Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Derivatives of one variableExplained in: Derivatives of One Variable, §4. The derivative: shrinking the step to zero.
Leads to: State, controls and measurementsExplained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §4. The state: what the robot keeps track of; Uncertainty in roboticsExplained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §2. Why a robot is never sure; Probabilistic motion modelsMotion model p(\mathbf x_t \mid u_t, \mathbf x_{t-1}): The probability distribution of a robot’s pose after a move, given its pose before and the control (command or odometry); it describes how uncertain motion is, so a filter can score possible end poses or draw them at random. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §2.2 The motion model and its density; Maps and landmarksMap: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §2.1 What a map is for; Configuration spaceConfiguration space (C-space): The set of all configurations of a robot, one point per placement of the whole robot, such as a box of (x, y, \theta) whose top and bottom faces are the same headings for a floor robot; motion planning looks for paths through it. Explained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §2.2 The configuration space of the floor robot.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A robot can only set its wheel speeds, but every task is stated in places: “go to the door”. A model of the robot’s motion connects the two, so that we can predict where wheel commands take the robot and choose the commands that reach a goal.



Figure 1: A small two-wheeled robot on a floor grid at x = 2 m, y = 1 m, facing 30 degrees left of the x-axis, with its own forward and left axes drawn on it
The only thing a wheeled robot can do so far is spin its motors, say the right wheel at 12 rad/s and the left at 8 rad/s, and nothing yet tells us where that takes it. Everything we want from it is about places: drive to the door, stay in the lane, park in the corner. So we need a model that answers two questions, one in each direction:

Prediction: if the wheels spin at 12 and 8 rad/s, where does the robot of Figure 1 go?
Control: to bear left towards the door at 0.3 m/s, turning at 0.5 rad/s, at what speeds should the wheels spin?

Figure 1 shows the robot from above: it stands 2 m along the x-axis and 1 m along the y-axis of a floor grid, and faces 30° to the left of the x-axis. Like most indoor robots, it has two driven wheels.
Both questions need a precise way to say where the robot is, and a rule linking wheel speeds to changes in that position. In this Note we build both for that robot:

three numbers that say where the robot is, together called its pose, and why position alone is not enough (Section 2);
why a rolling wheel’s spin tells us its speed over the floor (Section 3);
the link from the two wheel speeds to how fast the robot drives forward and turns, derived from one fact about turning bodies, and the link back (Section 4);
how those speeds move the robot over the floor, and how to predict its path step by step (Section 5);
why the robot cannot slide sideways, and why it can still reach every pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading. (Section 6).

Cars and trailers follow the same model with stricter limits; the car-like robots Note later in this chapter covers them.
2. Pose: where the robot is


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Both opening questions first need a way to say where the robot is, and position alone does not tell us where it will go next: we also need the direction it faces. Position (x, y) plus heading (G-2284)Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading. \theta, measured in an agreed frame, is the pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading..


2.1 Why we need a frame
“The robot is at (2, 1)” means nothing until we say measured from where, and along which directions. Figure 2 shows the problem: measured from the corner of the room, A, a robot is at (2, 1); measured from the corner of a rug, B, the same robot is at (1, 0.5).

Figure 2: The same robot measured from two frames: from the room corner A it is at (2, 1), from the rug corner B at (1, 0.5)
So we first agree on a reference: a corner of the room as the origin, with an x-axis along one wall and a y-axis along the other. Such a choice of origin and axes is a coordinate frame (G-2281)Coordinate frame: A chosen origin and set of axes used to give positions as numbers; every position or pose is stated relative to some frame. Explained in §2.1 Why we need a frame.. The frame fixed to the room is the world frame (G-2282)World frame: The coordinate frame fixed to the surroundings (for example a corner of the room), in which the robot’s pose is given. Explained in §2.1 Why we need a frame.; every position in this Note is measured in it.
2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading
Take two robots at the same spot, (2, 1), both driving forward at 0.5 m/s for one second. One faces along the x-axis, the other along the y-axis:

















Robot facesWhere it is after 1 salong x(2.5, 1)along y(2, 1.5)
Figure 3 plays the two runs side by side. Watch the two robots leave the same spot at the same speed: after one second they stand in different places, because they face different ways.

Figure 3: Two robots start at (2, 1) and drive forward at 0.5 m/s for one second, one facing along x and one along y; the orange line is the path so far. The last frame shows the one facing along x at (2.5, 1) and the one facing along y at (2, 1.5)
To predict motion we must also record the direction the robot faces, its heading (G-2284)Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading.: the angle \theta from the world x-axis to the robot’s forward direction.
Angles are measured counter-clockwise, so a robot facing along y has \theta = 90^\circ.
Together, position and heading are the robot’s pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading.. For the robot in Figure 1:

x is its position along the world x-axis, 2 m;
y is its position along the world y-axis, 1 m;
\theta is its heading, 30°.

2.3 Why angles are measured in radians


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

In radians, the arc travelled by a point turning about a centre is simply radius times angle, with no conversion factor; every formula in this Note relies on that.


The heading is an angle, and when the robot turns, its wheels travel along arcs. So we will often need this: a point at distance d from a centre turns by some angle; how far does it travel along its arc? A full turn travels the whole circumference, 2\pi d, and a part of a turn travels the same part of the circumference.
Try it in degrees, with d = 0.5 m and a turn of 30°. Thirty degrees is one twelfth of a full turn:
\text{arc} = \frac{30}{360} \times 2\pi \times 0.5
= 0.262 \text{ m}
Multiplying the radius by the angle in degrees gives nonsense:
0.5 \times 30 = 15 \text{ m}
Degrees need the extra factor 2\pi / 360 every time. So we measure angles in a unit that already contains it: the radian (G-2285)Radian: The unit of angle at which the arc of a circle is as long as its radius; a full turn is 2\pi rad, and with radians an arc is simply radius times angle. Explained in §2.3 Why angles are measured in radians., where a full turn is 2\pi radians. Then 30° is:
30 \times \frac{2\pi}{360} = 0.524 \text{ rad}
and the arc is radius times angle, with nothing else. With our numbers:

d is the point’s distance from the centre, 0.5 m;
\Delta\theta is the angle it turns, 0.524 rad (30°);
arc is the distance it travels along its circle, in m.

\text{arc} = d \times \Delta\theta
0.5 \times 0.524 = 0.262 \text{ m}
Figure 4 shows where the radian comes from. Bend a piece of string as long as the radius onto the circle: the angle it covers is one radian, about 57.3°. Keep laying radius-long pieces round the rim, and a full turn takes 6.283 of them, which is why a full turn is 2\pi radians.

Figure 4: A string as long as the radius is bent onto the circle and covers 1 radian; laying radius-long pieces round the rim, a full turn takes 6.283 of them
This arc rule is the reason all of these work in radians:

the wheel formula (Section 3);
the turning formulas (Section 4);
the cosine and sine functions of Python’s numpy.

3. The differential-drive robot


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The prediction question starts at the wheels: two motorised wheels on one axle are enough to drive anywhere and even to spin on the spot. If a wheel rolls without slipping (G-2290)Rolling without slipping: A wheel moving so that its contact point does not skid: it moves forward by its radius times the angle it turns and never slides sideways, which is what lets wheel turns predict motion. Explained in §3.2 Why wheel spin gives ground speed: rolling without slipping., its speed over the floor is its radius times its spin rate, so 12 rad/s gives 0.6 m/s.


3.1 Why two wheels and a caster
A differential-drive (G-2288)Differential drive: A robot with two independently driven wheels on one axle (plus a caster); it steers by running the wheels at different speeds and can spin on the spot. Explained in §3.1 Why two wheels and a caster. robot has two driven wheels on a common axle, each turned by its own motor. The differential drive is the most common way to drive an indoor robot (LaValle §13.1.2.2), because two motors are enough for everything: driving, turning and spinning on the spot (Section 4.4). Two wheels on one axle would tip over, so a third, free-swivelling caster wheel (G-2289)Caster wheel: A free-swivelling, undriven wheel, like the one under an office chair; it supports a robot without steering it. Explained in §3.1 Why two wheels and a caster., like the wheel under an office chair, holds the robot up without steering it (LaValle §13.1.2.2).
There is no steering wheel. The robot turns only through the difference between its two wheel speeds, and that is where the name “differential” comes from.

Figure 5: Top view of a differential-drive robot: right and left wheels of radius r, the distance L between them, the caster at the back, and the midpoint of the axle
The robot’s position (x, y) is the midpoint of the axle, the black dot in Figure 5. The figure also shows the only two measurements the model needs, with the values we use throughout. Both can be measured with a ruler:

r is the wheel radius, 0.05 m;
L is the wheel separation, the distance between the two wheels, 0.2 m.

3.2 Why wheel spin gives ground speed: rolling without slipping


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A wheel that does not skid lays its rim down on the floor as it turns, so it moves forward by exactly the length of rim it turns.


A motor tells us how fast the wheel spins, in radians (G-2285)Radian: The unit of angle at which the arc of a circle is as long as its radius; a full turn is 2\pi rad, and with radians an arc is simply radius times angle. Explained in §2.3 Why angles are measured in radians. per second. What we need is how fast the robot moves over the floor, in metres per second. The link is the wheel’s grip.
A wheel rolls without slipping (G-2290)Rolling without slipping: A wheel moving so that its contact point does not skid: it moves forward by its radius times the angle it turns and never slides sideways, which is what lets wheel turns predict motion. Explained in §3.2 Why wheel spin gives ground speed: rolling without slipping. when the point touching the floor does not skid. Each bit of rim that comes down touches the floor once and stays put while touching. So the wheel moves forward by exactly the length of rim it has turned (Figure 6). One full turn lays down the whole circumference, with the wheel radius r, 0.05 m:
\text{circumference} = 2\pi \times r
= 6.283 \times 0.05
= 0.314 \text{ m}

Figure 6: A wheel of radius 0.05 m rolls one full turn along the floor; a marked point on its rim traces the turn, and the wheel ends 0.314 m further on
A part of a turn lays down the same part of the rim, which is the arc rule of Section 2.3: radius times angle. So a wheel moves over the floor at its radius times its spin rate. For one wheel:

u is its spin rate, in rad/s;
r is its radius, 0.05 m;
v_{\text{wheel}} is its speed over the floor, in m/s.

v_{\text{wheel}} = r\ u
For our two wheels:

u_R is the right wheel’s spin rate, 12 rad/s;
u_L is the left wheel’s spin rate, 8 rad/s;
v_R is the right wheel’s speed over the floor, in m/s;
v_L is the left wheel’s speed over the floor, in m/s.

v_R = 0.05 \times 12 = 0.6 \text{ m/s}
v_L = 0.05 \times 8 = 0.4 \text{ m/s}


                  
                  Extra 
                  
                

Real wheels slip a little, more on smooth floors and in fast turns. The formula then overestimates the distance moved, and a robot that tracks its position by counting wheel turns slowly drifts away from the truth. Later Notes on motion models and wheel odometry deal with that error.


The two wheel speeds, 0.6 and 0.4 m/s, do not yet say how the whole robot moves; Section 4 turns them into the robot’s own motion.
4. From wheel speeds to robot speeds and back


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The prediction question continues: the right and left wheel speeds, 0.6 and 0.4 m/s, give how fast the robot drives forward, their average (0.5 m/s), and how fast it turns, their difference divided by the wheel separation (1 rad/s). Both follow from one fact, that a turning rigid body circles a single point, and run backwards the same formulas answer the control question.


4.1 Why we describe motion by linear and angular velocity
Wheel speeds are what the motors take, but they are an awkward way to think. Asked how to drive to the door, nobody says “right wheel 0.35 m/s, left wheel 0.25 m/s”; we say “not too fast, and bear left”. So we describe the motion of the whole robot with two numbers that match that way of thinking (Figure 7):

how fast the midpoint between the wheels moves along the heading (G-2284)Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading., the direction the robot faces, in metres per second: its linear velocity (G-2291)Linear velocity v: How fast a robot’s reference point (for a differential drive, the middle of the axle) moves along its heading, in m/s; for a differential drive, the average of the two wheel speeds, so it sets how fast the robot advances. Explained in §4.1 Why we describe motion by linear and angular velocity. v;
how fast the heading \theta changes, in radians (G-2285)Radian: The unit of angle at which the arc of a circle is as long as its radius; a full turn is 2\pi rad, and with radians an arc is simply radius times angle. Explained in §2.3 Why angles are measured in radians. per second, positive to the left: its angular velocity (G-2292)Angular velocity \omega: How fast a robot’s heading changes, in rad/s, positive to the left; for a differential drive, the difference of the wheel speeds divided by the wheel separation. Explained in §4.1 Why we describe motion by linear and angular velocity. \omega (omega).


Figure 7: A robot with a straight arrow for its linear velocity v along the heading and a curved arrow for its angular velocity omega, positive to the left
A controller decides v and \omega; this section finds the formulas that convert them to wheel speeds and back.
4.2 Why the robot turns about a point on its axle line


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Each wheel can only move straight ahead, square to the axle. The only centre the whole body can turn about that allows this lies on the axle line.


When a rigid body turns, every point of it moves on a circle around one centre, and its velocity at each moment points square to the line from that centre. Our two wheels must move straight ahead, because they cannot slide sideways (Section 6). Straight ahead is square to the axle. So the line from the centre to each wheel must be the axle line itself: the centre lies somewhere on the line through the axle.
That centre, the point the whole robot turns about at this moment, is the instantaneous centre of curvature (ICC) (G-2529)Instantaneous centre of curvature (ICC): The point a turning robot’s whole body circles at a given moment; for a differential drive it lies on the axle line at distance R = v/\omega from the midpoint, so it fixes how fast each wheel must move. Explained in §4.2 Why the robot turns about a point on its axle line.; “instantaneous” because it moves whenever the wheel speeds change. Its distance from the robot’s midpoint is the turning radius (G-2293)Turning radius R: The distance from the point a robot is turning about (the instantaneous centre of curvature, ICC) to the robot’s reference point; R = v / \omega, so it says how tight a turn is. Explained in §4.2 Why the robot turns about a point on its axle line. R.
Figure 8 plays one second of our robot’s turn, with wheel speeds 0.6 and 0.4 m/s. Watch the axle line swing about the ICC: the right wheel, the midpoint and the left wheel all turn by the same angle, and the one farther out covers the longer arc.

Figure 8: Our robot turns about the green ICC for one second at 1 rad/s. The grey axle line swings about the ICC, and the right wheel (red), the midpoint (orange) and the left wheel (purple) trace arcs along their dashed circles; the arrows show their speeds. The last frame: all three have turned 1 rad, and their arcs are 0.6, 0.5 and 0.4 m long, the same as their distances from the ICC, so they move at 0.6, 0.5 and 0.4 m/s
The whole body turns by the same angle in each second, the angular velocity (G-2292)Angular velocity \omega: How fast a robot’s heading changes, in rad/s, positive to the left; for a differential drive, the difference of the wheel speeds divided by the wheel separation. Explained in §4.1 Why we describe motion by linear and angular velocity. \omega, in rad/s. By the arc rule of Section 2.3, a point at distance d from the centre then travels \omega times d metres per second. Points farther out move faster (Figure 8):
\text{speed} = \omega \times \text{distance}
For a left turn, the right wheel sits half the wheel separation, 0.1 m, farther out than the midpoint, and the left wheel 0.1 m closer in. For our robot:

\omega is the angular velocity, the angle the whole body turns per second, in rad/s;
R is the turning radius, the midpoint’s distance from the ICC, in m;
L is the wheel separation, 0.2 m;
v_R is the right wheel’s speed over the floor, 0.6 m/s;
v_L is the left wheel’s speed over the floor, 0.4 m/s;
v is the midpoint’s speed, the linear velocity (G-2291)Linear velocity v: How fast a robot’s reference point (for a differential drive, the middle of the axle) moves along its heading, in m/s; for a differential drive, the average of the two wheel speeds, so it sets how fast the robot advances. Explained in §4.1 Why we describe motion by linear and angular velocity., in m/s.

Each wheel’s line with our numbers first, then in symbols:
0.6 = \omega \thinspace(R + 0.1)
v_R = \omega \thinspace(R + L/2)
0.4 = \omega \thinspace(R - 0.1)
v_L = \omega \thinspace(R - L/2)
v = \omega \thinspace R
4.3 Wheel speeds to linear and angular velocity


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Subtracting the two wheel equations isolates the angular velocity \omega; adding them isolates the linear velocity v.


The symbols are the ones listed in Section 4.2: the wheel speeds v_R and v_L, the wheel separation L, the turning radius (G-2293)Turning radius R: The distance from the point a robot is turning about (the instantaneous centre of curvature, ICC) to the robot’s reference point; R = v / \omega, so it says how tight a turn is. Explained in §4.2 Why the robot turns about a point on its axle line. R, the linear velocity (G-2291)Linear velocity v: How fast a robot’s reference point (for a differential drive, the middle of the axle) moves along its heading, in m/s; for a differential drive, the average of the two wheel speeds, so it sets how fast the robot advances. Explained in §4.1 Why we describe motion by linear and angular velocity. v and the angular velocity (G-2292)Angular velocity \omega: How fast a robot’s heading changes, in rad/s, positive to the left; for a differential drive, the difference of the wheel speeds divided by the wheel separation. Explained in §4.1 Why we describe motion by linear and angular velocity. \omega.
Subtract the left-wheel line of Section 4.2 from the right-wheel line, then add the two; our numbers first, each followed by the same step in symbols:
0.6 - 0.4 = \omega\thinspace(R + 0.1) - \omega\thinspace(R - 0.1)
v_R - v_L = \omega\thinspace(R + L/2) - \omega\thinspace(R - L/2)
0.2 = 0.2\thinspace\omega
v_R - v_L = \omega\thinspace L
\omega = 0.2 / 0.2 = 1 \text{ rad/s}
\omega = \frac{v_R - v_L}{L}
0.6 + 0.4 = \omega\thinspace(R + 0.1) + \omega\thinspace(R - 0.1)
v_R + v_L = \omega\thinspace(R + L/2) + \omega\thinspace(R - L/2)
1.0 = 2\thinspace\omega\thinspace R
v_R + v_L = 2\thinspace\omega\thinspace R
1.0 = 2\thinspace v
v_R + v_L = 2\thinspace v
v = 1.0 / 2 = 0.5 \text{ m/s}
v = \frac{v_R + v_L}{2}
R = 0.5 / 1 = 0.5 \text{ m}
R = v / \omega
The midpoint moves at the average speed of the wheels because it sits halfway between them. The formula for \omega says why a wide robot turns more lazily: the same speed difference has to swing a longer axle. With a speed difference of 0.2 m/s:

















Wheel separation LAngular velocity \omega0.2 m1 rad/s0.4 m0.5 rad/s
Going from the wheel speeds to the robot’s motion is the forward kinematics (G-2294)Forward kinematics (wheeled robot): Working out the robot’s linear and angular velocity from its wheel speeds, used to predict where the robot goes. Explained in §4.3 Wheel speeds to linear and angular velocity. of the robot. The forward kinematics answers half of the prediction question of Section 1; Section 5 finishes it.
4.4 Four ways to drive


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Equal wheel speeds drive straight, opposite speeds spin on the spot, one stopped wheel pivots about that wheel, and anything else drives on a circle.


The two formulas predict four kinds of motion. Figure 9 plays each one for two seconds; the green dot is the ICC.

Figure 9: Four motions of the robot, each played for two seconds with its trail: equal wheel speeds drive straight; opposite speeds spin in place; a stopped left wheel pivots about that wheel; unequal speeds drive on a circle of radius 0.5 m








































Wheel speeds v_R, v_L (m/s)Linear velocity v (m/s)Angular velocity \omega (rad/s)Turning radius R (m)Motion0.5, 0.50.50nonestraight line0.2, −0.2020spin on the spot0.4, 00.220.1pivot about the left wheel0.6, 0.40.510.5circle to the left
Why each happens:

Straight line. Equal speeds have no difference, so \omega = 0: nothing turns the heading (G-2284)Heading \theta: The angle from the world x-axis to the direction a robot faces, measured counter-clockwise; it decides which way the robot moves when it drives forward. Explained in §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading.. The ICC is infinitely far away.
Spin on the spot. Opposite speeds add up to zero, so v = 0: the midpoint stays put while the heading turns.
Pivot. A stopped wheel does not move, so it must be the ICC itself; the table confirms a turning radius (G-2293)Turning radius R: The distance from the point a robot is turning about (the instantaneous centre of curvature, ICC) to the robot’s reference point; R = v / \omega, so it says how tight a turn is. Explained in §4.2 Why the robot turns about a point on its axle line. of 0.1 m, exactly half the wheel separation.

The spin on the spot is what makes the differential drive (G-2288)Differential drive: A robot with two independently driven wheels on one axle (plus a caster); it steers by running the wheels at different speeds and can spin on the spot. Explained in §3.1 Why two wheels and a caster. so easy to steer: it can face any direction first and then drive straight (LaValle §13.1.2.2). A car cannot, as the car-like robots Note later in this chapter shows.
4.5 Back again: the wheel speeds for a wanted motion


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

To drive with linear velocity (G-2291)Linear velocity v: How fast a robot’s reference point (for a differential drive, the middle of the axle) moves along its heading, in m/s; for a differential drive, the average of the two wheel speeds, so it sets how fast the robot advances. Explained in §4.1 Why we describe motion by linear and angular velocity. v and angular velocity (G-2292)Angular velocity \omega: How fast a robot’s heading changes, in rad/s, positive to the left; for a differential drive, the difference of the wheel speeds divided by the wheel separation. Explained in §4.1 Why we describe motion by linear and angular velocity. \omega, run the right wheel faster than v and the left wheel slower, each by \omega times half the wheel separation L.


The control question of Section 1 goes the other way: the controller has chosen v and \omega and must send wheel commands. Going from v and \omega to the wheel speeds is the inverse kinematics (G-2295)Inverse kinematics (wheeled robot): Working out the wheel speeds that give a wanted linear and angular velocity, used by a controller to command the motors. Explained in §4.5 Back again: the wheel speeds for a wanted motion. of the robot. Solve the two formulas of Section 4.3 for the wheel speeds. For the control question:

v is the wanted linear velocity, 0.3 m/s;
\omega is the wanted angular velocity, 0.5 rad/s;
L is the wheel separation, 0.2 m;
v_R is the right wheel’s speed over the floor, in m/s;
v_L is the left wheel’s speed over the floor, in m/s.

v_R = v + \omega L/2
v_L = v - \omega L/2
Each wheel runs at the midpoint’s speed, plus or minus the extra speed it needs for being half an axle farther out or closer in. Then divide by the wheel radius to get the spin rates for the motors.
Worked example. We want 0.3 m/s while bearing left at 0.5 rad/s. The extra speed for half an axle:
\omega L/2 = 0.5 \times 0.1 = 0.05 \text{ m/s}
The wheel speeds:
v_R = 0.3 + 0.05 = 0.35 \text{ m/s}
v_L = 0.3 - 0.05 = 0.25 \text{ m/s}
The spin rates u_R and u_L of the right and left wheels, with the wheel radius 0.05 m:
u_R = 0.35 / 0.05 = 7 \text{ rad/s}
u_L = 0.25 / 0.05 = 5 \text{ rad/s}
Figure 10 shows why the two wheels differ. The wanted motion is a circle of radius 0.6 m (the turning radius (G-2293), v divided by \omega)Turning radius R: The distance from the point a robot is turning about (the instantaneous centre of curvature, ICC) to the robot’s reference point; R = v / \omega, so it says how tight a turn is. Explained in §4.2 Why the robot turns about a point on its axle line.; the right wheel runs on the outside of it and must cover more ground in the same time than the left wheel on the inside.

Figure 10: The wanted motion, v = 0.3 m/s and omega = 0.5 rad/s, is a circle of radius 0.6 m: the outer right wheel needs 0.35 m/s, the midpoint 0.3 m/s and the inner left wheel 0.25 m/s
As a check, feeding 7 and 5 rad/s back into the forward kinematics (G-2294)Forward kinematics (wheeled robot): Working out the robot’s linear and angular velocity from its wheel speeds, used to predict where the robot goes. Explained in §4.3 Wheel speeds to linear and angular velocity. of Section 4.3 must return 0.3 m/s and 0.5 rad/s, and it does (the Python box below).

Python: both directions in four lines.
r, L = 0.05, 0.2               # wheel radius, wheel separation (m)
def forward(uR, uL):           # spin rates (rad/s) -> v (m/s), omega (rad/s)
    return r * (uR + uL) / 2, r * (uR - uL) / L
def inverse(v, omega):         # v, omega -> spin rates (rad/s)
    return (v + omega * L / 2) / r, (v - omega * L / 2) / r
inverse(0.3, 0.5)              # about (7.0, 5.0)
forward(7, 5)                  # about (0.3, 0.5): back where we started

The formulas now link wheel speeds and v, \omega in both directions, and the control question has its answer: spin the right wheel at 7 rad/s and the left at 5 rad/s. Still open: where 0.5 m/s and 1 rad/s take the robot over the floor.

The robot knows its linear velocity (G-2291)Linear velocity v: How fast a robot’s reference point (for a differential drive, the middle of the axle) moves along its heading, in m/s; for a differential drive, the average of the two wheel speeds, so it sets how fast the robot advances. facing along x (\theta = 0^\circ): all of the speed goes into x, none into y;

In between, the speed is shared. Draw the velocity as an arrow of length v at angle \theta (Figure 11). The arrow is the long side of a right-angled triangle whose two short sides are the x speed and the y speed.

\cos\theta is the side along x divided by the long side;

6. The robot cannot slide sideways


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

One last check on the control question: can wheel commands reach every place, even one straight to the side? Rolling wheels forbid sideways motion, which limits which way the robot can move at each moment but not which poses (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Why does this deserve a section? Many route planners assume a robot can move in any direction from where it stands. A route that needs a step sideways cannot be followed by our robot or by a car, so those planners cannot be used as they are (MR §13.3.3). So we need to know exactly what the rule forbids, and what it does not.
6.1 The rule: no sideways motion
A wheel rolls along its own direction but grips against sliding sideways (LaValle §13.1.2.1). So the robot’s midpoint can move forward or backward, never along its own left–right axis. In words: the robot’s velocity has no part pointing to its left.

Its two inputs are “drive forward” (v) and “turn” (\omega); “slide sideways” is not among them. So the robot has two inputs for the three numbers of its pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. 6.2 Can the robot still get everywhere?


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Not sliding sideways limits which way the robot can move right now, not where it can end up. A limit like that is called nonholonomic.


The robot cannot move to its left. Can it still get to a spot 0.5 m to its left? Yes, with three legal moves (Figure 13, which starts the robot at the origin, facing along x):

Spin 90° to the left on the spot.
Drive 0.5 m forward.
Spin 90° back to the right.

RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-007-.title: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements
RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-007-.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Conditional probabilityExplained in: Joint, Marginal and Conditional Probability, §4. Conditional probability; Probability distributionsProbability distribution: A list (or curve) of every possible outcome of a random variable with its probability, adding up to 1; it says how likely each outcome is, so the chance of any event can be worked out from it. Explained in: Random Variables and Probability Distributions, §3. Probability distributions as tables; Differential-drive kinematicsExplained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §5.2 The kinematic model; PosePose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading.
Leads to: Probabilistic motion modelsMotion model p(\mathbf x_t \mid u_t, \mathbf x_{t-1}): The probability distribution of a robot’s pose after a move, given its pose before and the control (command or odometry); it describes how uncertain motion is, so a filter can score possible end poses or draw them at random. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §2.2 The motion model and its density; BeliefBelief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition; Choosing the search stateSearch state: What a search keeps for each vertex: the quantities that decide which moves are allowed and what they cost, and nothing more, such as (cell, charge left) for a robot with a battery; leaving one out breaks the Markov property and can hide routes. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §10. Choosing the search state: the Markov rule.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A robot’s sensors and wheels are never exact, so one reading can fit many places and one move can end in several. The robot therefore keeps a probability for every place it could be, instead of a single guess.



Figure 1: A hallway of 10 cells of 1 m, numbered 0 to 9 and joined into a loop, with doors at cells 1, 3 and 7. The robot’s sensor says “door”. The robot could be at any of the three doors, so each of those cells gets probability 0.33
So far the kinematic model (G-2297)Kinematic model: Equations that give how a robot’s configuration changes from its speed inputs alone, ignoring masses and forces, such as \dot{x} = v\cos\theta, \dot{y} = v\sin\theta, \dot{\theta} = \omega; used to predict motion at low speed. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §5.2 The kinematic model predicts where wheel commands take a robot: wheels at 12 and 8 rad/s drive it round a circle of radius 0.5 m. That prediction assumes wheels that never slip. Real wheels slip, so a command “move 2” can end 1, 2 or 3 cells on, and a robot that only counts such moves soon does not know where it is. This Note adds the answer: keep a probability for every place. We leave the floor for a hallway of cells, because one number per place keeps the counting small (Section 4.1 returns to the floor).
A delivery robot drives along the hallway of Figure 1, the hallway the belief and grid-filter Notes of this chapter return to. It has a map (G-2331)Map: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §2.1 What a map is for: 10 cells of 1 m each, numbered 0 to 9, with doors at cells 1, 3 and 7. The hallway is a loop, so one step to the right of cell 9 is cell 0. The robot has a sensor that says “door” or “wall” for the cell beside it. Its sensor now says “door”. Where is it?
There is no single answer. Three cells fit that reading, and the robot has no reason to prefer one of them. A robot that picks one cell and forgets the rest is wrong two times out of three. A robot that keeps all three, each with probability 1/3, still has the true cell among them.
This Note builds that idea step by step:

why a robot can never be sure: five sources of uncertainty, and how errors pile up when the robot only counts its moves (Section 2);
why the robot keeps a probability for every place instead of one best guess (Section 3);
what the robot must keep track of, its state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in §4.1 State: from one number to many., and when a state is complete (Section 4);
the two streams of data it receives, controls and measurements (G-2317)Measurement z_t: What a robot’s sensors report about the world at time t, such as “door”, a laser scan or a camera image; it does not change the state but tells the robot something about it, which narrows its distribution. Explained in §5.1 Measurements and controls., and their order in time (Section 5);
why moving makes the robot less sure and sensing makes it more sure (Section 6).

2. Why a robot is never sure


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A move of 2 cells can end 1, 2 or 3 cells on, and a reading can be wrong, because every part of a robot adds uncertainty: the world changes, sensors are limited and noisy, wheels slip, models are simplified and computers must answer in time. Errors in counted moves add up, so a robot that only counts its moves gets more and more lost: after 8 moves it is where it thinks only with probability 0.33.


2.1 Why counting moves is not enough: dead reckoning
The simplest way to know where we are is to start at a known place and add up our own moves: “I started at 0 m and moved 2 m eight times, so I am at 16 m.” The method is dead reckoning (G-2311)Dead reckoning: Working out a robot’s position from a known start by adding up its own moves, without looking at its surroundings; simple, but its error grows with every move, so it needs readings to correct it. Explained in §2.1 Why counting moves is not enough: dead reckoning.: working out the position from a known start plus the robot’s own motion, with no look at the surroundings. Facing north at 1 m/s for 3 s, a robot reckons it is 3 m north of where it started, without checking anything.
The trouble is that the moves themselves are not exact. Our hallway robot is told “move 2”, two cells of 1 m. Because its wheels sometimes slip or spin on, the real move is (Labbe ch.2):





















Real moveProbability1 cell (it falls short)0.12 cells0.83 cells (it runs on)0.1
We count positions in whole cells, so a move that falls well short counts as 1 cell and one that runs on counts as 3. The hallway robot moves this way throughout the chapter.
Figure 2 plays what happens to a robot that starts surely at 0 m on a long straight track (so that eight moves of 2 m do not wrap round the 10 m loop) and is told “move 2” eight times without looking around. The bars show the probability of each true position; the red dashed line is where the robot thinks it is.

Figure 2: Dead reckoning without readings: after 1, 2, 4 and 8 moves of 2 m the probability of each true position spreads wider; after 8 moves the robot is exactly where it thinks (16 m) with probability 0.33 only
The chance that the robot is exactly where it thinks shrinks with every move:



































MovesRobot thinksChance it is exactly thereStandard deviation12 m0.800.45 m24 m0.660.63 m48 m0.490.89 m816 m0.331.26 m
The last column is the standard deviation (G-1870)Standard deviation of a random variable: The square root of a random variable’s variance, in the units of X; it says how far values typically fall from the expected value. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4.1 Variance term by term of the true position: the typical distance between the true position and the reckoned one, so it says how widely the robot may be off. Why does it grow? One move has variance 0.2 m², the average squared miss from the commanded 2 m:
0.1 \times (1 - 2)^2 = 0.1
0.8 \times (2 - 2)^2 = 0
0.1 \times (3 - 2)^2 = 0.1
\text{variance} = 0.1 + 0 + 0.1 = 0.2
The moves slip independently (G-934)Independent events: Events where one happening does not change the probability of the other; for them the probability that both happen is the product of their probabilities. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Independent Events, §2. The definition, one move’s slip not changing the chances of the next, and for independent moves the variances addExplained in: Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem, §4.2 Mean and variance of the sample means. After 8 moves:
\text{variance} = 8 \times 0.2 = 1.6
\text{standard deviation} = \sqrt{1.6}
= 1.26 \text{ m}
The standard deviation keeps growing, more slowly than the number of moves but without limit. Dead reckoning is good over short stretches; over longer ones its error grows until something outside the robot corrects it. The notebook RO-007-why-a-robot-is-never-sure.ipynb checks the table with 100 000 simulated robots.
2.2 Five sources of uncertainty
Slipping wheels are only one cause. The textbook on probabilistic robotics (G-2313)Probabilistic robotics: The approach in which a robot keeps a probability distribution over what might be the case (such as where it is) instead of one best guess, so it can handle ambiguous readings and recover from errors. Explained in §3.2 Why a single best guess gets lost., robotics that reasons with probabilities, lists five (Thrun et al. 2005 ch.1, as given in Khamis L5), shown in Figure 3:

Figure 3: Five sources of uncertainty around a robot: the environment, the sensors, the robot’s actuation, the models and the computation, each with an example

The environment. The world is not fully predictable: people walk past, doors open and close, chairs move. A person who steps between the robot and the wall makes a distance sensor read much less than the true distance to the wall.
The sensors. A sensor sees only so far and so finely; a camera cannot see through walls. Eight distance sensors around a robot tell it how far the nearest obstacle is in eight directions, which is usually not enough to say where it is in a room. And every reading carries sensor noise (G-2312)Sensor noise: Small random errors in a sensor’s readings, so the same quantity measured twice gives slightly different numbers (a wall 2 m away reads 1.92 to 2.07 m); it is one reason a robot cannot take a reading at face value. Explained in §2.2 Five sources of uncertainty.: small random errors, so the same wall measured again from the same spot gives slightly different numbers.
The robot’s actuation. Motors and wheels do not do exactly what they are told. A command to move 1 m gives 95 cm one time and 1.1 m the next; gears slip and wear.
The models. Every model simplifies. The kinematic model (G-2297)Kinematic model: Equations that give how a robot’s configuration changes from its speed inputs alone, ignoring masses and forces, such as \dot{x} = v\cos\theta, \dot{y} = v\sin\theta, \dot{\theta} = \omega; used to predict motion at low speed. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §5.2 The kinematic model, the equations that turn wheel speeds into motion, assumes wheels that never slip.
The computation. A robot must decide in time, so its algorithms take shortcuts and approximate (Khamis L5).

In Figure 4, watch sensor noise and the environment at work on one wall: no two readings of the wall agree exactly, and while a person walks through the beam the readings fall far short of the wall. A distance sensor stands 2.00 m from a wall and takes 200 readings. The 190 readings of the wall itself spread from 1.92 m to 2.07 m, because of sensor noise. The 10 readings taken while a person walked past are between 0.61 m and 1.16 m, nowhere near the wall.

Figure 4: Animation: a distance sensor 2.00 m from a wall takes 200 readings (simulated), one at a time. Top: the beam and the distance the sensor reports (dot). Bottom: the histogram of the readings so far, one bar per 0.02 m, on the same metre scale. The wall’s readings pile up around 2.00 m; after the 100th reading a person walks through the beam, and the next 10 readings land where the person is. The last frame holds all 200: 190 readings of the wall between 1.92 and 2.07 m, and 10 readings of the person between 0.61 and 1.16 m
So no reading and no move can be taken at face value. Section 3 starts with the reading: “door” fits three cells, and the robot must still say where it is.
3. Keep a distribution, not one best guess


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

This section answers the opening question for one reading: “door” fits cells 1, 3 and 7. A robot that keeps one guess throws the other two away and gets lost when it guessed wrong; a robot that keeps a probability for every cell keeps the true one among its candidates.


3.1 Why one reading fits many places
Back to the hallway. For this section we make two simplifications: the moves are exact and the door sensor never errs. At the start the robot knows nothing, so each of the 10 cells has the same probability. We write:

n is a cell number, 0 to 9;
P(n) is the probability that the robot is in cell n, a number from 0 to 1; the ten cells’ probabilities add up to 1.

P(\text{each cell}) = \frac{1}{10} = 0.1
The sensor says “door”. Three cells have a door (1, 3 and 7) and nothing favours one of them, so each gets a third:
P(1) = P(3) = P(7) = \frac{1}{3} = 0.33
The other seven get 0, as Figure 1 shows. The same thing happens in two dimensions. A robot in a room whose laser scan shows “a flat wall 1 m straight ahead” could stand 1 m from any straight stretch of any wall, facing it (Figure 5). The reading rules out spots near a corner or facing the door, where the scan would look different, but it leaves many poses (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, positions together with a heading.

Figure 5: A room 7 m by 4 m with a door. The scan shows a flat wall 1 m ahead; every pose 1 m from a straight stretch of wall, facing it, fits the reading, so candidate poses line all four walls
Such a list of every possible value with its probability, adding up to 1, is a probability distribution (G-1571)Probability distribution: A list (or curve) of every possible outcome of a random variable with its probability, adding up to 1; it says how likely each outcome is, so the chance of any event can be worked out from it. Explained in: Random Variables and Probability Distributions, §3. Probability distributions as tables. Ours has three separate peaks, so it is a multimodal (G-1275)Multimodal: Having more than one mode, that is more than one peak (two peaks: bimodal), such as a robot’s belief peaking at three doors; it shows the data point to several separate values, so one mean or one best guess would hide them. Explained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §5. Mode distribution: the robot is not in three places at once, it has narrowed its position down to one of three (Labbe ch.2).
3.2 Why a single best guess gets lost
A robot could instead keep only one value: its best guess, a point estimate (G-1507)Point estimate: A single number computed from sample data as the best guess for an unknown population parameter. Explained in: Estimating a Population Mean with the Central Limit Theorem, §1. Overview of its position. Figure 6 runs both robots side by side. The true robot is in cell 1 (red square).

Figure 6: Animation: after the reading “door” the distribution keeps cells 1, 3 and 7 while a best guess picks cell 7; after “move 2” the candidates become cells 3, 5 and 9; after a second “door” only cell 3 fits, while the best guess at cell 9 expected a wall and is lost
Step by step:

Reading “door”. The distribution keeps cells 1, 3 and 7. The best-guess robot must pick one and picks cell 7. With three equal candidates, a guess is right only one time in three.
Control “move 2”. Every candidate moves with the robot: cells 1, 3 and 7 become 3, 5 and 9. The best guess becomes cell 9.
Reading “door” again. Of cells 3, 5 and 9, only cell 3 has a door. Each other candidate would have read “wall”, which does not match. So the distribution is now certain: cell 3, with probability 1.

The best-guess robot expected a wall at cell 9 and read “door”. It now knows its guess was wrong, but it threw the other candidates away at step 1, so it has nothing to fall back on: it is lost. The robot that kept the whole distribution found its place, because it remembered every place the readings allowed (Labbe ch.2).
Keeping the whole distribution is the central idea of probabilistic robotics (G-2313)Probabilistic robotics: The approach in which a robot keeps a probability distribution over what might be the case (such as where it is) instead of one best guess, so it can handle ambiguous readings and recover from errors. Explained in §3.2 Why a single best guess gets lost.: the robot computes a probability distribution (G-1571)Probability distribution: A list (or curve) of every possible outcome of a random variable with its probability, adding up to 1; it says how likely each outcome is, so the chance of any event can be worked out from it. Explained in: Random Variables and Probability Distributions, §3. Probability distributions as tables over what might be the case, instead of a single best guess, so it can handle ambiguous readings and recover from errors (Thrun 2000). The probability distribution a robot keeps over where it might be is its belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition, defined later in this chapter.
3.3 Why noisy sensors forbid crossing places out
Section 3.2 crossed out every cell that did not match a reading. Crossing out works only for a perfect sensor. A real door sensor errs. The sensor of our hallway robot, used throughout the chapter, behaves like this:




















Robot is atReads “door”Reads “wall”a door cell0.60.4a wall cell0.20.8
A robot that still crosses out non-matching cells throws away its true cell every time the reading is wrong. In Section 3.2 the true robot stood at a door both times (cells 1 and 3). The chance that both readings say “door” is:
0.6 \times 0.6 = 0.36
So the chance that at least one says “wall”, and the true cell is crossed out, is:
1 - 0.36 = 0.64
Nearly two times in three, the robot would delete the cell where it really is. (The two readings err independently (G-934), which is why their probabilities multiply.)Independent events: Events where one happening does not change the probability of the other; for them the probability that both happen is the product of their probabilities. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Independent Events, §2. The definition
So with a noisy sensor the robot does not cross out; it weights. A reading of “door” makes each door cell 3 times as likely as each wall cell, because the sensor reads “door” 3 times as often at a door as at a wall (Labbe ch.2):
\frac{0.6}{0.2} = 3
Three door cells and seven wall cells make 16 equal shares, and the probability P of a cell (Section 3.1) is its shares out of 16:
3 \times 3 + 7 \times 1 = 16
P(\text{each door}) = \frac{3}{16} = 0.1875
P(\text{each wall}) = \frac{1}{16} = 0.0625
Check: the ten cells add up to 1.
3 \times 0.1875 + 7 \times 0.0625 = 1
Figure 7 plays the same reading on the cells, for the perfect sensor and the noisy one. Every cell starts at 0.1; watch each one be multiplied by the chance of reading “door” there, and then every cell be divided by the sum of the products, so that the ten add up to 1 again. The noisy sensor ends at the same 0.1875 and 0.0625 as the shares.

Figure 7: Animation of one reading “door” for a perfect sensor (top, blue) and the noisy sensor (bottom, purple). Every cell starts at 0.1 and is multiplied by the chance of reading “door” there: 1 at a door and 0 at a wall for the perfect sensor (products 0.1 and 0), 0.6 and 0.2 for the noisy sensor (products 0.06 and 0.02). The products add up to 0.3 and 0.32, and each cell is divided by its sensor’s sum. The last frame: the perfect sensor gives 0.33 to each door cell and 0 to each wall cell; the noisy sensor gives 0.1875 to each door cell and 0.0625 to each wall cell
The wall cells keep a small probability, so one wrong reading lowers the true cell but never deletes it; later readings can lift it again. How a reading turns into these numbers in general is Bayes’ theoremBayes’ theorem: The rule that reverses a conditional probability: from P(B \mid A) it gives P(A \mid B), so a belief about A can be updated after seeing B; P(A \mid B) = P(B \mid A) P(A) / P(B). Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Bayes’ Theorem, §4.1 From the counts to the formula, which this chapter later applies to the robot’s readingsExplained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §3.1 Why the robot needs Bayes’ theorem. So far the answer to “where is it?” has been one cell number; Section 4 asks what a robot must track in general.
4. The state: what the robot keeps track of


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

“Where is it?” asks for the robot’s state: in the hallway one number, its cell. In general the state is every quantity the robot needs to predict what happens next: its pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, often its speeds, and the things around it that can change. A state is complete when knowing it now makes the past useless for predicting the future.


4.1 State: from one number to many
In the hallway the robot needs one number, its cell. A robot on a floor needs three, its pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading: position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°).
The collection of quantities the robot keeps track of because they decide what happens next is its state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in §4.1 State: from one number to many.. In the hallway run of Section 3.2 the robot is in cell 3 at time 2:

t is the time step, counted 0, 1, 2 and so on, here 2;
x_t is the whole state at time t, not only the position x of a pose; in the hallway it is the robot’s cell number, here 3.

x_2 = 3
Depending on the robot and the task, the state can also include:

the pose of the robot;
the speeds of the robot, when it does not stop the moment its motors stop (Section 4.2);
the positions of things around it: fixed things such as walls and doors are kept in a map (G-2331)Map: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §2.1 What a map is for, while things that move, such as people, go into the state, often with their speeds.

4.2 Why the speed can belong to the state
Figure 8 plays two robots on a smooth floor with their motors switched off, from one second ago to one second from now: watch robot B roll to 2 m, where robot A stands, so that for a moment the two positions are the same, and then roll on. Both are at 2 m right now. Robot A has been standing still; robot B is rolling at 0.5 m/s.

Figure 8: Animation of two robots on a smooth floor with their motors off, from one second ago to one second from now. Robot A (blue) stands still at 2 m. Robot B (purple) rolls at 0.5 m/s: from 1.5 m up to 2 m, where now both robots are at 2 m and their positions look the same, then on to 2.5 m; dashed boxes mark where B was. The last frame: in one second A is still at 2 m and B is at 2.5 m
One second later:























RobotPosition nowSpeed nowPosition in 1 sA2 m0 m/s2 mB2 m0.5 m/s2.5 m
Their positions now are the same, but their futures differ. If the state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in §4.1 State: from one number to many. were the position alone, we could not predict where each robot goes, while their positions one second ago (2 m and 1.5 m) would tell us. The past would carry information the state lacks. With the speed added, the state (2 \text{ m}, 0.5 \text{ m/s}) predicts robot B’s next position by itself, and the past adds nothing.
4.3 Complete state and the Markov property
That test gives the definition. A state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in §4.1 State: from one number to many. is a complete state (G-2315)Complete state: A state that, once known, makes earlier states, controls and measurements useless for predicting the future (position plus speed for a coasting robot, not position alone); it lets the robot keep only its latest estimate. Explained in §4.3 Complete state and the Markov property. if knowing it now, the earlier states, commands and sensor readings, called controls and measurements (G-2317)Measurement z_t: What a robot’s sensors report about the world at time t, such as “door”, a laser scan or a camera image; it does not change the state but tells the robot something about it, which narrows its distribution. Explained in §5.1 Measurements and controls., tell us nothing more about the future (Thrun et al. 2005 §2.3.1). For robot B:

position only: not complete, because the position one second ago improves the prediction;
position and speed: complete, because nothing from the past improves it.

A sequence of states with this property, where the future depends on the past only through the present, has the Markov property (G-2316)Markov property: The property of a sequence of states that the future depends on the past only through the present state; it lets a filter forget the history and work from the latest state alone. Explained in §4.3 Complete state and the Markov property.. We want it because it lets the robot forget its history: to predict and to update its belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition, its probability for every place, it needs only the latest state, not every reading since it was switched on. The Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm, which updates the belief after every move and every reading, is built on it.
In practice no robot’s state is truly complete: people move, gears wear, the floor changes. Robots still treat their state as complete, and the methods of this chapter work well when the leftover effects are small (Thrun 2000). The robot never sees its state directly; Section 5 names the two kinds of data it does receive.
5. Controls and measurements: two streams of data


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The robot answers “where is it?” from two kinds of data. Controls, such as “move 2”, change its state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in §4.1 State: from one number to many., here its cell; measurements, such as “door”, only report on it. A control comes first, then the measurement in the new state.


5.1 Measurements and controls
The data that reaches a robot comes in two kinds (Thrun 2000; Khamis L5):


A measurement (G-2317)Measurement z_t: What a robot’s sensors report about the world at time t, such as “door”, a laser scan or a camera image; it does not change the state but tells the robot something about it, which narrows its distribution. Explained in §5.1 Measurements and controls. z_t is what the sensors report about the world at time t: our door sensor’s “door”, a laser scan of distances, a camera image. In the hallway at time 1:
z_1 = \text{door}


A control (G-2532)Control u_t: Information about how a robot’s state changed between two time steps, such as the command “move 2” or a count of how far the wheels turned; it changes the state, so a filter uses it to predict where the robot went, which spreads its probability distribution. Explained in §5.1 Measurements and controls. is information about how the state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in §4.1 State: from one number to many. changed: the command “move 2”, or a count of how far the wheels turned. We write it u_t, the same symbol as the control input (G-2298)Control input u: The numbers we choose to drive a robot, such as u = (v, \omega); the model turns them into motion. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §5.2 The kinematic model of a robot model. In the hallway at time 2:
u_2 = \text{move 2}


We keep them apart because they do opposite things to the robot’s knowledge (Section 6). A control causes the state to change; a measurement does not change the state, it only tells the robot something about it.
5.2 The order in time
The robot starts in some state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in §4.1 State: from one number to many. x_0. Then each time step has two parts:

a control u_t moves the robot from x_{t-1} to x_t;
the robot takes a measurement (G-2317)Measurement z_t: What a robot’s sensors report about the world at time t, such as “door”, a laser scan or a camera image; it does not change the state but tells the robot something about it, which narrows its distribution. Explained in §5.1 Measurements and controls. z_t in the new state x_t.

Figure 9 builds this chain one event at a time on the hallway run: watch each control (green) carry the robot to its next state, and each measurement (orange) come out of the state it was read in.

Figure 9: Animation of the order of events, one at a time. Top: the chain of states x0, x1, x2, x3 (blue circles); each control u (green box) points into the state it produces, each measurement z (orange box) points out of the state it was read in. Under the chain, the hallway run: from x0 = cell 1, u1 stay gives x1 = cell 1 with z1 door; u2 move 2 gives x2 = cell 3 with z2 door; u3 move 2 gives x3 = cell 5 with z3 wall. Bottom: the hallway with doors at cells 1, 3 and 7; the red square, the robot’s true cell, moves with each control. The last frame holds the whole chain
Controls point into the states (green arrows), because they change them; measurements point out of the states (orange arrows), because each one is produced by the state the robot is in. The robot never sees the states themselves, only the controls it sent and the measurements it received. Working out the states from those two streams is localization (G-2318)Localization: Working out a robot’s pose in a known map from the controls it sent and the measurements it received; needed because the pose itself cannot be measured directly. Explained in §5.2 The order in time. when the state is the robot’s pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, its position and heading, in a known map (Thrun 2000).
How likely each next state is after a control, and each reading in a given state, are the two models every method in this chapter needs. The motion model (G-2319)Motion model p(\mathbf x_t \mid u_t, \mathbf x_{t-1}): The probability distribution of a robot’s pose after a move, given its pose before and the control (command or odometry); it describes how uncertain motion is, so a filter can score possible end poses or draw them at random. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §2.2 The motion model and its density is the first; the measurement model (G-2374)Measurement model p(z \mid \mathbf{x}, m): The density of getting sensor readings z if the robot were at pose \mathbf{x} in map m (also sensor or observation model); read over poses it is a likelihood that tells a filter which poses fit the readings. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §2.2 Why we need a measurement model is the second. Before those models, Section 6 shows what each stream does to the hallway robot’s distribution.
6. Moving makes the robot less sure, sensing makes it more sure


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Here the whole opening problem comes back at once: moves that slip and a sensor that errs. Every uncertain move widens the robot’s distribution (its standard deviation (G-1870), the typical distance of a cell from the average, grows from 0 to 0.63 m in two moves)Standard deviation of a random variable: The square root of a random variable’s variance, in the units of X; it says how far values typically fall from the expected value. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4.1 Variance term by term; every informative reading narrows it (to 0.42 m). Neither alone is enough: moves alone drift, readings alone are ambiguous, and together they pin the robot down.


Now we drop both simplifications: the moves are the noisy moves of Section 2.1, and the sensor is the noisy sensor of Section 3.3. Take a robot that knows it is in cell 3, as after Section 3.2. It drives two moves of 2 cells without a reading in between, and then reads its sensor. Figure 10 plays the four stages.

Figure 10: Animation: the robot is sure it is in cell 3; after one noisy move the probabilities are 0.1, 0.8, 0.1 at cells 4, 5, 6; after a second move 0.01, 0.16, 0.66, 0.16, 0.01 at cells 5 to 9; the noisy reading “door” lifts the door cell 7 to 0.853 and lowers cells 6 and 8 to 0.069
Control u_3 spreads the distribution. From cell 3 the robot ends in cell 4, 5 or 6 with the move probabilities of Section 2.1: 0.1, 0.8 and 0.1.
Control u_4 spreads it further. Each way of making two moves multiplies the two move probabilities, because the moves slip independently (G-934)Independent events: Events where one happening does not change the probability of the other; for them the probability that both happen is the product of their probabilities. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Independent Events, §2. The definition: one slip does not change the chances of the other. Ending in cell 7, four cells on, happens in three ways, and the probability P(7) of ending in cell 7 is their sum:
\text{2 then 2}: 0.8 \times 0.8 = 0.64
\text{1 then 3}: 0.1 \times 0.1 = 0.01
\text{3 then 1}: 0.1 \times 0.1 = 0.01
P(7) = 0.64 + 0.01 + 0.01 = 0.66
The same counting gives the whole distribution:





















Cell56789Probability0.010.160.660.160.01
Measurement z_4 = “door” sharpens it. The robot weights each cell as in Section 3.3: it multiplies each probability by the chance of reading “door” there, 0.6 at the door cell 7 and 0.2 at the wall cells:
\text{cell 7}: 0.66 \times 0.6 = 0.396
\text{cells 6, 8}: 0.16 \times 0.2 = 0.032
\text{cells 5, 9}: 0.01 \times 0.2 = 0.002
What is left no longer adds up to 1:
0.396 + 2 \times 0.032 + 2 \times 0.002
= 0.464
Dividing each by that sum gives the probability of each cell given the reading, a conditional probability (G-444)Conditional probability: The probability of an event given that another event has happened: P(A \mid B); it updates a probability with what is now known, such as the chance of reading “door” once the robot is known to be at a door. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Conditional Probability, §2. The definition:

P(n \mid \text{door}) is the probability that the robot is in cell n, given that it read “door” (the bar reads “given”), a number from 0 to 1.

P(7 \mid \text{door}) = \frac{0.396}{0.464} = 0.853
P(6 \mid \text{door}) = \frac{0.032}{0.464} = 0.069
P(5 \mid \text{door}) = \frac{0.002}{0.464} = 0.004
Cells 8 and 9 get the same as cells 6 and 5. The standard deviation of the distribution after each stage tells the story in one number:

























StageStandard deviationsure in cell 30 mafter u_30.45 mafter u_40.63 mafter z_40.42 m
Moves add uncertainty because the robot cannot tell which of the possible outcomes happened; readings remove it because they make places that do not fit less likely, or rule them out (Thrun 2000). So a robot needs both streams of data:

with moves alone it drifts, as in Section 2.1;
with readings alone it stays ambiguous, as the three doors of Section 3.1 show;
with both, each reading is checked against where the moves say the robot can be, and the places that fit everything gain probability, as in Section 3.2 and here.

7. Summary








































IdeaWhat it saysWhy it mattersDead reckoningadd up the robot’s own moves from a known startits error grows without limit, so it needs readings to correct itFive sources of uncertaintyenvironment, sensors, actuation, models, computationno reading or move can be taken at face valueDistribution, not best guesskeep a probability for every possible statethe truth stays among the candidates when a reading is ambiguousState x_tthe quantities that decide what happens nextit is what the robot estimatesComplete statethe past adds nothing once the state is knownthe robot can forget its history (Markov property)Control u_t, measurement z_tdata that changes the state, data that reports on itcontrols spread the distribution, measurements narrow it

“Where is it?” after the reading “door” has no single answer: cells 1, 3 and 7 each get 0.33, because all three fit the reading equally, so a single guess would be right only one time in three. A move and a second “door” then leave only cell 3; with slipping moves and the noisy sensor, two moves and a “door” give cell 7 probability 0.853.
Dead reckoning (G-2311)Dead reckoning: Working out a robot’s position from a known start by adding up its own moves, without looking at its surroundings; simple, but its error grows with every move, so it needs readings to correct it. Explained in §2.1 Why counting moves is not enough: dead reckoning. drifts: after 8 noisy moves the robot is where it thinks with probability 0.33, because independent errors add up (variances add).
Uncertainty comes from five places, so a robot must plan for imperfect readings and moves rather than hope for perfect ones.
A single best guess, once contradicted, has nothing left, so the robot keeps every candidate.
With a noisy sensor the robot weights places instead of crossing them out, because crossing out would delete the true place whenever a reading is wrong (64 percent of the time over two readings at two doors, with a sensor that sees a door 60 percent of the time).
The state holds what decides the future: pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, speeds when the robot coasts and moving things around it; it is complete when the past adds nothing, which lets the robot keep only its latest belief.
A control comes first and changes the state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in §4.1 State: from one number to many.; a measurement follows and reports on it, so each step of a filter is “move, then look”.
Moves widen the distribution (standard deviation (G-1870) 0 to 0.63 m in two moves)Standard deviation of a random variable: The square root of a random variable’s variance, in the units of X; it says how far values typically fall from the expected value. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4.1 Variance term by term and readings narrow it (0.63 to 0.42 m), so the robot needs both.

The robot can now say where it might be as a probability for every cell, and why moves spread it and readings narrow it. Where this fits

Convex optimisation problems; PosePose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading.
Leads to: Beam modelBeam model: The measurement model of a range finder that mixes four densities for one reading (measurement noise, unexpected objects, failures, random readings) with weights that add up to 1, so no single odd reading can rule out the true pose. Explained in: Range Sensors: the Beam Model, §5.1 The mixture; Landmark measurement modelLandmark measurement model: The density of a landmark reading (range, bearing) given a pose and the map: a Gaussian of the range error times a Gaussian of the bearing error, with the errors taken as independent; it scores how well a guessed pose explains what the robot saw. Explained in: Landmark Measurement Model, §4. The landmark measurement model; Graphs and state spacesState space: All the states a problem can be in, joined by the moves between them, such as the robot’s 76 cells or the arrangements of a Rubik’s cube; it is a graph, so planning becomes finding a path from the start state to a goal state. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §2.2 Any problem of states and moves is a graph; Obstacle region and free spaceFree space: All configurations at which the robot touches no obstacle, C_{\text{free}}, the C-space without the obstacle region; a planner looks for a path that stays inside it. Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point

2. Why a robot needs a map


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A map (G-2331)Map: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in §2.1 What a map is for. is the robot’s model of its surroundings: a list of the objects that matter, with where they are. Localization compares readings with it, and planning searches it for routes.


2.1 What a map is for
A reading such as “the pink pole is 2.236 m away, to the left” says where things are relative to the robot. To turn it into “where am I?”, the robot needs to know where those things are in the room. A map gives exactly that: the robot compares what it sees with the map and keeps the poses where the two agree. Planning needs the map too: a route to the door must go round the table.
A map (G-2331)Map: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in §2.1 What a map is for. is a list of the objects in the environment that matter to the robot, with their positions and properties (Thrun et al. 2005 §6.2). We write it as a list of objects:

m_i is object number i of the map, such as the pink pole at (1 m, 3 m);
N is the number of objects, 2 when the map holds only the two poles (Section 3);
m is the whole map, the list of all N objects.

m = \lbrace m_1,\ m_2,\ \dots,\ m_N \rbrace
Fixed things, such as walls and furniture, belong in the map; things that move, such as people, belong in the robot’s state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §4.1 State: from one number to many, the quantities it keeps track of, instead. What goes in the map is settled; how much of the room it records is not.
