4.4 Why work in log odds
Two reasons:

Adding is cheaper than multiplying and rescaling. A map can hold millions of cells, each updated at every scan; one addition per cell is the cheapest update possible, and every cell can be updated at the same time (Freiburg mapping slides: the log odds (G-1116) update “only requires to compute sums”)Log-odds: The natural log of the odds, \ln(p/(1-p)): it turns a probability between 0 and 1 into any number (0 at p = 0.5), so a model such as logistic regression can predict it with a straight line, and the sigmoid turns it back into a probability. Explained in: Gradient Boosting for Classification, §4. Stage 1: the log-odds of class 1.
Probabilities near 0 or 1 round off. Run 40 readings of “open” in ordinary probabilities. The odds (G-1376)Odds: How often an event happens divided by how often it does not, e.g. 5 placed to 3 not placed is 5/3; unlike a probability, odds have no upper limit, so evidence updates them by one multiplication, and their log can be predicted with a straight line. Explained in: Gradient Boosting for Classification, §4. Stage 1: the log-odds of class 1 become 3 to the power 40, about 12 billion billion, and the computer stores p(\text{open}) as exactly 1.0. After that, a reading of “closed” changes nothing, because 1.0 times anything, divided by itself, is still 1.0. In log odds the same run reaches 43.94, and a “closed” reading moves it to 43.25, as it should. The notebook shows both.

5.1 Three questions about a run
Now the second half of the opening question: what else the same cell probabilities tell us. Filtering is what a robot needs while it drives. Smoothing and the most likely path are for looking back over a recorded run, for example to draw the path it took.
5.2 Smoothing with the forward-backward algorithm
At t = 1 the filter knew only the first reading, so cells 1, 3 and 7 were equally likely (Figure 11, blue bars). Later readings settle it. A robot at cell 3 at t = 1 would be at cell 5 at t = 2, a wall, and would have read “door” there only 20 percent of the time. A robot at cell 1 would be at cell 3, a door. So the reading at t = 2 points back to cell 1.
The forward-backward algorithm (G-2471)Forward-backward algorithm: The method that computes smoothed beliefs in an HMM by multiplying a forward pass (evidence up to t) by a backward pass (evidence after t) and rescaling; it uses every reading of a recorded run for each time step. Explained in §5.2 Smoothing with the forward-backward algorithm. makes this exact. The algorithm combines two quantities for every cell x and time t (J&M App. A):

the forward probability (G-2472)Forward probability \alpha_t: The probability of the readings up to time t together with being in state x at t; the histogram filter before rescaling, carrying the evidence from the past. Explained in §5.2 Smoothing with the forward-backward algorithm. \alpha_t(x): the probability of the readings up to t and of being in cell x at t. It is the histogram filter (G-2461)Histogram filter (discrete Bayes filter): The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position. Explained in §2.1 Why cells. before rescaling; at t = 1 it is 0.06 at the doors and 0.02 at the walls (Section 2.2);
the backward probability (G-2473)Backward probability \beta_t: The probability of the readings after time t, given state x at t, computed from the last step backwards starting at 1; it carries the evidence from the future. Explained in §5.2 Smoothing with the forward-backward algorithm. \beta_t(x): the probability of the readings after t, given cell x at t. It is computed from the end backwards, starting from 1 at the last step; for cell 1 at t = 1 it is 0.4144 (worked below).

Why does a plain product work? The steps use two facts:

the Markov property (G-2316)Markov property: The property of a sequence of states that the future depends on the past only through the present state; it lets a filter forget the history and work from the latest state alone. Trying every path is hopeless for long runs: with 10 cells and T steps there are 10 to the power T paths, 1000 for our 3 steps but a 1 followed by 100 zeros for 100 steps (J&M App. A).

x' is a cell at time t - 1, where the path may come from;

p(z_t \mid x) is the chance of the reading z_t in cell x (0.6 for “door” at cell 3);

The robot can now run the Bayes filter on a computer, one number per cell, and look back over a recorded run. Still missing: cells multiply with every extra state variable, 7.2 million for one 30 m floor; the particle filter (G-2492)Particle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in: Particle Filter, §4. The particle filter, step by step keeps samples only where the belief is, and the Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system keeps a belief shaped like a single bell-shaped curve, a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is, as two numbers.

Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Sampling distribution and standard errorExplained in: Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem, §3. Sampling distributions; LikelihoodLikelihood: How probable the observed data is under given parameter values; read as a function of the parameters with the data fixed. Explained in: Probability vs Likelihood, §2.2 Likelihood: from the event back to the parameter; Probabilistic motion modelsMotion model p(\mathbf x_t \mid u_t, \mathbf x_{t-1}): The probability distribution of a robot’s pose after a move, given its pose before and the control (command or odometry); it describes how uncertain motion is, so a filter can score possible end poses or draw them at random. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §2.2 The motion model and its density; Bayes filterBayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm; Histogram filterHistogram filter (discrete Bayes filter): The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position. Explained in: Grid Filters: Histogram Filter and Binary Bayes Filter, §2. The histogram filter.
Compare with: Histogram filterHistogram filter (discrete Bayes filter): The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position. Explained in: Grid Filters: Histogram Filter and Binary Bayes Filter, §2. The histogram filter; Kalman filterKalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system; Extended Kalman filterExtended Kalman filter (EKF): The Kalman filter for nonlinear motion and sensor models: it moves the mean through the nonlinear functions and uses their Jacobians at the latest estimate in place of F and H, so it can track unimodal beliefs through nonlinear models. Explained in: Extended Kalman Filter, §4. The extended Kalman filter.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A particle filter keeps the robot’s belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition as a cloud of guesses. Each reading reweighs the guesses, resampling keeps the good ones, and each move shifts them all; the cloud can take any shape, including several peaks at once.



Figure 1: A corridor that loops round a block, opened out from 0 to 10 m, with three doors set back into the right-hand wall; the robot at 2.1 m reads 1.46 m to the side. Below: the map, the reading expected at each position
So far the robot can run the Bayes filter with a histogram filter (G-2461)Histogram filter (discrete Bayes filter): The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position. Explained in: Grid Filters: Histogram Filter and Binary Bayes Filter, §2.1 Why cells: one probability per cell of the 10-cell hallway. The histogram filter breaks when the state grows: a floor robot’s pose (x, y, \theta), its position and heading, already needs 7.2 million cellsExplained in: Grid Filters: Histogram Filter and Binary Bayes Filter, §3.1 Why the number of cells explodes. This Note keeps the belief as a cloud of samples instead, placed only where the robot may be.
A robot is somewhere in the corridor of Figure 1. It has a map of the corridor, but it does not know where it is. Its side sensor reads 1.46 m, which means “a door is beside me”. Three doors fit that reading, so the reading’s answer to “where am I?” is “at door 1, door 2 or door 3, about equally likely”: a belief with a peak at each door. These peaks are the belief’s three modes (G-1251)Mode: The value that appears most often in the data, so it sits under the highest peak of a histogram or a distribution curve; it gives a centre for data that are not numbers, and a belief with several peaks has several modes. Explained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §5. Mode, so the belief is multimodal (G-1275)Multimodal: Having more than one mode, that is more than one peak (two peaks: bimodal), such as a robot’s belief peaking at three doors; it shows the data point to several separate values, so one mean or one best guess would hide them. Explained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §5. Mode.
The Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm gives the rule for updating such a belief. Two other ways of running it struggle here:

the grid filter, or histogram filter (G-2461)Histogram filter (discrete Bayes filter): The Bayes filter run on a space cut into cells, keeping one probability per cell; sensing multiplies each cell by p(z \mid x) and rescales, moving slides and blurs the list. It makes the Bayes filter computable for a continuous position. Explained in: Grid Filters: Histogram Filter and Binary Bayes Filter, §2.1 Why cells, stores one number per cell, which is fine on a 10 m line but grows very fast with the number of state variables;
the Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system stores the belief as a single bell-shaped curve, a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is, and one Gaussian has only one mode (Section 3.1).

The particle filter (G-2492)Particle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in §4. The particle filter, step by step. stores the belief as a set of sample guesses instead. This Note builds it on the corridor of Figure 1:

why a cloud of samples can stand for a belief, and how accurate it is (Section 3);
the three steps, move, weigh and resample, worked by hand and then run on the corridor (Section 4);
the low-variance sampler (G-2499)Low-variance sampler (systematic resampling): A way to resample with one random start between 0 and 1/M and M pointers 1/M apart along the stacked weights; it keeps every particle with weight at least 1/M, adds little randomness and runs in time proportional to M. Explained in §4.3 Resample: copy the heavy particles, drop the light ones., the standard way to resample (Section 4.3);
what goes wrong with too few particles (G-2491)Particle: One sample guess of the full state, such as a position of 1.6 m, together with a weight; a particle filter keeps M of them so that together they stand for the belief. Explained in §3.3 Weighted samples., and the fixes (Section 5).

2. The running example and the Bayes filter in brief


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

To tell the three doors apart, the robot has a map, a noisy side sensor and wheels that slip. The Bayes filter turns these into a belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition with two steps per round: predict with the motion, update with the reading.


2.1 The corridor, the sensor and the motion
The corridor loops round a block and is 10 m around, so position 10 m is position 0 m again. 2.2 The Bayes filter in brief
The robot’s belief \text{bel}(x_t) is a probability distribution over where it is at time t, given every command and reading so far (belief (G-2433))Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition. The Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm updates it in two steps per round.
At step t:

x_t is the robot’s position at step t, in m (2.10 m at the first reading, which the filter never sees);
x_{t-1} is its position one step earlier, in m;
u_t is the command, a move of 2.5 m;
z_t is the side sensor’s reading, in m (1.46 m at the first reading);
\text{bel}(x_{t-1}) is the belief one step earlier, a density over positions, in probability per metre;
p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1}) is the motion model, the density of the new position given the command and the old position, in probability per metre;
\int \ldots\ dx_{t-1} adds over every previous position x_{t-1};
\overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) (read “bel bar”) is the predicted belief, after the move and before the reading;
p(z_t \mid x_t) is the sensor model of Section 2.1, in probability per metre;
\eta is the number that makes the total 1;
\text{bel}(x_t) is the belief after the reading.

Predict with the command u_t: every place x_{t-1} the robot may have been sends probability to the places the move may take it.
\overline{\text{bel}}(x_t) = \int p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1})
\qquad \times\ \text{bel}(x_{t-1})\ dx_{t-1}
Update with the reading z_t: multiply by how well each place explains the reading, then rescale so the total is 1.
\text{bel}(x_t) = \eta\ p(z_t \mid x_t)\ \overline{\text{bel}}(x_t)
The update is Bayes’ theorem (G-269)Bayes’ theorem: The rule that reverses a conditional probability: from P(B \mid A) it gives P(A \mid B), so a belief about A can be updated after seeing B; P(A \mid B) = P(B \mid A) P(A) / P(B). Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Bayes’ Theorem, §4. The formula and its proof with the predicted belief as the prior.
The two formulas are exact, but they hold whole curves, and an integral over a curve cannot be computed for most maps and sensors (Labbe ch.12). Every Bayes-filter variant is a way of storing the curve so that the two steps become sums a computer can do. The particle filter (G-2492)Particle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in §4. The particle filter, step by step. stores it as samples.

3.2 Samples stand for a distribution: the Monte Carlo idea
Suppose we could draw guesses of the robot’s position from its belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. 4.2 Weigh: the update step


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A particle (G-2491)Particle: One sample guess of the full state, such as a position of 1.6 m, together with a weight; a particle filter keeps M of them so that together they stand for the belief. Explained in §3.3 Weighted samples.’s weight is the height of the sensor curve, centred on the reading the particle expects, at the reading we got.


The idea. The reading is 1.46 m. A particle in front of a door expects 1.5 m: close, so it explains the reading well. A particle beside plain wall expects 1.0 m: 0.46 m off, more than three sensor standard deviations, so it explains the reading badly. The weight turns “explains well” into a number.
The weight. For particle m:

x^{[m]} is its position, in m (1.6 m for particle 2 below);
z is the reading, 1.46 m;
p(z \mid x^{[m]}) is the sensor model of Section 2.1, the density of the reading z at that position, in probability per metre (2.567 for particle 2);
w^{[m]} is the particle’s weight, the same number (2.567 for particle 2) until it is normalised below.

For each particle we ask the sensor model how likely the reading z is if the robot were where the particle says:
w^{[m]} = p(z \mid x^{[m]})
The result is the importance weight (G-2494)Importance weight: The weight a particle gets from a reading: the height of the sensor model p(z \mid x) at that reading, normalised over all particles; it says how well the particle explains what the robot sensed. Explained in §4.2 Weigh: the update step. of the particle: the height of the Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is, centred on the particle’s expected reading h(x^{[m]}), at the reading z (Figure 5). The weight is a height, not an area: the area under a density over a single point is zero, and the height is what a likelihood (G-1086)Likelihood: How probable the observed data is under given parameter values; read as a function of the parameters with the data fixed. Explained in: Probability vs Likelihood, §2.2 Likelihood: from the event back to the parameter is. The height is a density, not a probability, so it can be larger than 1.

4.3 Resample: copy the heavy particles, drop the light ones


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Resampling draws a fresh set of M particles from the weighted set, each pick in proportion to weight, so the computation goes where the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition is. The low-variance sampler does it with one random number and keeps every particle whose weight is at least 1/M, one over the number of particles M.


Why resample. After weighing, the two wall particles (G-2491)Particle: One sample guess of the full state, such as a position of 1.6 m, together with a weight; a particle filter keeps M of them so that together they stand for the belief. Explained in §3.3 Weighted samples. carry a weight of 0.0031 each; after a few more readings, most of 100 particles would carry weights near zero. They still cost a motion step and a sensor check each round but add almost nothing to the belief. Worse, a particle’s weight only ever shrinks or grows by multiplication, so a few particles soon carry nearly all the weight and the cloud behaves as if it had two or three particles (Labbe ch.12 calls this degeneracy).
The idea. Draw M new particles from the weighted set, with replacement (G-2125)With replacement: Sampling in which each drawn item is put back, so it can be drawn again. Explained in: Bagging: Bootstrap Aggregation, §2.3 Drawing with replacement, each draw picking particle i with probability equal to its weight w^{[i]}. A heavy particle is picked several times, a light one probably never. The new particles all get the weight 1/M again: the copies have taken the place of the weight. This step is resampling (G-2498)Resampling (particle filter): Drawing a fresh set of M particles, with replacement, from the weighted set, each pick in proportion to weight, then giving all weight 1/M; heavy particles are copied and light ones dropped, so computation goes where the belief is. Explained in §4.3 Resample: copy the heavy particles, drop the light ones.; it is the same “draw rows in proportion to weight” as upsampling in AdaBoostUpsampling (resampling by weight): Drawing a new dataset of the same size in which each row is picked with probability equal to its weight, so heavily weighted rows appear more often for the next model. Explained in: AdaBoost Step by Step, §9. Step 7: upsampling, a new dataset drawn by weight.
Plain resampling. Lay the weights end to end along the line from 0 to 1, so each particle owns a stretch as long as its weight (Figure 6, top). Draw M independent random numbers between 0 and 1; each picks the particle whose stretch it lands in. Less randomness. All pointers move together with the one random start, so the number of copies a particle gets can only be the whole number just below or just above M times its weight. For particle 3:
5 \times 0.3313 = 1.66
so it gets 1 or 2 copies. Over 100,000 repeats (notebook):

























MethodAverage copies of particle 3Standard deviation of copiesShare of repeats with no copyLow-variance1.6550.4750.000Plain1.6541.0520.135
Both give the same average, so neither favours any particle; the low-variance sampler’s standard deviation is less than half as large. The low-variance sampler also needs one pass along the list, a running time proportional to M, against M \log M for plain resampling with a search per draw (Freiburg PF slides; Labbe ch.12).

Python: the low-variance sampler in four lines.
def low_variance(w, rng):
    M = len(w)
    pointers = rng.uniform(0, 1 / M) + np.arange(M) / M
    return np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(w), pointers, side="right")
np.cumsum(w) gives the stretch ends; np.searchsorted(..., side="right") returns, for each pointer, the index of the first stretch that ends beyond it. x = x[low_variance(w, rng)] is the new particle set.

One answer from a cloud, and a trap. A controller usually wants one position. In symbols:

M is the number of particles, 100 here;
x^{[m]} is particle m‘s position, in m;
w^{[m]} is its weight, a number from 0 to 1, the weights adding up to 1;

The usual choice is the weighted mean of the particles:

After reading 3 it gives 7.05 m; the robot is at 7.08 m. After reading 2, the same formula gives 5.73 m, between the two clusters, in front of plain wall (the black diamond in frame 5 of Figure 8). 4.6 The algorithm
Putting the steps together gives the particle filter of Thrun Table 4.3, as also given in the Freiburg PF slides. Inputs: the particle (G-2491)Particle: One sample guess of the full state, such as a position of 1.6 m, together with a weight; a particle filter keeps M of them so that together they stand for the belief. Explained in §3.3 Weighted samples. set \mathcal X_{t-1} from the last round, the command u_t and the reading z_t. The other symbols are listed in Section 2.2 and Section 3.3.

For each particle m = 1, \ldots, M:

move: sample x_t^{[m]} from p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1}^{[m]});
weigh: set w_t^{[m]} = p(z_t \mid x_t^{[m]}).


Normalise the weights so they add up to 1.
Resample: draw M particles from the weighted set in proportion to the weights (low-variance sampler (G-2499))Low-variance sampler (systematic resampling): A way to resample with one random start between 0 and 1/M and M pointers 1/M apart along the stacked weights; it keeps every particle with weight at least 1/M, adds little randomness and runs in time proportional to M. Explained in §4.3 Resample: copy the heavy particles, drop the light ones.; they form \mathcal X_t, each with weight 1/M.

Every line uses the models only to draw a sample or to evaluate a density. No model needs to be linear, smooth or Gaussian: our map is a step, which a Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system could not use (Section 3.1). With 100 particles the loop found the right door; with fewer, it can fail.
5. Particle deprivation


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

If no particle (G-2491)Particle: One sample guess of the full state, such as a position of 1.6 m, together with a weight; a particle filter keeps M of them so that together they stand for the belief. Explained in §3.3 Weighted samples. is near the true state, no step can create one there, and the filter settles on a wrong answer. More particles and fewer, smarter resamplings are the fixes.


5.1 Too few particles
The cloud can hold the three doors of Figure 1 only if some particles (G-2491)Particle: One sample guess of the full state, such as a position of 1.6 m, together with a weight; a particle filter keeps M of them so that together they stand for the belief. Explained in §3.3 Weighted samples. sit at each of them. Resampling only copies particles that exist, and the move step only shifts them a little. So once every particle near the true position has been dropped, the filter has no way back. Losing the particles near the true state is particle deprivation (G-2501)Particle deprivation: The failure in which no particles are left near the true state, so the filter settles confidently on a wrong answer; caused by too few particles or unlucky resampling, and fought with more particles and fewer resamplings. Explained in §5.1 Too few particles. (Thrun §4.3).
With few particles it happens often. Figure 9 first runs 5 particles and 100 particles on the same three readings. Watch the 5: none starts at door 1, where the robot starts, so they follow the one particle at door 3 and end tight at door 1, the wrong door, while the 100 end at door 3. The last frame shows that this is not bad luck: we ran the corridor example 1000 times for each particle count and counted how often the filter ended at the right door.

With 5 particles, the start often has no particle at door 1, the robot’s true door, or resampling drops the few there; the filter then follows whatever survived, with full confidence. Too few particles make the filter overconfident: it reports one tight cluster at the wrong door. The average share it gives door 3 shows the same bias: 0.432 with 5 particles against the exact 0.956 (notebook); a small particle set gives a biased belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition (Thrun §4.3).
The problem grows with the number of state variables. A cloud of 100 points covers a 10 m line densely, but spread over a room’s (x, y, \theta) the same 100 points leave wide gaps, so the number of particles needed grows very fast with the state’s dimension (Labbe ch.12).
5.2 Other fixes


More particles. The direct fix, paid for in computation (Labbe ch.12).


Resample less often. Each resampling throws away variety. One rule resamples only when the weights have become uneven: when the effective number of particles (G-2491)Particle: One sample guess of the full state, such as a position of 1.6 m, together with a weight; a particle filter keeps M of them so that together they stand for the belief. Explained in §3.3 Weighted samples. falls below half of M, the number of particles (Labbe ch.12). In symbols:

w^{[m]} is the weight of particle m, a number from 0 to 1, the weights adding up to 1;
\sum_m adds over all M particles;
\hat N_{\text{eff}} is the effective number of particles, how many particles of equal weight the cloud is worth.

\hat N_{\text{eff}} = 1 / \textstyle\sum_m (w^{[m]})^2
With equal weights it equals M; with all weight on one particle it equals 1.


A very accurate sensor is a trap. If the sensor curve is much narrower than the gaps between particles, almost every particle gets a weight near zero and the cloud collapses onto one or two. Pretending the sensor is noisier than it is, or using more particles, keeps enough particles alive (Labbe ch.12).

Explained in: Probability vs Likelihood, §2.2 Likelihood: from the event back to the parameterHow probable the observed data is under given parameter values; read as a function of the parameters with the data fixed.Normalisation (of weights) (G-1347)Normalisation (of weights): Dividing every weight by their sum so they add up to 1. Explained in: AdaBoost from Scratch in Python, §6. Normalising and drawing the next datasetDividing every weight by their sum so they add up to 1.With replacement (G-2125)With replacement: Sampling in which each drawn item is put back, so it can be drawn again. Explained in: Bagging: Bootstrap Aggregation, §2.3 Drawing with replacementSampling in which each drawn item is put back, so it can be drawn again.

RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-017-.title: Kalman Filter
RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-017-.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Expected value and variance of a random variableExpected value E[X]: The average value we would get over many repeats: each possible value times its probability, added up (the probability-weighted average of a random variable). Also called the long-run mean and written \mu. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §3. Expected value; Normal distributionNormal distribution: A symmetric, bell-shaped distribution: most values sit near the mean and they get rarer the further out we go; its mean and standard deviation set its centre and width. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is; Derivatives of one variableExplained in: Derivatives of One Variable, §4. The derivative: shrinking the step to zero; Multivariate normal distributionMultivariate normal distribution: The bell-shaped (normal) distribution for several numbers at once, a vector; it is set by a mean vector (its centre) and a covariance matrix (its spread and how the numbers vary together). Explained in: Gaussian Mixture Models, §7.1 The multivariate normal; Bayes filterBayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm.
Leads to: Extended Kalman filterExtended Kalman filter (EKF): The Kalman filter for nonlinear motion and sensor models: it moves the mean through the nonlinear functions and uses their Jacobians at the latest estimate in place of F and H, so it can track unimodal beliefs through nonlinear models. Explained in: Extended Kalman Filter, §4. The extended Kalman filter; Filter consistencyExplained in: Extended Kalman Filter, §5. Consistency: is the filter telling the truth about itself?.
Compare with: Particle filterParticle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in: Particle Filter, §4. The particle filter, step by step.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A robot has two noisy ways to know where it is: its commands, which drift, and its sensor, which jumps. The Kalman filter blends them with the weight that makes the result as certain as possible, and it does so one step at a time from two numbers.


Figure 1 plays ten seconds of a robot in a corridor, one step per frame, with its two sources of position: its commands (grey) and a ceiling beacon (orange). Watch the grey gap between the commands-only path and the truth: each step keeps the last gap and adds a new wheel slip, so the commands stay behind the truth at every step. The orange gap of the beacon starts fresh each step and swings from one side of the truth to the other. The last frame adds the Kalman filter (blue), which misses by less than either.

Figure 1: Ten steps of a robot in a corridor, one step per frame: the true position (black), the commands alone (grey, dashed) and the beacon readings (orange crosses). Each frame draws this step’s gap from each source to the truth: the commands’ gap is the last gap plus a new wheel slip, the beacon’s gap is new every time. The last frame adds the Kalman filter estimate (blue) and each one’s average miss (RMSE) over the ten steps: commands 0.27 m, beacon 0.51 m, Kalman filter 0.17 m
The particle filter (G-2492)Particle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in: Particle Filter, §4. The particle filter, step by step lets the robot’s belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition, its probability for each possible position, take any shape, but every particle must be moved and weighed every round. When the belief is a single bell-shaped curve, a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is, two numbers carry all of it; this Note builds that filter, the Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in §2.5 The linear Gaussian system.. It needs a new world. The three doors of the looped corridor give a belief with a peak at each door: three modes (G-1251)Mode: The value that appears most often in the data, so it sits under the highest peak of a histogram or a distribution curve; it gives a centre for data that are not numbers, and a belief with several peaks has several modes. Explained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §5. Mode, so the belief is multimodal (G-1275)Multimodal: Having more than one mode, that is more than one peak (two peaks: bimodal), such as a robot’s belief peaking at three doors; it shows the data point to several separate values, so one mean or one best guess would hide them. Explained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §5. Mode, and one Gaussian cannot hold it. Here a ceiling beacon reports the position itself, so the belief has a single mode: it is unimodal (G-2528)Unimodal: Having a single mode (one peak); a unimodal belief can be held by one Gaussian, so the Kalman filter needs only its mean and variance. Explained in §1. Overview..
A delivery robot drives along a straight corridor. Every second it is commanded to move 0.5 m. A ceiling beacon system also reports its position once a second. Neither source is good enough on its own (Figure 1):

The commands give a smooth path, but they drift: each step’s error is the last step’s error plus a new wheel slip, so the error carries over and piles up. Over the ten steps of Figure 1, the commands alone miss the true position by 0.27 m on average (the root mean squared error (G-1705), RMSE)Root mean squared error (RMSE): The square root of the average squared error (MSE), so the error is back in the output’s units. Explained in: Regression Metrics: MAE, MSE, RMSE, R² and Adjusted R², §4. Root mean squared error (RMSE).
The beacon jumps: each reading’s error is new, with no memory of the last one, so it never piles up, but it can swing from one side to the other between two seconds. Its readings miss by 0.51 m on average.

Figure 2 runs both sources for 60 steps from a known start. The commands’ error moves only a little each step, but the moves add up, and its band of two standard deviations (G-1871)Standard deviation: How far values typically lie from the mean; divide by n - 1 for a sample (pandas default) or by n for a population (NumPy default). Explained in: Understanding Your Data: Seven First Questions, §7.1 Count, mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum, twice the error’s typical size, widens with the number of steps (Section 2.4). With:

t is the number of steps since the start, from 1 to 60 in Figure 2;
0.1 m is the standard deviation of one step’s wheel slip.

The band reaches this far either side of zero, in m:
2 \times 0.1 \times \sqrt{t}
The beacon’s error lands somewhere new each step, but its band stays at ±0.8 m. After about 16 steps the commands are the worse source.

Figure 2: One simulated run of 60 steps from a known start, one frame per step. Top: the errors now, with an arrow from each last value; the commands’ error moves a little each step and wanders off, the beacon’s lands somewhere new each step, the Kalman filter’s stays near zero. Bottom: the errors so far; the commands’ band of two standard deviations widens, the beacon’s stays at ±0.8 m, the Kalman filter’s settles at ±0.38 m
Over the ten steps of Figure 1, the Kalman filter’s estimate misses by 0.17 m, better than either (notebook). In Figure 2 (blue), its error stays near zero, and its band settles at ±0.38 m, half the beacon’s, and does not widen. The filter gets there by asking, at every step, how far to trust each source, and the answer is a number we derive: the Kalman gain (G-2508)Kalman gain K: The weight the update gives to the reading, K = \bar{p}/(\bar{p} + R) in one dimension: the weight that makes the updated variance smallest, near 1 when the prediction is vague and near 0 when the reading is. Explained in §4.3 The best weight: the Kalman gain.. The Note builds the filter on this corridor, one step at a time, in the order of kalmanfilter.net and Becker’s book:

why a Gaussian belief stays Gaussian, so two numbers are enough (Section 2);
the predict step, which carries the drift: the Gaussian moves and widens (Section 3);
the update step, which uses the beacon: the gain derived as the weight that makes the estimate’s variance (G-2076)Variance of a random variable: How spread out a random variable’s values are: the expected squared distance from its expected value, \mathrm{Var}(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2]. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4. Variance of a random variable, the spread of its error, smallest (Section 4);
the ten steps of Figure 1 by hand (Section 5);
the matrix form, which estimates a speed that is never measured, then observability (G-2517)Observability: Whether a system’s whole state can be worked out from its readings and commands over time; a filter needs it before it can pin down every state variable. Explained in §6.5 Observability: can the readings pin down the state?., whether the readings can pin down the whole state, and the filter as the source of the state a controller needs (Section 6);
how to choose the two noise settings: Q, the variance of the wheel slip, 0.01 m², and R, the variance of the beacon’s error, 0.16 m² (Section 7).

2. Why two numbers are enough: the linear Gaussian system


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

To weigh the drifting commands against the jumping beacon at every step, the filter must carry its belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition in a few numbers. If the motion and the sensor are linear functions (G-2527)Linear function: A function y = ax + b: a fixed multiple of the input plus a constant, whose graph is a straight line; passing a normal variable through it gives another normal variable, which is why the Kalman filter is exact for linear models. Explained in §2.3 A linear function keeps a Gaussian a Gaussian. of the state (the output y is a fixed multiple a of the state x plus a constant b, y = ax + b, whose graph is a straight line) with added Gaussian noise, a Gaussian belief stays Gaussian, so a mean and a variance (G-2076)Variance of a random variable: How spread out a random variable’s values are: the expected squared distance from its expected value, \mathrm{Var}(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2]. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4. Variance of a random variable carry the whole belief.


2.1 The Bayes filter in brief
The robot’s belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition is a probability distribution over its position. The Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm updates it once a second, in rounds numbered by the step t. At step t:

x_t is the robot’s position, in m;
\text{bel}(x_t) is the belief, the probability distribution over the position x_t;
u_t is the command, 0.5 m forward;
z_t is the beacon’s reading, in m;
p(x_t \mid u_t, x_{t-1}) is the motion model, the probability of each new position given the command and the last position x_{t-1};
p(z_t \mid x_t) is the sensor model, the probability of each reading given the position.

Each round has two steps:

predict with the command u_t, spreading the belief by the motion model;
update with the reading z_t, multiplying by the sensor model and rescaling to a total of 1.

For a general belief these steps act on whole curves, which is costly: the particle filter (G-2492)Particle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in: Particle Filter, §4. The particle filter, step by step needs hundreds of samples to store one. The Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in §2.5 The linear Gaussian system. instead uses the case in which the belief is always a Gaussian, which needs no samples at all.
2.2 A Gaussian is two numbers
A Gaussian, also called a normal distribution (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is, is fixed by its mean (where the peak is) and its variance (G-2076)Variance of a random variable: How spread out a random variable’s values are: the expected squared distance from its expected value, \mathrm{Var}(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2]. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4. Variance of a random variable (how wide it is). If the belief is normal, it is enough to store:

\hat{x} is the estimate, the mean, our best single guess, in m;
p is its variance, how unsure we are, in m².

The robot’s first guess, marked with the subscript 0 for the start, is that it starts at the dock, give or take about 1 m:
\hat x_0 = 0 \text{ m}
p_0 = 1 \text{ m}^2
The true start is 0.3 m; the filter does not know that, and this start error is part of the commands’ drift. Two numbers are enough only if the predict and update steps keep the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition Gaussian, which the rest of this section checks.
2.3 A linear function keeps a Gaussian a Gaussian


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Passing a normal variable x through a linear function y = ax + b (a fixed multiple a of x plus a constant b), whose graph is a straight line, gives another normal variable y: the mean goes through the line and the variance is multiplied by a^2, the slope squared.


The predict step shifts the belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition by the command, so we first check what a linear function does to a Gaussian, on a small example:

x is a normal variable with mean 1 and standard deviation (G-1871)Standard deviation: How far values typically lie from the mean; divide by n - 1 for a sample (pandas default) or by n for a population (NumPy default). Explained in: Understanding Your Data: Seven First Questions, §7.1 Count, mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum, the typical distance from the mean, 0.5;
y is the value the line below gives for x.

y = 2x + 1
Every value of x is stretched by 2 and shifted by 1, so the whole curve is stretched by 2 and shifted by 1. Its shape stays a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is (Figure 3). The mean goes through the line:
\text{mean of } y = 2 \times 1 + 1 = 3
The standard deviation is stretched by the slope:
\text{standard deviation of } y = 2 \times 0.5 = 1
Make interactive
Figure 3: x with mean 1 and standard deviation 0.5 (top) is passed through the line y = 2x + 1; the result y (right) is a Gaussian with mean 3 and standard deviation 1. Both axes and both density panels use the same scale, so the line rises 2 for every 1 across and the curve of y is twice as wide and half as tall. Histograms of 5000 samples sit on the formula curves
Why the mean goes through the line and the variance gets a^2, the slope squared. The mean of y is the average of all the y values, and every y is 2x + 1. Two samples of x, 0.5 and 1.5, have mean 1 and variance 0.25, like x in Figure 3. Through the line they become 2 and 4:
\text{mean of } y = \frac{2 + 4}{2}
= \frac{(2 \times 0.5 + 1) + (2 \times 1.5 + 1)}{2}
= \frac{2 \times 0.5 + 2 \times 1.5 + 1 + 1}{2}
= \frac{2 \times (0.5 + 1.5) + 2 \times 1}{2}
= 2 \times \frac{0.5 + 1.5}{2} + 1
= 2 \times 1 + 1
= 3
The same steps for any samples, through any line:

n is the number of samples, 2 above;
x_i is sample number i, 0.5 and 1.5 above;
\mu is the mean of the samples, 1 above;
a is the line’s slope, 2 above;
b is the line’s shift, 1 above;
y_i is sample x_i after the line, 2 and 4 above;
\sum means add upExplained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §3. Mean, here over i from 1 to n.

\text{mean of } y = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i
= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (a x_i + b)
= \frac{1}{n}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{n} a x_i + \sum_{i=1}^{n} b\Big)
= \frac{1}{n}\Big(a\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i + n b\Big)
= a\thinspace\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i + b
= a\mu + b
The variance (G-2076)Variance of a random variable: How spread out a random variable’s values are: the expected squared distance from its expected value, \mathrm{Var}(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2]. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4. Variance of a random variable of y, written \text{Var}(y), is the average squared distance of the y values from their mean, a\mu + b:
\text{Var}(y) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \big(y_i - (a\mu + b)\big)^2
= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (a x_i + b - a\mu - b)^2
= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (a x_i - a\mu)^2
= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \big(a\thinspace(x_i - \mu)\big)^2
= \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} a^2\thinspace(x_i - \mu)^2
= a^2\thinspace\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \mu)^2
= a^2\thinspace\text{Var}(x)
With our numbers:
\text{Var}(y) = 4 \times 0.25 = 1
The shift b moves the Gaussian without widening it. That the result is still a Gaussian, not some other shape, is a property of the normal distribution (Freiburg KF slides; Labbe ch.4). The command is such a shift, but each step also adds a wheel slip, a second error.
2.4 Adding independent errors adds variances
The robot’s next position is its present position plus the commanded 0.5 m plus a random slip. The estimate moves by the same 0.5 m. The error is the true position minus the estimate. With:

x is the robot’s present true position, in m;
\hat{x} is the present estimate, in m;
w is the next step’s wheel slip, in m, with mean 0 and a standard deviation of 0.1 m;
e is the present error, the true position minus the estimate, in m.

The next error:
(x + 0.5 + w) - (\hat{x} + 0.5)
= x - \hat{x} + w
= e + w
The present error has mean 0, because the estimate is the mean, and variance (G-2076)Variance of a random variable: How spread out a random variable’s values are: the expected squared distance from its expected value, \mathrm{Var}(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2]. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4. Variance of a random variable p, the estimate’s variance, 1 m² at the start (Section 2.2). The slip has mean 0 and does not depend on e, so the two errors are independent. Their variances add, where \text{Var} stands for the variance:
\text{Var}(e + w) = \text{Var}(e) + \text{Var}(w)
Why. Take a present error of 1 m or −1 m and a slip of 0.1 m or −0.1 m, all four pairs equally likely. Square each next error:
(1 + 0.1)^2 = 1 + 0.2 + 0.01
(1 - 0.1)^2 = 1 - 0.2 + 0.01
(-1 + 0.1)^2 = 1 - 0.2 + 0.01
(-1 - 0.1)^2 = 1 + 0.2 + 0.01
Average the four squares; each +0.2 cancels a −0.2:
\text{Var}(e + w) = 1 + 0.01
The same in symbols:
(e + w)^2 = e^2 + 2ew + w^2
Averaged, the 2ew parts cancel the same way: whatever e is, the slip is as often negative as positive.
\text{Var}(e + w) = \text{Var}(e) + \text{Var}(w)
So every slip adds its variance, and the commands’ drift grows step by step.
2.5 The linear Gaussian system
Sections 2.3 and 2.4 give the two facts the Kalman filter needs: a linear function keeps a Gaussian a Gaussian, and independent errors add their variances (G-2076)Variance of a random variable: How spread out a random variable’s values are: the expected squared distance from its expected value, \mathrm{Var}(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2]. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4. Variance of a random variable. Both apply to a linear Gaussian system (G-2507)Linear Gaussian system: A system whose next state and whose readings are linear functions of the state plus normal noise, starting from a normal belief; in it the belief stays normal, so the Kalman filter is exact. Explained in §2.5 The linear Gaussian system., a system that meets three conditions (Freiburg KF slides; Thrun §3.2):

the next state is a linear function of the state and the command, plus normal noise;
the reading is a linear function of the state, plus normal noise;
the first belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definition, before any command or reading, is normal.

Our robot meets all three. At step t:

x_t is the robot’s true position, in m;
u_t is the command, 0.5 m forward;
w_t is the wheel slip, the source of the commands’ drift, normal with mean 0 and variance Q = 0.01 m² (a standard deviation of 0.1 m);
z_t is the beacon’s reading, in m;
v_t is the beacon’s error, the source of its jumps, normal with mean 0 and variance R = 0.16 m² (a standard deviation of 0.4 m).

The next position is the last position plus the command plus the slip:
x_t = x_{t-1} + u_t + w_t
The reading is the position plus the beacon’s error:
z_t = x_t + v_t
Both are linear with normal noise, which meets conditions 1 and 2. The first belief, mean 0 m and variance 1 m² (Section 2.2), is normal, which meets condition 3. So the belief stays Gaussian at every step, and the Kalman filter computes its mean and variance exactly. It is the Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithm with nothing approximated (Freiburg KF slides). Its first step, predict, is where the drift enters.
3. Predict: the Gaussian moves and widens


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The command moves the estimate; the slip widens it. The predicted variance (G-2076)Variance of a random variable: How spread out a random variable’s values are: the expected squared distance from its expected value, \mathrm{Var}(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2]. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4. Variance of a random variable, how unsure the prediction is, is the old variance plus the slip’s variance Q, 0.01 m².


The idea. First the drift of Figure 1: why do the commands alone miss by 0.27 m? The robot is commanded 0.5 m, so our best guess moves 0.5 m. But each command adds a slip we cannot see, so we are less sure than before, and the doubt piles up.
The standard terms. The random slip the motion adds at each step is the process noise (G-2509)Process noise Q: The random part of the motion the model leaves out (wheel slip, pushes), given as its variance or covariance Q; it widens the belief at every predict step and is usually set by tuning. Explained in §3. Predict: the Gaussian moves and widens. (kalmanfilter.net). The estimate before the step’s reading is the predicted estimate (G-2512)Predicted estimate (a priori): The estimate and its variance after the predict step and before the step’s reading, \bar{x} and \bar{p}; it says what the model alone expects. Explained in §3. Predict: the Gaussian moves and widens., also called the prior or a priori estimate.
The formulas. At each step:

\hat{x} is the estimate after the last step, in m (0 m at the start);
p is its variance, in m² (1 m² at the start);
u is the command, 0.5 m;
Q is the slip’s variance, 0.01 m²;
\bar{x} is the predicted estimate, in m;
\bar{p} is its variance, in m².

The mean goes through the motion; the variances add (Section 2.4):
\bar{x} = \hat{x} + u
\bar{p} = p + Q
Step 1 on the corridor. From the first guess:
\bar x_1 = 0 + 0.5 = 0.5 \text{ m}
\bar p_1 = 1 + 0.01 = 1.01 \text{ m}^2
Frame “step 1: predict” of Figure 7 (Section 5) shows the Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is, the bell-shaped belief, moving 0.5 m and widening a little.
If the robot drove with no readings at all, the variance would grow by Q every step. After 100 steps:
p = 1 + 100 \times 0.01 = 2 \text{ m}^2
\sqrt{2} = 1.4 \text{ m standard deviation}
The growing variance is the drift of Figure 1: the commands alone only ever widen the Gaussian, so a beacon reading is needed to pull the variance down.
4. Update: the gain that makes the estimate most certain


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The new estimate is a weighted average of the prediction and the reading. 6.4 One step in matrix form, and the speed nobody measured
We run one step of these lines on the corridor’s first reading. At the start, marked with the subscript 0:

\hat{\mathbf x_0} is the first estimate, a vector of 2 entries: position 0 m and speed 0 m/s;
P_0 is its covariance matrix, 2 × 2: variance (G-2076)Variance of a random variable: How spread out a random variable’s values are: the expected squared distance from its expected value, \mathrm{Var}(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2]. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4. Variance of a random variable 1 m² for position and 1 m²/s² for speed on the diagonal, and no covariance, 0, off it;
F is the state transition matrix of Section 6.2, with rows (1, 1) and (0, 1);
Q is the process noise covariance of Section 6.2, 0.01 m² and 0.001 m²/s² on the diagonal.

\hat{\mathbf x_0} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \cr0 \end{bmatrix}
P_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \cr0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
Predict. The mean stays at zero. P_0 is the identity matrix, so F P_0 F^{\mathsf T} is F F^{\mathsf T}. Each entry is a row of F times a row of F:
\text{top left: } 1 \times 1 + 1 \times 1 = 2
\text{off-diagonal: } 1 \times 0 + 1 \times 1 = 1
\text{bottom right: } 0 \times 0 + 1 \times 1 = 1
F P_0 F^{\mathsf T} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \cr1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
Adding Q gives the predicted covariance matrix for step 1:
\bar P_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 2.01 & 1 \cr1 & 1.001 \end{bmatrix}
The position variance has grown from 1 to 2.01, because an unknown speed adds an unknown distance. The off-diagonal 1 is new: the prediction now links the two errors. If the robot is further along than predicted, it was probably faster.
Update with the first reading z_1 = 0.82 m. The innovation variance S is the predicted position variance plus the beacon’s variance R, 0.16 m²:
S = 2.01 + 0.16 = 2.17
The measurement matrix H, the row (1, 0), picks the first column of \bar P_1:
\bar P_1 H^{\mathsf T} = \begin{bmatrix} 2.01 \cr1 \end{bmatrix}
Dividing by S gives the gain K, one weight for position and one for speed:
K = \begin{bmatrix} 2.01 / 2.17 \cr1 / 2.17 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 0.9263 \cr0.4608 \end{bmatrix}
The prediction was 0, so the innovation (G-2511)Innovation: The gap between a reading and the reading the prediction expected, z - H\bar{x}; the update moves the estimate by the gain times this gap, and its size is used to check the filter. Explained in §4.4 The updated estimate and its variance., the reading minus the predicted reading, is the whole reading, 0.82 m. The new state:
\text{position: } 0.9263 \times 0.82 = 0.760
\text{speed: } 0.4608 \times 0.82 = 0.378
\hat{\mathbf x_1} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.760 \cr0.378 \end{bmatrix}
One position reading has given a speed estimate of 0.378 m/s. The gain’s second entry is the covariance divided by S: through the link in \bar{P}, a position innovation becomes a speed correction.

6.5 Observability: can the readings pin down the state?
Could we do the same with a speed sensor and no position sensor? No. Every position, shifted by the same amount, gives exactly the same speed readings, so no number of speed readings can tell where the robot is.
A system is observable (G-2517)Observability: Whether a system’s whole state can be worked out from its readings and commands over time; a filter needs it before it can pin down every state variable. Explained in §6.5 Observability: can the readings pin down the state?. if its whole state can be worked out from its readings (and commands) over time (FBS §8.1). Figure 9 runs two filters for ten steps, one reading position and one reading only speed, one predict or update per frame: each predict raises the variance of the position estimate, each update lowers it. With the speed sensor, the variance after each update is higher than the step before, up to 2.68 m² after ten steps; with the position sensor it falls to 0.066 m² (notebook). A Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in §2.5 The linear Gaussian system. on an unobservable system runs without error messages but cannot shrink the uncertainty in the hidden direction, so checking observability comes before building the filter.

Blue: the filter reads position (measurement matrix H = [1, 0]); the variance after each update falls every step, to 0.066 m². Red: the filter reads only speed (H = [0, 1]); each drop is smaller than the rise before it, so the variance after each update climbs every step, to 2.68 m² in the last frame
6.6 The state a controller needs: the filter as an observer
The speed estimate of Section 6.4 is what a controller needs. A controller that holds the robot at 0.5 m/s must know the speed; one that stops it at a door must know the position. Many controllers need the whole state, but sensors give only part of it (FBS §8.1). Something must rebuild the missing parts.
The obvious attempt is to run the model alone, with no readings: each step, multiply the last estimate by the state transition matrix F. Running the model alone is dead reckoning (G-2311)Dead reckoning: Working out a robot’s position from a known start by adding up its own moves, without looking at its surroundings; simple, but its error grows with every move, so it needs readings to correct it. Explained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §2.1 Why counting moves is not enough: dead reckoning: any error in the start or in the model is never corrected. The fix is feedback: compare the reading with what the estimate predicts, and correct the estimate by a gain times the gap. With:

\bar{\mathbf{x}} is the estimate the model predicts, a vector of 2 entries: position, in m, and speed, in m/s;
z is the beacon’s reading, in m;
H is the measurement matrix of Section 6.2, the row (1, 0), which turns the state into the reading the sensor should give;
L is the observer’s gain, a vector of 2 entries: how far to correct the position and the speed per metre of gap; for the Kalman filter at step 1, 0.9263 and 0.4608;
\hat{\mathbf{x}} is the corrected estimate, a vector of 2 entries.

\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \bar{\mathbf{x}} + L\thinspace(z - H\bar{\mathbf{x}})
A model run alongside the real system and corrected this way is a state observer (G-2516)State observer: A model run alongside the real system and corrected by a gain times the gap between the measured and the predicted reading, so it rebuilds states no sensor measures for a controller to use; the Kalman filter is the observer with the best gain for the given noises. Explained in §6.6 The state a controller needs: the filter as an observer. (FBS §8.2). Figure 10 draws the observer as a loop with step 1’s numbers. Follow the beacon’s reading z, 0.82 m, and the model’s predicted reading, 0 m, to their gap; the gap times the gain L corrects the model’s estimate, which goes on to the controller and back into the model for the next step. No sensor reads the speed, yet the estimate that leaves the loop has one, 0.378 m/s.

Figure 10: The state observer as a loop, with step 1’s numbers. The model runs beside the robot: it carries the last estimate one step on with the state transition matrix F, giving the prediction of position and speed (0 m and 0 m/s at step 1), and the measurement matrix H turns the prediction into the predicted reading, 0 m. The beacon’s reading z, 0.82 m, minus the predicted reading is the gap, 0.82 m. The gain L, 0.9263 for position and 0.4608 for speed, times the gap corrects the prediction into the estimate: 0.760 m and 0.378 m/s. The estimate goes on to the controller, which commands the robot’s motors, and back into the model for the next step. The dashed frame is the observer
The size of the gain L is a trade-off: a large gain corrects errors fast but passes the sensor’s noise straight into the estimate (FBS §8.2). The Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in §2.5 The linear Gaussian system. is the observer whose gain, L = K, is the best compromise for the given noises (FBS §8.2). The controller then uses \hat{\mathbf{x}} in place of the true state (FBS §8.3), which is why the Kalman filter sits between the sensors and the controller in most robots. Every gain so far rested on two noise settings we were simply given: the slip’s variance Q and the beacon’s variance R.

7.1 R: measure the sensor

Explained in §4.1 Two estimates of one position. R is the variance of the beacon’s error, the jumps of Figure 1, so it can be measured: put the robot on a mark at a known position and record many readings (kalmanfilter.net). 7.2 Q: tune the motion noise
The slip’s variance Q is harder: it covers everything the motion model leaves out (slips, pushes, a wheel radius slightly wrong), so there is no datasheet for it, and it is set by tuning against data (Labbe ch.8). Each wrong choice fails in its own way. We simulated 2000 runs of 50 steps in which the true slip variance (G-2076)Variance of a random variable: How spread out a random variable’s values are: the expected squared distance from its expected value, \mathrm{Var}(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2]. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4. Variance of a random variable is 0.01, and ran three filters on them, each scored by its RMSE, the typical size of its error (Figure 11):

The readings alone give 0.399 m. Too small a Q trusts the commands and drifts like them; too large a Q follows every jump of the beacon (Labbe ch.4, “Incorrect process variance”; kalmanfilter.net, where a too-small Q causes a lag error). Only the ratio matters. Multiply the slip’s variance Q, the beacon’s variance R and the starting variance all by 10. The first predicted variance \bar{p}, the starting variance plus Q, is then 10 times larger too, and so is every later one. So every gain has a 10 on top and below:
K = \frac{10\thinspace\bar{p}}{10\thinspace\bar{p} + 10\thinspace R}
= \frac{\bar{p}}{\bar{p} + R}
The gains and the estimates are the same; the notebook finds a largest difference of exactly 0. What a filter designer really chooses is how much the model is trusted relative to the sensor.
How to tell when it is wrong without knowing the truth. Explained in §4.4 The updated estimate and its variance., the gaps between each reading and its prediction, are not: a well-tuned filter’s innovations look like random noise of the size its own innovation variance S (Section 6.3) predicts. Explained in §6.2 The model as matrices.The matrix that carries the state one step forward in a linear model, such as F = [[1, 1], [0, 1]] for position and speed with 1 s steps (position plus speed, speed unchanged).Measurement matrix H (G-2515)Measurement matrix H: The matrix that turns the state into the reading the sensor should give, such as H = [1, 0] for a sensor that sees position but not speed. Explained in §6.6 The state a controller needs: the filter as an observer.A model run alongside the real system and corrected by a gain times the gap between the measured and the predicted reading, so it rebuilds states no sensor measures for a controller to use; the Kalman filter is the observer with the best gain for the given noises.Particle filter (G-2492)Particle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in: Particle Filter, §4. The particle filter, step by stepA Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors.Belief (G-2433)Belief: The robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state. Explained in: Belief: What the Robot Knows, §4.2 The definitionThe robot’s probability for each possible state given all its commands and readings, \text{bel}(x_t) = p(x_t \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}); a short summary of the history that says how strongly the evidence points to each state.Gaussian distribution (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution isAnother name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements.Mode (G-1251)Mode: The value that appears most often in the data, so it sits under the highest peak of a histogram or a distribution curve; it gives a centre for data that are not numbers, and a belief with several peaks has several modes. Explained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §5. ModeThe value that appears most often in the data, so it sits under the highest peak of a histogram or a distribution curve; it gives a centre for data that are not numbers, and a belief with several peaks has several modes.Multimodal (G-1275)Multimodal: Having more than one mode, that is more than one peak (two peaks: bimodal), such as a robot’s belief peaking at three doors; it shows the data point to several separate values, so one mean or one best guess would hide them. Explained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §5. ModeHaving more than one mode, that is more than one peak (two peaks: bimodal), such as a robot’s belief peaking at three doors; it shows the data point to several separate values, so one mean or one best guess would hide them.Root mean squared error (RMSE) (G-1705)Root mean squared error (RMSE): The square root of the average squared error (MSE), so the error is back in the output’s units. Explained in: Regression Metrics: MAE, MSE, RMSE, R² and Adjusted R², §4. Root mean squared error (RMSE)The square root of the average squared error (MSE), so the error is back in the output’s units.Standard deviation (G-1871)Standard deviation: How far values typically lie from the mean; divide by n - 1 for a sample (pandas default) or by n for a population (NumPy default). Explained in: Understanding Your Data: Seven First Questions, §7.1 Count, mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximumHow far values typically lie from the mean; divide by n - 1 for a sample (pandas default) or by n for a population (NumPy default).Variance of a random variable (G-2076)Variance of a random variable: How spread out a random variable’s values are: the expected squared distance from its expected value, \mathrm{Var}(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2]. Explained in: Random Variables as Functions, Expected Value and Variance, §4. Variance of a random variableHow spread out a random variable’s values are: the expected squared distance from its expected value, \mathrm{Var}(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2].Bayes filter (G-2446)Bayes filter: The algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption. Explained in: The Bayes Filter: Predict, Then Update, §4.4 The algorithmThe algorithm that keeps a robot’s belief up to date one step at a time: a prediction step after each command and a correction step after each reading; it gives the exact belief without storing the history, under the Markov assumption.Derivative (G-595)Derivative: The slope of a function at a point: how fast the output changes as the input changes there. It is zero at the lowest point of a smooth curve, which is how training finds a minimum. Explained in: Derivatives of One Variable, §4.1 From secant to tangentThe slope of a function at a point: how fast the output changes as the input changes there. It is zero at the lowest point of a smooth curve, which is how training finds a minimum.Power rule (G-1540)Power rule: The rule for differentiating a power of x: bring the power down in front and lower the power by one, (x^n)' = n x^{n-1}. Explained in: PCA: Problem Formulation and Step-by-Step Solution, §3.3 The covariance matrixA square table with every feature’s variance on the diagonal and every pair’s covariance off it, so it sums up how the data spreads and which features move together; PCA takes its eigenvectors.Multivariate normal distribution (G-1283)Multivariate normal distribution: The bell-shaped (normal) distribution for several numbers at once, a vector; it is set by a mean vector (its centre) and a covariance matrix (its spread and how the numbers vary together).
