RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-018-.title: Extended Kalman Filter
RO/localization/02-bayes-filters/RO-018-.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Chi-square testsChi-square test: A test of whether categorical counts match expected counts (goodness of fit) or whether two categorical columns are related (independence). Explained in: Chi-square Tests, §2. The chi-square statistic; Derivatives of one variableExplained in: Derivatives of One Variable, §4. The derivative: shrinking the step to zero; Jacobian and matrix gradientsExplained in: The Jacobian and Gradients of Matrices, §4. The Jacobian; Kalman filterKalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system.
Compare with: Particle filterParticle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in: Particle Filter, §4. The particle filter, step by step.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Most robot sensors and motions are nonlinear functions of the state, and a nonlinear function bends a Gaussian out of shape. The extended Kalman filter replaces each nonlinear function by its tangent line at the current estimate and then runs the ordinary Kalman filter; checking its innovations (G-2511)Innovation: The gap between a reading and the reading the prediction expected, z - H\bar{x}; the update moves the estimate by the gain times this gap, and its size is used to check the filter. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §4.4 The updated estimate and its variance tells us whether its variance can be trusted.



Figure 1: Top: a radio beacon on the corridor wall at 6 m, 2 m to the side; the robot reads its straight-line distance to it. Bottom: that distance as a function of position, a curve with its lowest point at 2 m under the beacon; positions 4 m and 8 m both read 2.83 m
With the Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system, the corridor robot blends its drifting commands and its jumping readings, and its estimate misses by 0.17 m, against 0.27 m for the commands alone and 0.51 m for the readings. The blend works because the belief stays a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is, a bell-shaped curve set by a mean and a variance, and because the ceiling system reports the position itself plus noise, a linear function (G-2527)Linear function: A function y = ax + b: a fixed multiple of the input plus a constant, whose graph is a straight line; passing a normal variable through it gives another normal variable, which is why the Kalman filter is exact for linear models. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.3 A linear function keeps a Gaussian a Gaussian of the position, whose graph is a straight line. Now the robot has a new sensor in the same corridor: a radio beacon fixed on the wall at 6 m along the corridor, 2 m to the side, and it measures its straight-line distance to the beacon (Figure 1). Such range sensors are common: radio beacons, GPS ranges to satellites, a lidar’s range to a landmark.
The reading is no longer the position plus noise. Its graph against the position is a curve (Figure 1), so no fixed multiple of the position plus a constant gives it: the reading is a nonlinear function (G-2530)Nonlinear function: A function whose graph is not a straight line, so it is not a fixed multiple of the input plus a constant, such as the beacon distance h(x) = \sqrt{(6 - x)^2 + 4}; it bends a Gaussian into another shape, which is why the Kalman filter cannot use it as it is and the extended Kalman filter linearises it. Explained in §1. Overview. of the position:

far from the beacon, the distance changes almost one for one with position, nearly a straight line;
under the beacon, the distance stops changing: it bottoms out at 2 m;
past the beacon, it grows again, so 4 m and 8 m give the same reading.

The Kalman filter needs linear models (Section 2), so it cannot use this reading as it is. This Note adds the extended Kalman filter, which straightens the curve at the current estimate, and a check that tells when the result has gone wrong:

pushing a Gaussian through a nonlinear function, and the tangent-line fix (Section 3);
the extended Kalman filter, step by step on the corridor (Section 4);
its limits: one Gaussian can hold only one side (Section 4.4);
consistency, whether the filter’s variance matches its real errors: the innovation, its covariance, and the NIS and NEES tests (Section 5).

2. The Kalman filter in brief, and why nonlinear functions break it


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The Kalman filter is exact only because linear functions (G-2527)Linear function: A function y = ax + b: a fixed multiple of the input plus a constant, whose graph is a straight line; passing a normal variable through it gives another normal variable, which is why the Kalman filter is exact for linear models. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.3 A linear function keeps a Gaussian a Gaussian, whose graphs are straight lines, keep a Gaussian a Gaussian. A nonlinear function, such as the beacon distance, does not.


To see why the nonlinear beacon distance of Figure 1 breaks it, recall what the Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system does. The Kalman filter keeps the belief as a mean \hat{x} and a variance p and runs two steps per round:

predict: move the mean by the command, 0.5 m, and add the process noise Q, the variance of each step’s wheel slip, 0.01 m², to the variance;
update: blend in the reading z with the Kalman gain (G-2508)Kalman gain K: The weight the update gives to the reading, K = \bar{p}/(\bar{p} + R) in one dimension: the weight that makes the updated variance smallest, near 1 when the prediction is vague and near 0 when the reading is. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §4.3 The best weight: the Kalman gain, which gives the reading the weight that makes the new variance smallest.

Both steps rest on one fact: a linear function keeps a Gaussian a GaussianLinear function: A function y = ax + b: a fixed multiple of the input plus a constant, whose graph is a straight line; passing a normal variable through it gives another normal variable, which is why the Kalman filter is exact for linear models. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.3 A linear function keeps a Gaussian a Gaussian, with the variance multiplied by the slope squared. The update also assumed the reading was a linear function of the position: a fixed number H times the position, plus the sensor’s noise. Our new reading is the straight-line distance to the beacon, 6 m along the corridor and 2 m to the side. With:

x is the robot’s position along the corridor, in m;
h(x) is the distance from position x to the beacon, the reading before the sensor’s noise, in m.

By Pythagoras, from the gap along the corridor and the 2 m across:
h(x) = \sqrt{(6 - x)^2 + 2^2}
For example, at 0.5 m:
h(0.5) = \sqrt{5.5^2 + 4}
= \sqrt{34.25} = 5.852 \text{ m}
No single number H turns position into this reading everywhere, so the five lines of the Kalman filter cannot be used as they are. The first guess is that of the Kalman filter: the estimate \hat{x} is 0 m, with variance p of 1 m². The beacon’s distance readings have a standard deviation of 0.1 m, so the measurement noise (G-2510)Measurement noise R: The random error of a sensor reading, given as its variance or covariance R; it sets how much the filter trusts each reading and is taken from the datasheet or measured in a calibration. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §4.1 Two estimates of one position is R = 0.01 m². Before the filter can use these readings, we need to know what the beacon distance does to a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is belief, a bell-shaped curve over positions.
3. Pushing a Gaussian through a nonlinear function


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A nonlinear function (G-2530)Nonlinear function: A function whose graph is not a straight line, so it is not a fixed multiple of the input plus a constant, such as the beacon distance h(x) = \sqrt{(6 - x)^2 + 4}; it bends a Gaussian into another shape, which is why the Kalman filter cannot use it as it is and the extended Kalman filter linearises it. Explained in §1. Overview., one whose graph is a curve, bends a Gaussian into a lopsided shape. Near a point, its graph looks like its tangent line, and a line keeps a Gaussian a Gaussian; that approximation is good when the Gaussian is narrow compared with the bend.


3.1 What a nonlinear function does to a Gaussian
The worst place is near the beacon, where the distance bottoms out at 2 m (Figure 1). Suppose the robot’s position there is a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is, a bell-shaped curve, with mean 5.5 m and standard deviation (sd) 0.5 m. What does the predicted reading look like? We cannot use a formula yet, so we use the Monte CarloExplained in: Particle Filter, §3.2 Samples stand for a distribution: the Monte Carlo idea way: draw 200,000 positions from the Gaussian, push each through the beacon distance h, and look at the results (notebook).
Figure 2 shows the result in its frame with input mean 5.5 m, sd 0.5 m. The readings pile up against 2 m, the smallest possible distance, with a long tail upwards: the Gaussian has become lopsided. Its lopsidedness, the skewness (G-1817)Skewness: A number for how lopsided a distribution is: 0 symmetric, positive right tail, negative left tail. Explained in: Univariate Analysis: Exploring One Column at a Time, §10. Skewness, is 1.89, where a Gaussian has 0. A Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system has no way to store that shape: it keeps only a mean and a variance. To keep the belief Gaussian, the filter needs a straight line in place of the curve.

Figure 2: A Gaussian of positions (top) pushed through the beacon curve (middle, black) gives the orange histogram of readings (right); the purple Gaussian is what the tangent line at the mean (purple dashed) predicts. The input’s mean steps from 1 m through 2.5 m and 4 m to 5.5 m, and then the input widens. Far from the beacon (mean 1 m) the two agree; near it (mean 5.5 m) the true readings are lopsided against 2 m, and with a wide input (sd 1.5 m) the tangent-line Gaussian is far too narrow
3.2 The tangent line: linearisation
Zoom in on any smooth curve and it looks straight. Near a point, the curve is close to its tangent line, the straight line that touches the curve there with the curve’s slope. Figure 3 zooms in on the beacon curve at two places at once, the window shrinking from 8 m to 0.1 m wide. Watch the gap between the curve and its tangent line: at 1 m it is already too small to see when the window is 2 m wide, while at 6 m, under the beacon, where the curve bends most, it is still visible at 0.5 m wide. So the tangent line can stand in for the curve close to where it touches, and the more the curve bends, the closer that has to be.

Figure 3: The beacon distance h(x) (black) and its tangent line (purple dashed) at x = 1 m (left, slope −0.928) and at x = 6 m under the beacon (right, slope 0), seen through a window that shrinks from 8 m through 2 m and 0.5 m to 0.1 m wide, with both axes on the same scale. Each panel gives the largest gap between curve and line inside the window, as a share of the window’s height: at 1 m it falls from 7.1% to 0.77%, 0.17% and 0.032%; at 6 m from 31% to 12%, 3.1% and 0.62%. The last frame, 0.1 m wide: in both panels the curve cannot be told from its tangent line
Replacing a function near a point by its tangent line is linearisation (G-1099)Linearisation: Replacing a function near a point by its tangent line (its first-order Taylor polynomial), so that a curve can be handled as a straight line close to that point, where straight-line methods apply. Explained in: Derivatives of One Variable, §6.3 Degree 1: the tangent line. In Figure 2 the tangent line is the purple dashed line, drawn at the input’s mean. With:

\mu is the position where the line touches the curve, in m (1 m in the example below);
h(\mu) is the beacon distance there, in m;
h'(\mu) is the derivative (G-595)Derivative: The slope of a function at a point: how fast the output changes as the input changes there. It is zero at the lowest point of a smooth curve, which is how training finds a minimum. Explained in: Derivatives of One Variable, §4.1 From secant to tangent of h at \mu, the slope of the curve there, in metres of distance per metre of position;
x is a position near \mu, in m.

h(x) \approx h(\mu) + h'(\mu)\thinspace(x - \mu)
The beacon distance is the square root of an inside part, so the chain rule (G-371)Chain rule: To differentiate a function of a function, multiply the outer derivative by the inner derivative. Explained in: The Derivative of the Sigmoid Function, §2. Two rules we need gives its slope: the slope of the square root times the slope of the inside part. With:

s(x) is the part under the square root, in m², 29 m² at 1 m;
dh/ds is the slope of h against s, in m per m², 0.0928 at 1 m;
ds/dx is the slope of s against x, in m² per m, −10 at 1 m.

At 1 m first, each line followed by the same step at any position x:
s(1) = (6 - 1)^2 + 4 = 29
s(x) = (6 - x)^2 + 4
h(1) = \sqrt{29} = 5.3852
h(x) = \sqrt{s(x)}
\frac{dh}{ds} = \frac{1}{2 \times 5.3852} = 0.0928
\frac{dh}{ds} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{s}} = \frac{1}{2h(x)}
\frac{ds}{dx} = -2 \times (6 - 1) = -10
\frac{ds}{dx} = -2\thinspace(6 - x)
h'(1) = 0.0928 \times (-10) = -0.928
h'(x) = \frac{1}{2h(x)} \times (-2)\thinspace(6 - x)
= \frac{-(6 - x)}{h(x)}
Driving 1 m towards the beacon from 1 m cuts the distance by about 0.93 m.
The tangent line is a straight line, and a straight line keeps a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is a Gaussian. So the predicted reading is a Gaussian whose mean is h(\mu) and whose standard deviation (sd) is the input’s sd times the size of the slope, where |h'(\mu)| is the slope without its sign:
\text{mean} \approx h(\mu)
\text{sd} \approx |h'(\mu)| \times \text{sd of } x
Carrying a mean and a standard deviation through a function this way, with its value and slope at the mean, is first-order uncertainty propagation (G-2519)First-order uncertainty propagation: Carrying a mean and a standard deviation through a function by its value and slope at the mean: mean out ≈ h(\mu), standard deviation out ≈ slope × standard deviation in (with a Jacobian, J P J^{\mathsf T}); accurate when the function is nearly straight across the standard deviation. Explained in §3.2 The tangent line: linearisation. (Labbe ch.9; Becker ch.13).
3.3 When the tangent line fails
The tangent line describes the curve well only near the point where it touches. The wider the Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is, and the more the curve bends inside it, the worse the approximation (Labbe ch.9; Freiburg EKF slides). Three of the frames of Figure 2, with the notebook’s numbers:

























Input GaussianTrue readings: mean, sdTangent line: mean, sdmean 1.0, sd 0.5 (curve nearly straight)5.39, 0.465.39, 0.46mean 5.5, sd 0.5 (near the bend)2.12, 0.142.06, 0.12mean 5.5, sd 1.5 (near the bend, wide)2.48, 0.572.06, 0.36
Near the bend, the tangent-line Gaussian puts its mean too low and is too narrow, so a filter using it would be too sure of itself. The tangent-line Gaussian even gives probability to readings below 2 m, which no position can produce. Both failures grow with the width of the input: with standard deviation 1.5 m, the tangent line misses the true standard deviation by more than a third.
3.4 Several variables: the Jacobian
The beacon distance has one input, the position, so one slope is enough. A robot’s pose (G-2280)Pose: Where a robot is and which way it faces: on a floor, its position (x, y) and heading \theta, such as (2 m, 1 m, 30°); needed because a robot at one spot drives off differently depending on its heading. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.2 Why position is not enough: the heading, where it is and which way it faces, has several numbers: its position x and y on the floor, in m, and its heading \theta, in radians. A function of several numbers has a slope for each pair of output and input. The table of all these slopes is the Jacobian (G-980)Jacobian: The table (matrix) of all first partial derivatives of a function with several inputs and outputs, one row per output and one column per input, J_{ij} = \partial f_i/\partial x_j; it shows how every output changes with every input near a point. Explained in: The Jacobian and Gradients of Matrices, §4.2 The formula: every partial derivative in one grid, and it plays the part of the slope: near a point, the function behaves like multiplying by that matrix.
For motion the Jacobian is called G, the motion Jacobian (G-2522)Motion Jacobian G: The table of slopes of the motion model at the last estimate, one row per new state variable and one column per old one; the EKF uses it to carry the covariance forward as G P G^{\mathsf T} + Q. Explained in §3.4 Several variables: the Jacobian., and it carries the covariance forward as the state transition matrix F does in the Kalman filter’s matrix formExplained in: Kalman Filter, §6.3 The five lines in matrix form. With:

P is the estimate’s covariance matrix, one row and one column per state variable: the variances on the diagonal and the covariances off it (for the corridor’s one number, the variance p);
G is the motion Jacobian, one row per new state variable and one column per old one (for the corridor, the single number 1);
G^{\mathsf T} is its transpose, G flipped over its diagonal.

The carried covariance is:
G P G^{\mathsf T}
With the tangent line for one number and the Jacobian for several, the Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system can now run on nonlinear models.
4. The extended Kalman filter


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The EKF predicts and updates with the nonlinear functions themselves, and uses their slopes at the current estimate wherever the Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system used its state transition matrix F and measurement matrix H.


4.1 The algorithm
The extended Kalman filter (EKF) (G-2520)Extended Kalman filter (EKF): The Kalman filter for nonlinear motion and sensor models: it moves the mean through the nonlinear functions and uses their Jacobians at the latest estimate in place of F and H, so it can track unimodal beliefs through nonlinear models. Explained in §4.1 The algorithm. uses that tangent line to run the Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system, which keeps a Gaussian belief as a mean and a covariance, on a nonlinear model such as the beacon distance: it linearises the nonlinear models at the latest estimate, every step (Freiburg EKF slides; Thrun §3.3; Labbe ch.11). The Kalman filter column of the table below uses the symbols listed in its matrix formExplained in: Kalman Filter, §6.3 The five lines in matrix form; bold letters are vectors. The EKF adds:

g is the motion model, the function that gives the predicted state from the command u and the last estimate \hat{\mathbf{x}} (on the corridor, the position plus 0.5 m);
G is the Jacobian (G-980)Jacobian: The table (matrix) of all first partial derivatives of a function with several inputs and outputs, one row per output and one column per input, J_{ij} = \partial f_i/\partial x_j; it shows how every output changes with every input near a point. Explained in: The Jacobian and Gradients of Matrices, §4.2 The formula: every partial derivative in one grid of g at the last estimate \hat{\mathbf{x}}, a matrix with one row per new state variable and one column per old one (on the corridor, the single number 1);
h is the sensor model, the function that gives the reading expected from a state (on the corridor, the beacon distance of Section 2);
H is the Jacobian of h at the prediction \bar{\mathbf{x}}, the measurement Jacobian (G-2521)Measurement Jacobian H: The slopes of the sensor model at the predicted state, one row per reading and one column per state variable; the EKF uses it to compute the innovation covariance and the gain, and its size says how much a reading tells about the state. Explained in §4.1 The algorithm., with one row per reading and one column per state variable (on the corridor, one number, −0.940 at step 1).

Each is linearised where the filter’s best guess is at the moment it is used. The lines:

4.2 Step 1 by hand
On the corridor every symbol is one number. At step 1, with the step number as a subscript:

\bar x_1 is the predicted position, in m;
\bar p_1 is its variance, in m²;
h(\bar x_1) is the reading the prediction expects, the beacon distance at \bar x_1, in m;
H is the measurement Jacobian, the slope of the beacon distance at \bar x_1, in metres of distance per metre of position;
z_1 is the beacon’s reading, 5.61 m;
S is the innovation variance, the variance the filter expects of the innovation, in m²;
K is the Kalman gain, which turns the innovation into a correction of the position, in metres of position per metre of distance;
\hat x_1 is the updated estimate, in m;
p_1 is its variance, in m².

Predict, as in the Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system, from the first guess, 0 m with variance 1 m², with the command 0.5 m and the slip’s variance Q, 0.01 m²:
\bar x_1 = 0 + 0.5 = 0.5 \text{ m}
\bar p_1 = 1 + 0.01 = 1.01 \text{ m}^2
Linearise the sensor at the prediction. The expected reading and the slope, kept to four digits because the variance below subtracts two nearly equal numbers:
h(0.5) = 5.852
H = -5.5 / 5.852 = -0.9398
Innovation. The innovation (G-2511)Innovation: The gap between a reading and the reading the prediction expected, z - H\bar{x}; the update moves the estimate by the gain times this gap, and its size is used to check the filter. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §4.4 The updated estimate and its variance is the gap between the reading and the reading the prediction expected. The reading is z_1 = 5.61 m:
z_1 - h(\bar x_1) = 5.61 - 5.852 = -0.242
The robot is 0.24 m closer to the beacon than predicted.
Gain. First the innovation variance, with the sensor’s variance R, 0.01 m²:
S = 0.9398^2 \times 1.01 + 0.01
= 0.892 + 0.01 = 0.902
then
K = 1.01 \times (-0.9398) / 0.902
= -1.0523
The gain is negative because the slope is: a shorter distance than expected means the robot is further along, so a negative innovation must move the estimate forward. Its size above 1 is expected too: it converts metres of distance into metres of position, and here the distance changes a little less than one for one.
Update:
\hat x_1 = 0.5 + (-1.0523)(-0.242)
= 0.5 + 0.255 = 0.755 \text{ m}
p_1 = (1 - (-1.0523)(-0.9398)) \times 1.01
= 0.01105 \times 1.01 = 0.0112 \text{ m}^2
The true position is 0.73 m. A check. After a reading this good, the position should be known about as well as the sensor allows, which is the sensor’s standard deviation divided by the slope:
\text{sd} = 0.1 / 0.94 = 0.106 \text{ m}
\text{sd}^2 = 0.106^2 = 0.0112 \text{ m}^2
matching p_1. The slope 0.94 set that precision, and the slope changes as the robot drives towards the beacon.

4.4 The limits of the EKF
One Gaussian holds one side. Positions 4 m and 8 m give the same reading, 2.83 m (Figure 1); so do 1 m and 11 m. Figure 5 feeds the same 16 readings, one step per frame, to a second EKF that starts at 11 m, on the far side of the beacon. Every reading fits the mirror position as well as the true one, so the filter follows the mirror path, confident and wrong: at step 1 it says 11.24 m when the robot is at 0.73 m, 10.5 m off, with only about 10 cm of uncertainty. Watch it move left while the robot moves right: only when the robot passes the beacon, where the mirror and the true path meet, does it come right (7.96 m against the true 7.86 m at step 16, notebook).

The last frame shows the whole run, both filters ending near the truth
A Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is, one bell-shaped curve, is unimodal (G-2528)Unimodal: Having a single mode (one peak); a unimodal belief can be held by one Gaussian, so the Kalman filter needs only its mean and variance. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §1. Overview, with a single mode (peak), so it cannot say “here or at the mirror place”; that belief has two modes, it is multimodal (G-1275)Multimodal: Having more than one mode, that is more than one peak (two peaks: bimodal), such as a robot’s belief peaking at three doors; it shows the data point to several separate values, so one mean or one best guess would hide them. Explained in: Measures of Central Tendency, §5. Mode, and a particle filter (G-2492)Particle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in: Particle Filter, §4. The particle filter, step by step, which stores the belief as a cloud of samples, can keep both until the readings decide (Labbe ch.12).
The other limits (Freiburg EKF slides; Labbe ch.11):

Strongly nonlinear models. Where the Gaussian is wide compared with the bend (Section 3.3), the linearised covariance is wrong, usually too small, and the filter becomes overconfident.
Jacobians must exist. A model with steps, like the door map of the particle filter (G-2492)Particle filter: A Bayes filter that stores the belief as a set of weighted samples (particles) and runs each round as move, weigh, resample; it can hold beliefs of any shape, such as a belief with three modes, one at each of three doors. Explained in: Particle Filter, §4. The particle filter, step by step (1.0 m beside wall, 1.5 m at a door), has slope 0 almost everywhere and no slope at the edges, so the EKF cannot use it.
Jacobians must be derived. Deriving them by hand is error-prone for big models; symbolic tools such as SymPy can do it (Labbe ch.11).

The unscented Kalman filter (G-2506)Kalman filter: The Bayes filter for a linear Gaussian system: it keeps the belief as a mean and a (co)variance and updates them with a predict step and an update step, blending a model’s prediction with a sensor reading so the result is as certain as possible. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §2.5 The linear Gaussian system pushes a few chosen sample points through the nonlinear function instead of a tangent line, and the particle filter pushes many; both avoid Jacobians at a higher cost (Labbe ch.9; Freiburg EKF slides). Each of these limits can leave the EKF wrong while its variance says it is sure, so it needs a check.
5. Consistency: is the filter telling the truth about itself?


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A filter is consistent when its real errors are as big as the variance it reports with its estimate: on average, error squared divided by variance comes to the number of variables. The innovations (G-2511)Innovation: The gap between a reading and the reading the prediction expected, z - H\bar{x}; the update moves the estimate by the gain times this gap, and its size is used to check the filter. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §4.4 The updated estimate and its variance allow the check without knowing the truth.


5.1 Why we need a check
To tell when the result has gone wrong, the filter’s own variance is no help. The EKF’s variance comes from tangent lines and from the noise variances we chose, the slip’s Q and the sensor’s R, 0.01 m² each, so it can be wrong without any error message: the mirror filter of Figure 5 reported about 10 cm of uncertainty while 10 m off. A controller or a planner that trusts a variance needs to know whether that variance matches the real errors. A filter whose errors match its own variance is consistent (G-2524)Consistent filter: A filter whose real errors are as large as its own reported covariance says, on average; only then can its uncertainty be trusted by a controller or planner. Explained in §5.1 Why we need a check. (Chen et al. 2018; Labbe ch.8). On a real robot the true errors are unknown, but the innovations (G-2511)Innovation: The gap between a reading and the reading the prediction expected, z - H\bar{x}; the update moves the estimate by the gain times this gap, and its size is used to check the filter. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §4.4 The updated estimate and its variance, the gaps between each reading and the reading the filter predicted, are not.
5.2 The innovation and its covariance
Every step, before it sees the reading, the filter predicts it. The filter also predicts how far off the reading will be. At step 1:

\bar{x} is the predicted position, 0.5 m;
h(\bar{x}) is the reading the filter predicts, the beacon distance at \bar{x}, 5.852 m;
z is the reading, 5.61 m;
H is the measurement Jacobian, the slope of the beacon distance at \bar{x}, −0.940;
\bar{P} is the prediction’s covariance matrix, here one number, the variance 1.01 m²;
H^{\mathsf T} is the transpose of H, H flipped over its diagonal; for one number, H itself;
R is the sensor’s variance, 0.01 m²;
S is the innovation covariance, in m².

The innovation (G-2511)Innovation: The gap between a reading and the reading the prediction expected, z - H\bar{x}; the update moves the estimate by the gain times this gap, and its size is used to check the filter. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §4.4 The updated estimate and its variance z - h(\bar{x}) has two independent sources of error, the prediction’s and the sensor’s. The prediction’s error reaches the reading through the slope H, so its variance is multiplied by H^2 (variance times slope squaredExplained in: Kalman Filter, §2.3 A linear function keeps a Gaussian a Gaussian); then the two independent variances addExplained in: Kalman Filter, §2.4 Adding independent errors adds variances:
S = H\bar{P}H^{\mathsf T} + R
This S is the innovation covariance (G-2523)Innovation covariance S: The variance the filter expects of its next innovation, S = H\bar{P}H^{\mathsf T} + R: prediction uncertainty seen through the sensor plus sensor noise; it scales the gain and is the yardstick for the NIS test. Explained in §5.2 The innovation and its covariance.: the variance the filter expects of its innovation (Labbe ch.8; Chen et al. 2018). At step 1, the innovation was −0.242 m with S = 0.902 m², a predicted standard deviation of:
\sqrt{S} = \sqrt{0.902} = 0.95 \text{ m}
So an innovation of 0.24 m was well within what the filter expected. Unlike the true error, the innovation is known on a real robot at every step, so it is the everyday test.
5.3 NIS: the innovation test, no truth needed
To turn each innovation (G-2511)Innovation: The gap between a reading and the reading the prediction expected, z - H\bar{x}; the update moves the estimate by the gain times this gap, and its size is used to check the filter. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §4.4 The updated estimate and its variance into one test number, divide its square by its predicted variance. At step 1:

y is the innovation, the reading minus the reading the filter predicted, −0.242 m;
S is its predicted variance, the innovation covariance, 0.902 m²;
\varepsilon_z is the test number, with no unit.

\varepsilon_z = y^2 / S
For several readings at once, y is a vector with one entry per reading, S is a matrix with one row and one column per reading, y^{\mathsf T} is y written as a row, and dividing by S becomes multiplying by its inverseExplained in: Multiple Linear Regression: The Normal Equation, §6. The normal equation S^{-1}:
\varepsilon_z = y^{\mathsf T} S^{-1} y
The number \varepsilon_z is the normalised innovation squared (NIS) (G-2526)NIS (normalised innovation squared): The squared innovation divided by its predicted covariance, y^{\mathsf T}S^{-1}y; for a consistent filter it follows chi-square with m degrees of freedom (one per reading) and averages m, so it tests consistency from readings alone, even on the robot. Explained in §5.3 NIS: the innovation test, no truth needed.. For step 1:
\varepsilon_z = 0.242^2 / 0.902 = 0.065
Why it should average 1. If the filter is consistent (G-2524)Consistent filter: A filter whose real errors are as large as its own reported covariance says, on average; only then can its uncertainty be trusted by a controller or planner. Explained in §5.1 Why we need a check., y follows a Gaussian (G-827)Gaussian distribution: Another name for the normal distribution: the symmetric, bell-shaped continuous distribution set by its mean and standard deviation, used to model many measurements. Explained in: The Normal Distribution, §2. What the normal distribution is, a bell-shaped curve, with mean 0 and variance S, so y / \sqrt{S} is a standard normal variable (mean 0, variance 1) and its square averages 1. A squared standard normal variable follows the chi-square distribution (G-378)Chi-square distribution: The shape the chi-square statistic \chi^2 follows when the null hypothesis H_0 is true: never negative, skewed to the right, with one parameter, the degrees of freedom. Explained in: Chi-square Tests, §3.1 Built from squared normal draws with 1 degree of freedom; with m readings at once, the NIS follows chi-square with m degrees of freedom and averages m (Chen et al. 2018). For one reading, 95 percent of a consistent filter’s NIS values lie below 3.84 (notebook), and an innovation two standard deviations out gives an NIS of 4.
On one run. Figure 6 plots 60 innovations with the band \pm 2\sqrt{S} the filter predicts. With the right sensor variance R, 0.01 m², 2 percent fall outside. A filter that assumes the sensor is twice as precise (R = 0.0025, a standard deviation of 0.05 m) predicts a narrower band, about ±0.24 m instead of ±0.32 m, and 13 percent fall outside: its innovations are bigger than its S allows (Labbe ch.8).

5.4 NEES: the error test, when the truth is known
In a simulation, or with a much better reference sensor, the true state is known and we can test the error itself. Divide the squared error by the filter’s variance. At step 1:

x is the true position, 0.73 m;
\hat{x} is the filter’s estimate, 0.755 m;
p is the filter’s variance, 0.0112 m²;
\varepsilon_x is the test number, with no unit.

\varepsilon_x = (x - \hat{x})^2 / p
For a state of n numbers, the error \tilde{\mathbf{x}}, the true state minus the estimate, is a vector of n entries, P is the filter’s covariance matrix, n rows by n columns, and dividing by P becomes multiplying by its inverse P^{-1}:
\varepsilon_x = \tilde{\mathbf{x}}^{\mathsf T} P^{-1} \tilde{\mathbf{x}}
The number \varepsilon_x is the normalised estimation error squared (NEES) (G-2525)NEES (normalised estimation error squared): The squared estimation error divided by the filter’s variance, \tilde{x}^{\mathsf T}P^{-1}\tilde{x}; for a consistent filter it follows chi-square with n degrees of freedom and averages n, so its average over simulated runs tests consistency when the truth is known. Explained in §5.4 NEES: the error test, when the truth is known. (Labbe ch.8; Chen et al. 2018). By the same argument it follows chi-square with n degrees of freedom and averages n, here 1. For step 1:
\varepsilon_x = (0.73 - 0.755)^2 / 0.0112
= 0.056
One value says little; the test averages many. We simulated 500 runs of 16 steps, ran three EKFs on each, set with different slip variances Q and sensor variances R, and averaged NEES and NIS at each step (Figure 7). If the filter is consistent (G-2524)Consistent filter: A filter whose real errors are as large as its own reported covariance says, on average; only then can its uncertainty be trusted by a controller or planner. 5.5 Reading the results

Both near 1: the filter’s variances match its real errors; it can be trusted.
Both well above 1: the filter is overconfident. Increase the noise it assumes; which one is told by tuning experiments such as those of choosing Q and RExplained in: Kalman Filter, §7.2 Q: tune the motion noise.
NEES rising over time: errors pile up faster than the filter allows, the mark of too small a slip variance Q: the filter trusts its motion model and stops listening to readings.
Values well below 1: the filter is too timid; its noises are too large, and it wastes information.

The innovations (G-2511)Innovation: The gap between a reading and the reading the prediction expected, z - H\bar{x}; the update moves the estimate by the gain times this gap, and its size is used to check the filter. Explained in: Kalman Filter, §4.4 The updated estimate and its variance should also look like random noise: centred on zero and with no slow trend. A trend means the model misses something, such as a bias or too little process noise (Labbe ch.8). NEES needs the truth, so it is a design-time test in simulation; NIS needs only the readings, so it can also run on the robot.

8. Key terms
Terms taught in this Note come first; linked terms are recaps, taught in the Note the link opens.













































































































TermMeaningNonlinear function (G-2530)Nonlinear function: A function whose graph is not a straight line, so it is not a fixed multiple of the input plus a constant, such as the beacon distance h(x) = \sqrt{(6 - x)^2 + 4}; it bends a Gaussian into another shape, which is why the Kalman filter cannot use it as it is and the extended Kalman filter linearises it. Explained in §1. RO/navigation/04-graph-search-and-config.title: Graphs and Uninformed Search
RO/navigation/04-graph-search-and-config.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: State, controls and measurementsExplained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §4. The state: what the robot keeps track of; Maps and landmarksMap: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §2.1 What a map is for.
Leads to: Dijkstra’s algorithmDijkstra’s algorithm: A search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals). Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §3.2 The algorithm: settle the nearest, update its neighbours; Priority queue and binary heapBinary heap: A tree filled level by level in which every entry is at most the entries below it, stored in a plain list; the smallest entry sits at the top and insert and remove each walk one path of about \log_2 N levels, so it makes a fast priority queue. Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §5.2 The binary heap; Iterative deepening and IDA*IDA (iterative-deepening A):** Iterative deepening with the limit on f = g + h instead of on moves, each new limit being the smallest f that passed the last; it returns the shortest route with an admissible heuristic while storing only the current route. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §7. Saving memory: iterative deepening and IDA; Forward state-space searchExplained in: Symbolic Task Planning: STRIPS and PDDL, §5.1 The state graph, built while searching; Symbolic task planningSymbolic task planning: Choosing a sequence of actions that reaches a goal, from a description of the world in true-or-false facts such as “the cup is on the table”; it decides the order of steps (go to the table, pick up, go to the door, put down) that a route search alone cannot. Explained in: Symbolic Task Planning: STRIPS and PDDL, §2.1 Facts and states; Basic motion planning problemBasic motion planning problem (piano mover’s problem): Given a robot, its obstacles, a start configuration and a goal configuration, find a continuous path in C-space between them through configurations where the robot touches no obstacle, or report that none exists; it states every collision-free motion task as one search through C-space. Explained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §6. The basic motion planning problem.
Compare with: Iterative deepening and IDA*IDA (iterative-deepening A):** Iterative deepening with the limit on f = g + h instead of on moves, each new limit being the smallest f that passed the last; it returns the shortest route with an admissible heuristic while storing only the current route. Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §7. Saving memory: iterative deepening and IDA; Connected components of free spaceConnected component (of free space): A piece of free space within which the robot can move from any configuration to any other without touching an obstacle; a path between two configurations exists only if both lie in the same component. Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §4.1 One piece or several.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A map says where the furniture is, not which way to go. Treating the free cells as places joined by moves turns the map into a graph, and searching the graph finds a route: breadth-first search finds the fewest moves to the door, 8 moves of 0.5 m.


The robot can now hold its room as a map (G-2331)Map: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §2.1 What a map is for, its list of what is where. In particular it has an occupancy grid (G-2340)Occupancy grid: A grid map that stores in each cell a number between 0 and 1, such as the probability that the cell is occupied, instead of a hard 0 or 1; the standard grid map of robotics, since sensors are never sure. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §5.2 Bitmaps and occupancy grids, the room cut into 0.5 m cells with a number in each cell for how much of it furniture covers. What still breaks: the robot at (2 m, 1 m), facing 30°, has to get out of the door, and nothing tells it which way to drive.
Figure 1 plays the first idea: drive straight ahead. Watch the robot leave its spot along its heading: after 1.35 m its centre meets the table’s edge.
The last frame shows the map as the robot holds it, 112 cells of which 36 are blocked, because furniture or a pole covers some part of them. The robot stands on the corner of the start cell S, which runs from 2.0 to 2.5 m along x and 1.0 to 1.5 m along y. The goal cell G sits just under the door, from 3.5 to 4.0 m along x and 3.5 to 4.0 m along y.

Figure 1: The robot at (2 m, 1 m) facing 30 degrees, drawn 1.6 times its real size so that it shows, drives straight ahead; its dashed orange path ends at a red cross where its centre meets the table’s edge after 1.35 m. The last frame shows the room’s 0.5 m grid: 36 grey blocked cells, 76 white free cells, the start cell S with the robot on its corner and the goal cell G under the door, and asks which free cells, in which order, lead from S to G
So the map holds the answer, 76 free cells, but not as a route: which free cells, in which order, take the robot from S to G? We turn the map into something a program can search, and search it; every number below is computed in the notebook RO-032-graphs-and-uninformed-search.ipynb:

the free cells as a graph of vertices and moves (Section 2);
the tree of every path from the start, and why listing it is wasteful (Section 3);
one search loop with a frontier and a visited list (Section 4), run in two orders: breadth-first (Section 5) and depth-first (Section 6);
how the work grows with the size of the problem (Section 7), and why exact planning is hard in general (Section 8);
building the graph in advance or on demand (Section 9), and what a search state must hold (Section 10).

2. The map as a graph


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

To choose a route, the robot first needs to know which cell it can step to from which. A graph says exactly that: the free cells are its vertices and the moves between neighbouring cells are its edges.


2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edges
To pick a route to the door, the robot first needs to know which cell it can step to from which. A metro map gives that kind of knowledge: stations are dots, and a line joins two dots when a train runs directly between them. The map leaves out everything else, the streets and the distances, because the question “can I get from here to there?” needs only the dots and the lines.
We do the same with the room. Each free cell becomes a dot, and two dots are joined when the robot can move directly between the cells: when the cells share a side, so one 0.5 m move left, down, up or right takes the robot across.
Figure 2 shows the result for our room. Look at the start cell S: four orange lines leave it, one for each move, because all four cells beside it are free.
Make interactive
Figure 2: The room’s 0.5 m grid with a blue dot at the centre of each of the 76 free cells and a blue line between every two free cells that share a side, 114 lines in all; the four lines from the start cell S are orange; the grey blocked cells have no dot
Dots joined by lines are a graph (G-2540)Graph: A set of vertices (points) joined by edges (lines), such as the room’s 76 free cells joined by 114 moves; it keeps only which places connect directly, so one search method works for maps, puzzles and any problem of states and moves. Explained in §2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edges., the standard model of places and the direct steps between them (LaValle §2.1). Its parts have names:

a vertex (G-2541)Vertex (graph): One point of a graph, such as one free cell of the room or one waypoint; the places a search moves between. Explained in §2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edges. is one dot, here one free cell, such as the start cell S;
an edge (G-2542)Edge (graph): A link between two vertices of a graph, such as one 0.5 m move between two free cells that share a side; it says the search can go directly from one vertex to the other. Explained in §2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edges. is one line, here one move between two free cells that share a side;
a path (G-2543)Path (graph): A chain of edges in which each edge starts where the last one ended, such as S, the cell above S and the cell above that; a route the robot can follow, and what a search returns. Explained in §2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edges. is a chain of edges, each starting where the last one ended, such as S, then the cell above S, then the cell above that: a path of 2 edges, 1.0 m.

Joining each cell to the cells that share a side with it, at most four, gives a 4-connected grid (G-2544)4-connected grid: A grid made into a graph by joining each cell to the up to four cells that share a side with it (left, down, up, right); the simplest graph of a grid map, with every move the same length. Explained in §2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edges. (CMU 16-350, heuristics). Our room’s graph has 76 vertices and 114 edges (notebook).
Formally, a graph is written as a pair of sets:

G is the graph;
V is its set of vertices, here the 76 free cells;
E is its set of edges, here the 114 pairs of free cells that share a side;
a set is a collection with no repeats, and curly brackets list its members: \lbrace1, 2, 3\rbrace is the set of the numbers 1, 2 and 3.

G = (V, E)
The graph says which moves exist, but not which ones to take; finding those is the search of Section 3 onwards.
2.2 Any problem of states and moves is a graph
The graph of Figure 2 came from a map, but the idea does not need a map. Anything that is in one situation at a time, and changes situation by a move, fits the same picture: each situation is a vertex, each move an edge (CS188 §1.2).

Our robot: the situation is its cell; a move is a 0.5 m step. The graph has 76 vertices.
A Rubik’s cube: the situation is the arrangement of the coloured squares; a move is one turn of a face. Each arrangement has 18 possible turns, so 18 edges leave every vertex (Korf 1997).

The situation a problem can be in is its state (G-2314)State x_t: The quantities a robot keeps track of at time t because they decide what happens next, such as its pose, its speeds and moving things around it; it is what localization and filtering estimate. Explained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §4.1 State: from one number to many, the quantities that decide what happens next. All the states together, with the moves between them, form the state space (G-2545)State space: All the states a problem can be in, joined by the moves between them, such as the robot’s 76 cells or the arrangements of a Rubik’s cube; it is a graph, so planning becomes finding a path from the start state to a goal state. Explained in §2.2 Any problem of states and moves is a graph.: a graph whose vertices are states and whose edges are the moves (CS188 §1.2.2).
Searching a state space means finding a path from the start state to a goal state, whatever the states stand for. Later Notes search a state space of facts, such as “the cup is on the table” (symbolic task planningSymbolic task planning: Choosing a sequence of actions that reaches a goal, from a description of the world in true-or-false facts such as “the cup is on the table”; it decides the order of steps (go to the table, pick up, go to the door, put down) that a route search alone cannot. Explained in: Symbolic Task Planning: STRIPS and PDDL, §1. Overview).
The grid’s 76 vertices are too many to follow by hand, so we also use a small graph of the same room (Figure 3). Its vertices are seven waypoints:

S, the start, at (2, 1);
A, B, C and D, the four corners of the table;
P, the pink pole, at (1, 3);
G, the door, at (3.6, 4).

Two waypoints are joined when the straight line between them misses the table and the cabinet and is at most 2.8 m long; the length limit keeps the graph small enough to trace by hand. In Figure 3, follow the edges out of S: there are three, to A, P and D. The straight line from S to the door is 3.4 m long, too long to be an edge.
Make interactive
Figure 3: The waypoint graph in the room: S at (2, 1), the table corners A (3, 1), B (5, 1), C (5.5, 2.5) and D (3.5, 3), the pink pole P (1, 3) and the door G (3.6, 4), with the table and cabinet shaded; 11 edges, each labelled with its length in metres: S–A 1.000, S–P 2.236, S–D 2.500, A–B 2.000, A–D 2.062, B–C 1.581, C–D 2.062, C–G 2.421, D–G 1.005, D–P 2.500, P–G 2.786
The waypoint graph has 7 vertices and 11 edges. In this Note only the edges matter, not their lengths: every edge counts as one move; the lengths come back in Dijkstra’s algorithmDijkstra’s algorithm: A search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals). Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §3.1 The fire picture.
With either graph in hand, the question is how to search it, and the simplest idea is to list every path.
3. The search tree: every path from the start


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Listing every path from the start that never revisits a vertex finds every route to the goal, but the list grows fast and contains the same vertex many times: 40 paths for the 7-waypoint graph.


Which of the routes from S reaches the door G? A program has no eyes to spot a good route on a picture, so the plainest method is to try them all: from S, write down each way to go on; from each of those, each way to go on again; and never let a path visit a waypoint it has already visited (CS188 §1.2.2). A path that reaches G is not extended.
Figure 4 grows that list on the waypoint graph, one new path per frame. The top shows the newest path in the room (orange); the bottom shows where it hangs in the list. Watch the bottom grow like a family tree: every path sits under the path it extends by one edge.

Figure 4: Top: the waypoint graph in the room with the newest path in orange. Bottom: the tree of paths growing one node per frame, level by level: level 0 is S; level 1 holds A, D, P; level 2 holds 8 paths and level 3 holds 11. Green nodes are paths that reach the door G and are not extended. The last frame outlines in purple the 3 nodes that end at waypoint D and states that the whole tree goes 6 levels deep, with 40 paths of which 14 reach G
The list of paths is the search tree (G-2546)Search tree: The tree of paths from the start: each node is a whole path, and its children extend it by one edge; listing it finds every route, but it repeats vertices and grows fast (40 paths for 7 waypoints). Explained in §3. The search tree: every path from the start.: each node is a whole path from the start, the top node, at level 0, is the path that has not moved yet, and the nodes on level 2 are the paths of 2 edges (CS188 §1.2.2). For the waypoint graph:

levels 0 to 6 hold 1, 3, 8, 11, 10, 5 and 2 paths, 40 in all;
14 of the 40 paths reach G; the first ones, on level 2, are S–D–G and S–P–G (notebook).

The tree is wasteful in two ways. First, it repeats work: waypoint D ends 3 nodes on levels 1 and 2 (S–D, S–A–D, S–P–D, the purple nodes in the last frame of Figure 4), and the tree grows everything below D three times. A state space graph holds each state once; a search tree can hold it many times, because each node carries the whole path that led to it (CS188 §1.2.2).
Second, the tree grows fast: on the grid of 76 cells, its level 8 alone holds 1,447 paths (Section 7). We need to grow only part of the tree, and never the same vertex twice.
4. Searching with a frontier and a visited list


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

To reach the door without exploring any place twice, keep two lists: the vertices waiting to be explored (the frontier) and those already explored (the visited list). Taking one vertex off the frontier and adding its new neighbours, over and over, reaches the door in 7 expansions on the waypoint graph, against 40 paths in the tree.


The tree of Section 3 grew the paths below D three times. The fix is the one we use for errands: a to-do list and a done list. The to-do list holds the places reached but not yet explored; the done list holds the places already explored, so they are never explored again.
The to-do list is the frontier (G-2547)Frontier (open list): The vertices a search has reached but not yet expanded, waiting to be taken off one at a time; which one comes off next is what makes one search differ from another. Explained in §4. Searching with a frontier and a visited list., also called the open list: the vertices the search has reached but not yet expanded. Expanding a vertex means taking it off the frontier and looking at its neighbours. The done list is the visited list (G-2548)Visited list (closed list): The vertices a search has already expanded; a search never expands them again, so it explores each vertex once (7 expansions on the waypoint graph instead of 40 paths). Explained in §4. Searching with a frontier and a visited list., also called the closed list or extended list: the vertices already expanded (CS188 §1.3, §1.4; LaValle §2.2.1; MIT 6.034).
For each vertex the search also records its parent (G-2576)Parent (back pointer): The vertex from which a search reached a vertex, stored with it during the search; following parents back from the goal gives the route. In A*, a cell’s parent changes whenever a shorter way in lowers its cost so far. Explained in §4. Searching with a frontier and a visited list., also called its back pointer: the vertex it was reached from, so the route can be read back at the end by following parents from the goal (LaValle §2.2.1). The loop (LaValle §2.2.1; CS188 §1.3):

Put the start S on the frontier.
Take a vertex off the frontier. If it is the goal G, stop, and read the route back from G along the parents.
Mark the vertex visited. Add each of its neighbours that is neither visited nor already on the frontier, and record the vertex as their parent.
Go back to step 2. If the frontier is empty, there is no route.

5. Breadth-first search: ring by ring


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Taking the vertex that has waited longest explores the grid in rings of equal moves from the start, so the first time the goal comes off the frontier, it is by the fewest moves: 8 moves, 4.0 m, after 57 expansions.


The loop of Section 4 needs an order in which to take vertices off the frontier, the vertices waiting their turn. The first answer is the one a ticket counter uses: serve whoever has waited longest. A frontier served this way, new arrivals joining the back and the next vertex leaving from the front, is a queue (G-2551)Queue (first in, first out): A list served in arrival order: new items join the back and the next item leaves from the front; as a search’s frontier it gives breadth-first search. Explained in §5. Breadth-first search: ring by ring., “first in, first out”.
The loop with a queue is breadth-first search (G-2550)Breadth-first search (BFS): A search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same. Explained in §5. Breadth-first search: ring by ring., BFS: it finishes every vertex one move from the start before any vertex two moves away (LaValle §2.2.2; CS188 §1.3.2). The run of Figure 5 was breadth-first.
Figure 6 runs breadth-first search on the room grid. A blue cell is visited, already expanded, and shows how many moves it is from S; an orange cell waits in the queue and shows its place in the queue.
Each frame is the moment one ring is finished: in frame “ring 1 done”, the 4 cells one move from S are blue and the 7 cells two moves away wait in the queue. Watch the blue region spread out from S like a ripple, one move further each frame, round the pink pole’s cells and up the left side of the table.

The last frame: the door’s cell G comes off the queue at the 57th expansion, and the route, outlined in green, runs 5 cells up from S and 3 to the right: 8 moves of 0.5 m, 4.0 m
The goal cell G comes off the queue at the 57th expansion. Read back along the parents, the route goes 5 cells up from S and then 3 cells right to G:
8 \times 0.5 = 4.0 \text{ m}
The rings hold 1, 4, 7, 9, 10, 9, 7, 6 and 5 cells for 0 to 8 moves. Without the stop at G, the search would go on to reach all 76 free cells, the farthest 18 moves from S (notebook).
Why the first route found has the fewest moves. Three facts about the queue give it:

Cells two moves from S join the queue only while cells one move away are being expanded, so they wait behind every cell one move away. The same holds for every ring: all of ring k, the cells k moves from S, leave the queue before any of ring k + 1.
A cell gets its parent the first time any neighbour reaches it. Rings are expanded in order, so that neighbour is in the lowest ring next to it, and the cell lands in the ring one further out.
So each cell’s ring is its fewest number of moves from S. G is in ring 8: no route reaches it in 7 moves.

The order in which a cell’s neighbours are tried can change which 8-move route is found, but not its length: with each of the 24 possible orders, the route has 8 moves (notebook). Fewest moves means shortest only because every move is 0.5 m long. Breadth-first search finds the cheapest route only when every edge costs the same (CS188 §1.3.2); the next Note lets the robot also move diagonally, and that condition fails.
Breadth-first search pays for its guarantee by finishing each whole ring before going one move further: 57 expansions to reach the door. The opposite order goes straight for depth.
6. Depth-first search: dive, then back up


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Taking the vertex that arrived last dives along one path until it is stuck, then backs up to the newest choice not yet tried. Depth-first search finds a route, but which one depends on the order the moves are tried: 22 moves, 11.0 m, on our grid, where breadth-first search found 8.


The second answer to the choice in Section 4 is the opposite of a queue: take the waiting vertex that arrived last. A pile of plates works this way: the plate put on top last is taken first. A frontier served from the end where vertices arrive is a stack (G-2553)Stack (last in, first out): A list served from the end where items arrive, like a pile of plates: the item put on last comes off first; as a search’s frontier it gives depth-first search. Explained in §6. Depth-first search: dive, then back up., “last in, first out”.
The loop with a stack is depth-first search (G-2552)Depth-first search (DFS): A search whose frontier is a stack, so it always extends the newest path and dives deep before backing up; it backs up to its last untried choice at dead ends and finds a route, but which one, and how long, depends on the order the moves are tried (22 moves where breadth-first search found 8). Explained in §6. Depth-first search: dive, then back up., DFS: it always extends the newest path, so it plunges deeper and deeper along one line (LaValle §2.2.2; CS188 §1.3.1).
When the search reaches a cell with no new neighbour, a dead end, the next cell off the stack hangs off an earlier cell. The search has gone back to the most recent choice it has not tried and taken the other branch.
Figure 7 runs depth-first search on the room grid, one expansion per frame, trying the moves in the order left, down, up, right; the first move tried is pushed last, so it sits on top. Python: one loop gives both searches; only the end of the frontier the next cell comes from differs. A deque (double-ended queue) can give its first item, popleft(), or its last, pop(). The stack takes new cells in reverse so that the first move tried ends on top.
from collections import deque
def search(start, goal, neighbours, depth_first=False):
    frontier, parent = deque([start]), {start: None}
    while frontier:
        cell = frontier.pop() if depth_first else frontier.popleft()
        if cell == goal:
            break
        new = [n for n in neighbours(cell) if n not in parent]
        for n in (reversed(new) if depth_first else new):
            parent[n] = cell
            frontier.append(n)
    route = [goal]
    while parent[route[-1]] is not None:
        route.append(parent[route[-1]])
    return route[::-1]

Both searches expand each cell at most once, thanks to the visited list (the cells already expanded), so on our grid both stop after at most 76 expansions. The tree of every path had 1,447 paths on level 8 alone. How the work grows as problems get bigger decides which searches are usable at all.
7. How fast the work grows: Big-O and exponential time


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Listing every path to the door multiplies the work by the number of choices at every level, 65,536 move sequences of 8 moves, while a search with a visited list touches each vertex and edge a fixed number of times, 304 steps on our grid. Big-O notation names such growth rates, ignoring constant factors.


7.1 Counting the work
The tree of every path to the door had 40 paths on the waypoint graph; the loop of Section 4 needed 7 expansions. To see why the gap matters, count how each grows with the depth of the goal.
On the grid, a robot that may make any of the 4 moves at each step has 4 choices for its first move, 4 for its second, and so on. After 8 moves:
4^8 = 65{,}536 \text{ move sequences}
The number of choices at each step of a search is its branching factor (G-2555)Branching factor b: The number of choices at each step of a search, such as 4 moves on a 4-connected grid or 18 turns of a Rubik’s cube; level d of a search tree holds up to b^d nodes, so it sets how fast the tree grows. Explained in §7.1 Counting the work. (CS188 §1.3). The symbols:

b is the branching factor, 4 on our grid;
d is a level of the tree, its number of moves from the start, 8 for the door.

Each level multiplies the sequences by b, so level d holds:
b^d \text{ sequences}
Figure 8 grows those levels one per frame. The grey bars count every sequence of d moves; the orange bars count the paths of d moves in our room that stay in free cells and never revisit a cell, the levels of the room’s search tree.
Both are drawn on an ordinary, linear axis, so the early levels look empty. Watch each grey bar dwarf all the bars before it.

Figure 8: Bar chart with one level d of the tree, its number of moves from the start, per frame, d from 0 to 8, on a linear axis. Grey bars: every sequence of d moves with 4 choices each, 4 to the power d: 1, 4, 16, 64, 256, 1,024, 4,096, 16,384 and 65,536. Orange bars: paths of d moves in the room that stay in free cells and never revisit a cell: 1, 4, 11, 30, 69, 158, 342, 728 and 1,447. The last frame: levels 0 to 8 hold 87,381 move sequences and 2,790 room paths; 16 of the 1,447 room paths on level 8 end at the door, while breadth-first search needed 57 expansions
The room’s tree grows more slowly, because walls and the no-revisit rule remove choices, but it still roughly doubles each level: 1,447 paths on level 8, of which 16 end at the door (notebook).
How big is the whole tree? Adding up its levels, the last level alone outweighs all the others. The symbols:

b is the branching factor, 4 on our grid;
d is the deepest level counted, 2 in the small check below;
N is the number of nodes on levels 0 to d together.

Our numbers first, with b of 4 and d of 2, then the same steps in symbols:
N = 1 + 4 + 16
N = 1 + b + b^2 + \dots + b^d
4N = 4 + 16 + 64
bN = b + b^2 + \dots + b^{d+1}
4N - N = 64 - 1
bN - N = b^{d+1} - 1
N = 63 / 3 = 21
N = \frac{b^{d+1} - 1}{b - 1}
Down to level 8 the tree holds 87,381 move sequences, and level 8 alone holds 65,536 of them, three quarters (notebook). So the work of listing every path is set by the last level, b^d.
Work that is multiplied by a constant factor, here b, each time the problem grows by one step is exponential time (G-734)Exponential time: Work that is multiplied by a constant factor with every step of the input size. Explained in: Memoization in Backpropagation, §3.2 Why it is slow, the same blow-up as computing the Fibonacci numbers by plain recursion.
A computer does about 10^8 simple steps per second (USACO Guide, time complexity). At one step per sequence:

A Rubik’s cube, with b = 18, has 3.57 \times 10^{12} move sequences of 10 turns, about 10 hours of work, and 1.27 \times 10^{25} of 20 turns, about 4 billion years (Korf 1997; notebook).
Breadth-first search with its visited list, the cells already expanded, grows differently. Each of the 76 cells comes off the queue once, and each of the 114 edges is looked at once from each of its two ends:
76 + 2 \times 114 = 304 \text{ steps}
Double the room and the steps roughly double; they do not multiply by 4 with every extra move.
7.2 Big-O notation
To compare searches we do not need the exact step counts, which depend on the computer and the code; we need how the count grows with the problem. So we keep only the fastest-growing part and drop constant factors: breadth-first search’s 304 steps grow in step with the number of vertices plus the number of edges, and listing every path grows like b^d (USACO Guide, time complexity).
Writing a growth rate this way is Big-O notation (G-2556)Big-O notation: A way to write how fast an algorithm’s work grows with the problem’s size, keeping only the fastest-growing part and dropping constant factors, such as O(V + E) for breadth-first search and O(b^d) for listing every path; it lets us compare methods without timing them. Explained in §7.2 Big-O notation.. With V now standing for the number of vertices, 76 on our grid, and E for the number of edges, 114, “breadth-first search is O(V + E)” reads “its work grows at most in proportion to the number of vertices plus the number of edges” (LaValle §2.2.2; USACO Guide, time complexity).
The formal version, with:

n is the size of the problem, such as the depth d;
f(n) is the exact work for size n, such as the tree size N;
g(n) is a simpler function, such as b^d;
c is a constant number, the same for every n;
the sign \le means “is at most”.

f(n) is O(g(n)) when, for all large enough n:
f(n) \le c\thinspace g(n)
The tree size is O(b^d) with c equal to 2, because the fraction of Section 7.1 is at most twice its last level when b is at least 2. With our numbers, b of 4 and d of 8:
\frac{4^9 - 1}{4 - 1} = 87{,}381
2 \times 4^8 = 131{,}072
87{,}381 \le 131{,}072
So, in Big-O terms:

listing every path takes O(b^d): exponential in the depth d;
breadth-first and depth-first search with a visited list take O(V + E): in proportion to the size of the graph (LaValle §2.2.2).

A search with a visited list is cheap in the size of its graph. The trouble is that for many robots the graph itself is enormous.
8. Why exact planning is hard: NP-hard and PSPACE-hard


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Each number a robot’s state needs multiplies the number of grid cells, so grids blow up exponentially with the number of numbers. Complexity theory says the general planning problem has no shortcut around this: it is PSPACE-hard, and even shortest paths among obstacles in 3D are NP-hard.


Our grid needs two numbers per state, x and y, and has 112 cells. Each further number multiplies the cells by its number of values:

x and y in 0.5 m cells: 14 times 8 is 112 cells;
add the heading, in 8 steps of 45°: 112 times 8 is 896 cells;
a robot arm with 6 joints, each angle in 100 steps: 100 to the power 6 is 10^{12} cells.

At 10^8 cells per second (USACO Guide, time complexity), only touching each of the arm’s cells once takes:
10^{12} / 10^8 = 10^4 \text{ s}
10^4 \text{ s} = 2.8 \text{ hours}
The search of Sections 4 to 6 is O(V + E), but V, the number of vertices, is itself exponential in the number of numbers per state. Is there a cleverer exact method that avoids this blow-up? Complexity theory sorts problems by how fast the best possible method’s work must grow, and its answer for planning is: almost certainly not.
The classes, in plain words. Two groups of problems matter first, and together they are P and NP (G-2557)P and NP: Two classes of problems: P, those a computer can solve with work that grows like a power of the input size (polynomial time), such as breadth-first search on a grid; NP, those whose “yes” answers can be checked in polynomial time once shown, such as surviving a known sequence of Tetris pieces. Whether every NP problem is also in P is unproved. Explained in §8. Why exact planning is hard: NP-hard and PSPACE-hard. (MIT 6.006 L23 notes):

P is the set of problems a computer can solve with work that grows like a power of the input size, n, n^2 or n^3, called polynomial time. Breadth-first search on a grid is in P: its O(V + E) grows like the first power of the grid’s size.
NP is the set of problems whose “yes” answers can be checked in polynomial time, once someone shows the answer. Tetris with every coming piece known is in NP: “can I survive these pieces?” is proved by showing the list of moves, which is quick to check by playing it, however hard it was to find.

Every problem in P is also in NP. Whether every problem in NP is also in P is the famous open question, and most computer scientists believe it is not (MIT 6.006 L23 notes; Wikipedia, P versus NP problem).
A problem is NP-hard (G-2558)NP-hard: Said of a problem at least as hard as every problem in NP: a polynomial-time method for it would give one for all of NP, and none is known, so it is expected to need exponential time in its worst cases; finding the shortest path among obstacles in 3D is NP-hard. Explained in §8. Why exact planning is hard: NP-hard and PSPACE-hard. when it is at least as hard as every problem in NP: a polynomial-time method for it would give one for every NP problem. No such method is known for any NP-hard problem, so we expect NP-hard problems to need exponential time in their worst cases (MIT 6.006 L23 notes; Wikipedia, NP-hardness).
Tetris with known pieces is NP-hard (MIT 6.006 L23 notes). So is finding the shortest path for a point among polyhedral obstacles in 3D (Canny and Reif 1987).
PSPACE is the set of problems that can be solved using memory that grows like a power of the input size, with no limit on time; it contains NP (Wikipedia, PSPACE). A problem is PSPACE-hard (G-2559)PSPACE-hard: Said of a problem at least as hard as every problem solvable with memory growing like a power of the input size (PSPACE, which contains NP); the general motion planning problem and Sokoban are PSPACE-hard, which is why practical planners give up exactness. Explained in §8. Why exact planning is hard: NP-hard and PSPACE-hard. when it is at least as hard as every problem in PSPACE, so at least as hard as every problem in NP too (Wikipedia, PSPACE). Two planning problems are PSPACE-hard (LaValle §6.5.1):

moving a body made of several linked parts through a world of obstacles from one placement to another, the general motion planning problem behind the piano mover’s problemExplained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §6. The basic motion planning problem (Reif 1979);
Sokoban, the puzzle of pushing boxes through a grid warehouse to target squares.

Figure 9 places these problems on one line of growing difficulty. Each class is everything to the left of its notch, and “-hard” is everything from the notch rightwards; a problem sitting on a notch is among the hardest of its class.
