Our floor robot is lucky: shortest paths among polygons in 2D can be found in polynomial time (Wikipedia, Euclidean shortest path). The hard results are about the general problem, with many linked parts or a third dimension.
Because exact planning is hopeless there, practical planners give up some exactness: a grid search is only as fine as its cells, so a gap narrower than a cell can be missed, and later chapters sample the space at random instead (LaValle §6.5.1). Even when the graph is not hopeless, it may be too big to build in full before searching.
9. Explicit and implicit graphs


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A graph can be built in full before the search (explicit) or made as the search goes, by a function that returns a vertex’s neighbours when asked (implicit). An implicit graph never makes the vertices the search does not reach, which is what makes large state spaces searchable.


Section 8 multiplied the cells by each extra number in the state. A planner for a robot’s position and heading shows what that does to the graph (CMU 16-350):

a 20 m by 20 m area in 0.25 m cells with 8 headings has 80 times 80 times 8, that is 51,200 states;
a 200 m by 200 m area in 0.25 m cells with 16 headings has 800 times 800 times 16, that is 10,240,000 states.

Building and storing all 51,200 states with their edges before the search is quick. Building 10 million, most of which the search never reaches, wastes time and memory.
So there are two ways to hand a graph to a search (CMU 16-350; CS188 §1.2.2):

an explicit graph (G-2560)Explicit graph: A graph built in full, every vertex and edge, before the search starts; simple and fine for small state spaces such as the room’s 76 cells. Explained in §9. Explicit and implicit graphs. is built in full, every vertex and edge, before the search starts; our room’s 76 vertices and 114 edges are small enough for that;
an implicit graph (G-2561)Implicit graph: A graph never built in full: the search starts from the start vertex and calls a function that returns a vertex’s neighbours when it is expanded, so only the vertices the search reaches are made; this is what makes state spaces of millions of states searchable. Explained in §9. Explicit and implicit graphs. is never built in full: the search starts from the start vertex and calls a function that returns a vertex’s neighbours when it is expanded, so only the vertices the search reaches are ever made.

Figure 10 contrasts the two on a small grid. On the left every dot and line exists before the search begins; on the right only the cells the search has reached exist, and the function neighbours(cell) makes the new ones when the red cell is expanded.

Figure 10: Left, explicit graph: a 6 by 4 grid of blue dots, all joined by lines before the search; our room has 76 vertices and 114 edges. Right, implicit graph: the same grid in faint grey dots; two blue cells have been reached, the red-ringed one is being expanded, and the function neighbours(cell), which reads the grid and returns the free cells left, down, up and right of it, has just made its three orange neighbours; grey cells are not made until the search reaches them
The search loop of Section 4 works unchanged on an implicit graph: it only ever asks for the neighbours of the vertex it is expanding. Our breadth-first search of Figure 6 was written that way: its neighbours function reads the occupancy grid and returns the free cells beside a cell when asked.
A Rubik’s cube can only be searched this way, because its state space is never written down; the search applies the 18 turns to the arrangement it is expanding (LaValle §2.2.2). Explicit graphs are typical for 2D problems in robotics and implicit graphs for problems with more dimensions (CMU 16-350).
An implicit graph is defined entirely by what a state holds and by the neighbours function, so choosing the state is the last decision left.
10. Choosing the search state: the Markov rule


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The search state must hold everything that decides which moves are allowed and what they cost. Leave out the robot’s battery charge, and a depth-first search finds no route to a door 8 moves away; put it in, and it finds one.


The implicit graph of Section 9 is only as good as its states. Suppose the robot’s battery holds enough for 12 moves, and each 0.5 m move uses one unit.

From there the door is 6 moves away, so every path through it runs flat. Later the search comes back to the cell below it with 11 units, but the purple cell is already visited, so it is never tried again.

The frame “stack empty after 42 expansions: no route” shows every cell the search reached; from the purple cell the door was 6 moves away. The last frame: with (cell, charge left) as the state, the same search finds a 12-move route, outlined in green, with the charge left written in each cell, after 182 expansions
The fault is in the state, not in the search. With the cell alone as the state, the moves allowed from a cell depend on the charge left, and the charge depends on the path that led there: on the history.
The search assumes the opposite, that a vertex’s neighbours and their costs depend only on the vertex itself (CMU 16-350). The assumption that only the present state matters is the Markov property (G-2316)Markov property: The property of a sequence of states that the future depends on the past only through the present state; it lets a filter forget the history and work from the latest state alone. Explained in: Why a Robot Is Never Sure: State, Controls and Measurements, §4.3 Complete state and the Markov property, the future depending on the past only through the present state, applied to search.
What a search keeps per vertex is its search state (G-2562)Search state: What a search keeps for each vertex: the quantities that decide which moves are allowed and what they cost, and nothing more, such as (cell, charge left) for a robot with a battery; leaving one out breaks the Markov property and can hide routes. Explained in §10. Choosing the search state: the Markov rule.: the quantities that decide which moves are allowed and what they cost, and nothing more (CS188 §1.2; CMU 16-350). Here the fix is to add the charge to the state: the same cell with 10 units left and with 2 units left are now different states. The last frame of Figure 11 runs the same depth-first search with (cell, charge left) as the state and finds a 12-move route after 182 expansions. The price is more states, one per cell and charge from 0 to 12:
76 \times 13 = 988 \text{ states}
Breadth-first search happens to survive the cell-only state in this example, because it reaches every cell first by the fewest moves, with the most charge left: it reaches the door with 4 units to spare (notebook). The rule does not depend on luck: a search state must hold what decides the next moves and costs, and every extra quantity multiplies the states, as in Section 8.
A Pac-Man that only has to reach a square needs its square as the state; one that must eat every dot needs its square plus a yes or no for each dot (CS188 §1.2). With the state chosen, the graph, the search loop and its cost are all in place for a room whose moves are all the same length.

Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Big-O notationBig-O notation: A way to write how fast an algorithm’s work grows with the problem’s size, keeping only the fastest-growing part and dropping constant factors, such as O(V + E) for breadth-first search and O(b^d) for listing every path; it lets us compare methods without timing them. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §7.2 Big-O notation; Breadth-first searchBreadth-first search (BFS): A search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same. 1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Once diagonal moves are allowed, routes with the same number of moves differ in length, so the fewest moves is no longer the shortest route. Dijkstra’s algorithm always settles the vertex nearest the start next, using a priority queue kept as a heap, and finds the shortest route to the door: 3.414 m, where breadth-first search returns 3.828 m.


So far the robot can turn its room into a graph and search it: on the grid of 0.5 m moves left, down, up and right, breadth-first search (G-2550)Breadth-first search (BFS): A search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §5. Breadth-first search: ring by ring finds the route to the door with the fewest moves, 8 moves, 4.0 m. What still breaks: our robot can spin on the spotExplained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §4.4 Four ways to drive and then drive in any direction, so it can also cut across a cell diagonally, 0.707 m instead of two moves of 0.5 m.
Figure 1 shows what breadth-first search does once diagonal moves are allowed. Breadth-first search returns a route of 6 moves, 3.828 m (orange, dashed), but another route of 6 moves is only 3.414 m long (green). Breadth-first search counts moves, so to it the two routes are equal, and it keeps whichever it finds first.

2. When moves have different lengths


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Allowing diagonal moves of 0.707 m beside straight moves of 0.5 m gives each edge its own cost. The length of a route is then the sum of its edge costs, and two routes of 6 moves can differ by 0.414 m.


2.1 Diagonal moves: the 8-connected grid
To reach the door by a shorter route, the robot must be allowed to cut corners of the grid. On the 4-connected grid (G-2544)4-connected grid: A grid made into a graph by joining each cell to the up to four cells that share a side with it (left, down, up, right); the simplest graph of a grid map, with every move the same length. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edges, where each cell is joined only to the cells sharing a side with it, going one cell right and one cell up takes two moves, 1.0 m. Our robot can turn on the spot to face the diagonal and drive straight there instead.
Figure 2 shows the moves this adds. From each cell the robot may now move to any of the 8 cells around it: 4 straight moves of 0.5 m and 4 diagonal moves. A diagonal move may not cut the corner of a blocked cell, because the robot would clip that cell on its way.

Explained in §2.1 Diagonal moves: the 8-connected grid. (CMU 16-350, heuristics). With the rule against cutting corners, our room’s 8-connected grid has the same 76 vertices as before and 190 edges instead of 114 (notebook).
How long is a diagonal move? It is the long side of the right-angled triangle in the middle of Figure 2, so Pythagoras’ rule gives it; its length is the Euclidean distance (G-715)Euclidean distance: The straight-line distance between two points. Explained in: Handling Missing Data: KNN Imputer, §4.1 The Euclidean distance, the straight-line distance, between the two cell centres. The symbols:

a is the side of a cell, 0.5 m, which is also the length of a straight move;
\ell is the length of a diagonal move, in m.

Our numbers first, then the same steps in symbols:
\ell^2 = 0.5^2 + 0.5^2
\ell^2 = a^2 + a^2
\ell^2 = 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5
\ell^2 = 2a^2
\ell = \sqrt{0.5} = 0.707 \text{ m}

A diagonal move covers the same ground as one move right and one move up, 1.0 m, in 0.707 m. The grid now has two kinds of moves, and that breaks breadth-first search.
2.2 Edge costs: the fewest moves is not the shortest
Breadth-first search treats every move as one step, but the robot cares about metres. In Figure 1 its route and the shortest route both have 6 moves. Adding up the metres, with 0.707 m for each diagonal move and 0.5 m for each straight move, the route breadth-first search returns, 4 diagonal and 2 straight moves:
4 \times 0.707 + 2 \times 0.5
= 2.828 + 1.0 = 3.828 \text{ m}
The shortest route, 2 diagonal and 4 straight moves:
2 \times 0.707 + 4 \times 0.5
= 1.414 + 2.0 = 3.414 \text{ m}
A graph in which every edge carries a number, its cost, is a weighted graph (G-2563)Weighted graph (edge cost): A graph in which every edge carries a number, its cost, such as a move’s length in metres (0.5 m straight, 0.707 m diagonal); the cost of a path is the sum of its edge costs, so the cheapest route need not have the fewest edges. Explained in §2.2 Edge costs: the fewest moves is not the shortest., and the cost of a path (G-2543)Path (graph): A chain of edges in which each edge starts where the last one ended, such as S, the cell above S and the cell above that; a route the robot can follow, and what a search returns. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §2.1 Cells and moves: vertices and edges, a chain of edges, is the sum of the costs of its edges (LaValle §2.2.2). Here an edge’s cost is its length in metres: 0.5 for a straight move, 0.707 for a diagonal. A cost could also be time or energy.
Breadth-first search goes wrong because it counts edges. Breadth-first search finishes all routes of 5 moves before any of 6, but among routes of 6 moves it cannot tell 3.414 m from 3.828 m; it keeps the first it finds, and which one that is depends on the order of the moves. 3. Dijkstra’s algorithm


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Dijkstra’s algorithm settles the vertices in order of their distance from the start: it always takes the unsettled vertex with the smallest distance found so far, which is then final, and offers each neighbour the route through it. On the waypoint graph it settles the door at 3.505 m by S–D–G.


3.1 The fire picture
To count metres, picture the waypoints as oil depots and the edges as pipelines (NPTEL DAA, Dijkstra). We set fire to the depot at S at time 0. The fire runs along every pipeline at the same speed, 1 m per second, and each depot catches fire when the first flame reaches it.
All flames move at the same speed, so the first flame to reach a depot came by the shortest route. A depot’s time of catching fire, in seconds, is therefore its shortest distance from S, in metres (DPV §4.4.1).
Figure 3 plays the fire on the waypoint graph. Burnt parts of pipelines are red, and each burnt waypoint shows the time it caught fire.
Under the room, a list keeps, for every waypoint not yet on fire, the arrival time of the first flame now on its way, smallest first. Such a list, which always hands out its smallest entry first instead of its oldest, is a priority queue (G-2568)Priority queue: A collection with two operations, insert an entry with a priority and remove the entry with the best priority (for Dijkstra’s algorithm, the smallest distance); it is what lets a search always pick its most promising vertex next. Explained in §5.1 Why a plain list is slow.. The queue’s first entry is always the next waypoint to catch fire. Watch two frames in particular:

frame “t = 2.236 s: P catches fire”: a flame starts from P towards the door G, due at 5.022 s, so G’s entry is 5.022;
frame “t = 2.500 s: D catches fire”: a flame from D is due at G after 1.005 m more, at 3.505 s, so G’s entry drops from 5.022 to 3.505.

3.2 The algorithm: settle the nearest, update its neighbours
A program cannot let a fire burn, but it does not need to: only the moments when a waypoint catches fire matter, and the next such moment always belongs to the waypoint with the earliest flame on its way, the first entry of the queue. Jumping from one such moment to the next is the algorithm. The symbols:

u is the vertex just settled, such as D;
v is one of its neighbours, such as G;
g(v) is the distance of v from S found so far, in m, such as 5.022 for G before D is settled;
c(u, v) is the cost of the edge from u to v, such as 1.005 m from D to G.

The steps (LaValle §2.2.2; DPV §4.4.1):

Set the start’s distance g(S) to 0 and put S in the queue; every other vertex has no distance yet.
Take the vertex u with the smallest g(u) off the queue. The vertex u is now settled: g(u) is its shortest distance.
For each neighbour v of u that is not settled: if the route through u is shorter than g(v), set g(v) to it, record u as the parent (G-2576)Parent (back pointer): The vertex from which a search reached a vertex, stored with it during the search; following parents back from the goal gives the route. In A*, a cell’s parent changes whenever a shorter way in lowers its cost so far. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §4. Searching with a frontier and a visited list of v, the vertex it was reached from, and put v in the queue with its new distance.
Go back to step 2 until the queue is empty.

These four steps are Dijkstra’s algorithm (G-2565)Dijkstra’s algorithm: A search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals). Explained in §3.2 The algorithm: settle the nearest, update its neighbours., published by Edsger Dijkstra in 1959 (Wikipedia, Dijkstra’s algorithm). Dijkstra’s algorithm is the search loop with a frontier and a visited listFrontier (open list): The vertices a search has reached but not yet expanded, waiting to be taken off one at a time; which one comes off next is what makes one search differ from another. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §4. Searching with a frontier and a visited list with one change: the frontier (G-2547)Frontier (open list): The vertices a search has reached but not yet expanded, waiting to be taken off one at a time; which one comes off next is what makes one search differ from another. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §4. Searching with a frontier and a visited list, the vertices waiting to be expanded, gives out the vertex with the smallest distance, not the oldest or the newest (LaValle §2.2.2). The settled vertices are its visited list (G-2548)Visited list (closed list): The vertices a search has already expanded; a search never expands them again, so it explores each vertex once (7 expansions on the waypoint graph instead of 40 paths). Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §4. Searching with a frontier and a visited list, the vertices already expanded.
Step 3 offers each neighbour the route through the vertex just settled and keeps the shorter of the two. When D is settled at 2.500, step 3 offers G the route through D. Our numbers first, then the same step in symbols:
g(G) = \min(5.022,\ 2.500 + 1.005)
g(v) = \min\big(g(v),\ g(u) + c(u, v)\big)
g(G) = \min(5.022,\ 3.505)
g(G) = 3.505

3.3 Why the nearest unsettled vertex is final
Step 2 settles D at 2.500 and never looks at it again. Could a route found later still reach D more cheaply? No; here is why.
When D is settled, the settled waypoints are S, A and P, and the queue holds D 2.500, B 3.000 and G 5.022. Any other route from S to D has to leave the settled waypoints somewhere, through a waypoint still in the queue, such as B. The symbols:

u is the first waypoint not yet settled on that other route, such as B;
g(u) is its entry in the queue, 3.000 for B;
r is the length of the rest of the route, from u on to D, in m: at least 0, because no edge is shorter than 0.

Our numbers first, then the same steps in symbols:
\text{other route} = 3.000 + r
\text{other route} = g(u) + r
3.000 + r \ge 3.000
g(u) + r \ge g(u)
3.000 \ge 2.500
g(u) \ge g(D)
So no later route can beat 2.500: D’s entry was the smallest in the queue, and every other route already costs at least the entry of the waypoint where it leaves the settled ones (DPV §4.4.2; Wikipedia, Dijkstra’s algorithm). Taking the best-looking step now and never revisiting it goes wrong in many problems; for Dijkstra’s algorithm the argument above proves it right.
The argument needs every edge cost to be at least 0. Lengths always are, but a cost can be negative in other problems, such as a taxi trip that earns money (DPV §4.6.1). Then a later route can undercut a settled vertex, and Dijkstra’s algorithm can return a wrong answer; the Bellman–Ford algorithm handles negative costs (Wikipedia, Dijkstra’s algorithm).
3.4 Stopping at the goal: uniform-cost search
The robot needs the distance to the door, not to every waypoint. Since a settled distance is final (Section 3.3), the search can stop as soon as the door is settled: on the waypoint graph that is the 6th settled waypoint, and C is never settled.
The test must come when the door is taken off the queue, not when it first enters it. G first entered the queue at 5.022, when P was settled, and that entry was wrong; only when G comes off is 3.505 sure (CS188 §1.3.3; Red Blob, introduction). Dijkstra’s algorithm stopped this way when the goal is settled is uniform-cost search (G-2567)Uniform-cost search: Dijkstra’s algorithm stopped as soon as the goal is taken off the priority queue, the name artificial intelligence books use; it finds the shortest route to the goal without settling the vertices farther away. Explained in §3.4 Stopping at the goal: uniform-cost search., the name artificial intelligence books use (CS188 §1.3.3; Wikipedia, Dijkstra’s algorithm).

5. The priority queue: finding the smallest fast


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Dijkstra’s algorithm needs a queue that hands out its smallest entry. A plain list makes either inserting or removing slow, about N^2 steps for N entries; a binary heap does both in about \log_2 N steps, so a million entries take about 0.2 s instead of hours.


5.1 Why a plain list is slow
Step 2 of Section 3.2 removes the entry with the smallest distance, again and again, while step 3 keeps inserting new ones. A collection that supports exactly these two operations, insert an entry with a priority and remove the entry with the best priority, is a priority queue (G-2568)Priority queue: A collection with two operations, insert an entry with a priority and remove the entry with the best priority (for Dijkstra’s algorithm, the smallest distance); it is what lets a search always pick its most promising vertex next. Explained in §5.1 Why a plain list is slow. (DPV §4.5; Wikipedia, Priority queue). For Dijkstra’s algorithm the best priority is the smallest distance.
The two obvious ways to keep one in a list each make one operation slow (Wikipedia, Priority queue):




















Kept asInsertRemove the smallestunsorted list1 step: add at the endlook at all N entriessorted listwalk up to N entries to its place1 step: take the first
For N inserts and N removals, either list costs about N times N steps. A grid of 10^6 cells, such as a 500 m by 500 m floor in 0.5 m cells, then needs about 10^{12} steps; at about 10^8 simple steps per second (USACO Guide, time complexity):
10^{12} / 10^8 = 10^4 \text{ s}
10^4 \text{ s} = 2.8 \text{ hours}
The heap of the next section needs about \log_2 N steps per operation, where \log_2 N is the power of 2 that gives N, such as 20 for a million (Section 5.2). For 10^6 inserts and removals:
10^6 \times 20 = 2 \times 10^7 \text{ steps}
2 \times 10^7 / 10^8 = 0.2 \text{ s}
5.2 The binary heap
A list keeps the smallest entry either hard to find or costly to maintain. A tree can keep it on top cheaply: we only demand that every entry be at most the entries just below it. Then the smallest entry is always at the top, while the rest of the tree is only partly in order, which is cheap to keep up.
A binary heap (G-2569)Binary heap: A tree filled level by level in which every entry is at most the entries below it, stored in a plain list; the smallest entry sits at the top and insert and remove each walk one path of about \log_2 N levels, so it makes a fast priority queue. Explained in §5.2 The binary heap. is such a tree, with two rules (DPV §4.5.2; Wikipedia, Binary heap):

each entry has at most two entries below it, and the tree is filled level by level, left to right, with no gaps;
every entry is at most the entries below it, so the smallest is at the top, which is what Dijkstra’s algorithm needs; with the rule turned round, a heap keeps the largest entry on top instead.

Its two operations keep both rules:

insert: put the new entry at the end of the bottom level, then, while it is smaller than the entry above it, swap the two (sift up);
remove the smallest: take the top entry, move the last entry of the bottom level to the top, then, while it is larger than the smaller of the entries below it, swap with that one (sift down).

In frame “remove the smallest: sift down”, after B 3.000 comes off, the last entry G 5.022 moves to the top, is larger than G 3.505 below it, and swaps down.

Why about log₂ N steps. A sift walks one path between the top and the bottom, one level per swap, so it takes at most as many swaps as the heap has levels. The levels hold 1, 2, 4, 8 entries and so on, each twice the one above. Adding them is the sum of the levels of a search treeExplained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §7.1 Counting the work, with a branching factor, the number of choices per step, of 2. The symbols:

n is the number of entries they hold.

Our numbers first, then the same steps in symbols:
n = 1 + 2 + 4
n = 1 + 2 + \dots + 2^{k-1}
n = 7 = 2^3 - 1
n = \frac{2^k - 1}{2 - 1} = 2^k - 1
Every extra level doubles the room, so N entries need only about \log_2 N levels. A million entries fit in 20 levels, because:
2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576
So insert and remove each take at most about 20 swaps for a million entries, instead of up to a million steps for a list.
5.3 Dijkstra’s algorithm with a heap
When step 3 lowers a vertex’s distance, as for G when D was settled, the vertex’s entry in the heap should go down too. The simplest way, used with Python’s heapq module, is not to change the old entry at all: push a new entry with the new distance, and when an entry comes off for a vertex already settled, skip it (Red Blob, implementation).
In Figure 5, G 5.022 is such a stale entry: it is still in the heap when G 3.505 comes off. Updating the entry in place also works, but needs a table from each vertex to its position in the heap (Wikipedia, Dijkstra’s algorithm).

Python: Dijkstra’s algorithm with Python’s heapq, which keeps a heap with the smallest entry on top in a plain list: heappush inserts and sifts up, heappop removes the smallest and sifts down. neighbours(v) returns each neighbour of v with the cost of the edge.
import heapq, math
def dijkstra(start, goal, neighbours):
    dist, parent = {start: 0.0}, {start: None}
    queue, settled = [(0.0, start)], set()
    while queue:
        d, v = heapq.heappop(queue)
        if v in settled:
            continue                          # a stale entry
        settled.add(v)
        if v == goal:
            break
        for n, cost in neighbours(v):
            if d + cost < dist.get(n, math.inf):
                dist[n], parent[n] = d + cost, v
                heapq.heappush(queue, (dist[n], n))
    return dist[goal]

V is the number of vertices, E the number of edges;
each heap operation takes about \log_2 V steps.

So Dijkstra’s algorithm with a heap takes O((V + E) \log V) steps, in the Big-O notation (G-2556)Big-O notation: A way to write how fast an algorithm’s work grows with the problem’s size, keeping only the fastest-growing part and dropping constant factors, such as O(V + E) for breadth-first search and O(b^d) for listing every path; it lets us compare methods without timing them. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §7.2 Big-O notation that keeps only the growth rate; with a plain list it takes O(V^2) (DPV §4.5; Wikipedia, Dijkstra’s algorithm). For a grid of 10^6 cells with diagonal moves, about 4 edges per cell:
(10^6 + 4 \times 10^6) \times 20 = 10^8
10^8 / 10^8 = 1 \text{ s}
With a plain list, V^2 is 10^{12} steps, the 2.8 hours of Section 5.1.
The heap makes each step of Dijkstra’s algorithm cheap, but not the number of steps. The search still spreads in rings in every direction, with no idea where the door is: it settled 54 cells to reach the door’s, including cells along the bottom wall that lead away from it.
6. Summary

With diagonal moves, the robot’s shortest route to the door is 3.414 m (2 diagonal and 4 straight moves), where breadth-first search returned 3.828 m, because breadth-first search counts moves and cannot tell two 6-move routes apart, while Dijkstra’s algorithm (G-2565)Dijkstra’s algorithm: A search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals). Explained in §3.2 The algorithm: settle the nearest, update its neighbours. counts metres.
In an 8-connected grid (G-2564)8-connected grid: A grid made into a graph by joining each cell to all 8 cells around it: 4 straight moves of one cell side and 4 diagonal moves of 1.414 cell sides (0.707 m for 0.5 m cells), usually without cutting the corner of a blocked cell; it gives shorter, less jagged routes than a 4-connected grid. Explained in §2.1 Diagonal moves: the 8-connected grid. a diagonal move is 0.707 m by Pythagoras’ rule, so the grid becomes a weighted graph (G-2563)Weighted graph (edge cost): A graph in which every edge carries a number, its cost, such as a move’s length in metres (0.5 m straight, 0.707 m diagonal); the cost of a path is the sum of its edge costs, so the cheapest route need not have the fewest edges. Explained in §2.2 Edge costs: the fewest moves is not the shortest., and a route’s cost is the sum of its edge costs.
Dijkstra’s algorithm works like a fire spreading at 1 m per second: each vertex settles at its shortest distance, so the waypoints settle in the order S 0, A 1.000, P 2.236, D 2.500, B 3.000, G 3.505, because the earliest flame to arrive came by the shortest route.
Each settled vertex offers its neighbours the route through it, and a neighbour keeps the shorter, so G’s distance dropped from 5.022 to 3.505 when D settled.
A settled distance is final, because any other route leaves the settled vertices through a queue entry that is already at least as large and adds only lengths of at least 0; with negative costs that fails.
Uniform-cost search (G-2567)Uniform-cost search: Dijkstra’s algorithm stopped as soon as the goal is taken off the priority queue, the name artificial intelligence books use; it finds the shortest route to the goal without settling the vertices farther away. Explained in §3.4 Stopping at the goal: uniform-cost search. stops when the goal comes off the queue, not when it first enters, because G’s first entry, 5.022, was wrong.
A priority queue (G-2568)Priority queue: A collection with two operations, insert an entry with a priority and remove the entry with the best priority (for Dijkstra’s algorithm, the smallest distance); it is what lets a search always pick its most promising vertex next. Explained in §5.1 Why a plain list is slow. hands out the smallest entry; kept as a binary heap (G-2569)Binary heap: A tree filled level by level in which every entry is at most the entries below it, stored in a plain list; the smallest entry sits at the top and insert and remove each walk one path of about \log_2 N levels, so it makes a fast priority queue. Explained in §5.2 The binary heap., a tree with every entry at most the entries below it, each insert or removal walks one path of about \log_2 N levels for N entries, so a million entries take about 0.2 s instead of hours with a list.

The robot can now find the shortest route to the door on any graph whose edges have costs. Still missing: Dijkstra’s algorithm spreads equally in every direction and settled 54 cells to reach the door; A* searchA search:* Dijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid). Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4. A: cost so far plus the guess adds an estimate of the distance still to go, so the search heads for the door.

RO/navigation/04-graph-search-and-config.title: A* and Heuristics
RO/navigation/04-graph-search-and-config.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Vector magnitude, distance and scalar operationsExplained in: Magnitude, Distance and Scalar Operations on Vectors, §2. Magnitude: the distance from the origin; Depth-first searchDepth-first search (DFS): A search whose frontier is a stack, so it always extends the newest path and dives deep before backing up; it backs up to its last untried choice at dead ends and finds a route, but which one, and how long, depends on the order the moves are tried (22 moves where breadth-first search found 8). Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §6. Depth-first search: dive, then back up; Dijkstra’s algorithmDijkstra’s algorithm: A search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals). Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §3.2 The algorithm: settle the nearest, update its neighbours.
Leads to: Forward state-space searchExplained in: Symbolic Task Planning: STRIPS and PDDL, §5.1 The state graph, built while searching.
Compare with: Breadth-first searchBreadth-first search (BFS): A search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §5. Breadth-first search: ring by ring; Dijkstra’s algorithmDijkstra’s algorithm: A search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals). Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §3.2 The algorithm: settle the nearest, update its neighbours.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Dijkstra’s algorithm finds the robot’s shortest route to the door, but it searches away from the door as much as towards it. Adding a guess of the distance left that never overestimates makes the search head for the door: A* finds the same 3.414 m route after 9 cells instead of 54.


The robot at (2 m, 1 m) can already find a route to the door on its map of the room, cut into 0.5 m cells, 76 of them free (occupancy grid (G-2340))Occupancy grid: A grid map that stores in each cell a number between 0 and 1, such as the probability that the cell is occupied, instead of a hard 0 or 1; the standard grid map of robotics, since sensors are never sure. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §5.2 Bitmaps and occupancy grids. The robot moves from a free cell to any of its 8 neighbours: 0.5 m straight or 0.707 m diagonally, and a diagonal move never cuts the corner of a blocked cell. The robot stands on the corner of the start cell S, which runs from 2.0 to 2.5 m along x and 1.0 to 1.5 m along y; the goal cell G sits just under the door, from 3.5 to 4.0 m along x and 3.5 to 4.0 m along y.
On this grid, Dijkstra’s algorithmDijkstra’s algorithm: A search that always settles the vertex with the smallest distance from the start found so far, which is then final, and offers each of its neighbours the route through it, keeping the shorter; with every edge cost at least 0 it finds the shortest route to every vertex (3.414 m to the door on the room grid with diagonals). Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §3.2 The algorithm: settle the nearest, update its neighbours finds the shortest route from S to G: 3.414 m. Dijkstra keeps an open list of the cells it has reached, the frontier (G-2547)Frontier (open list): The vertices a search has reached but not yet expanded, waiting to be taken off one at a time; which one comes off next is what makes one search differ from another. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §4. Searching with a frontier and a visited list, and always takes off the cell nearest to S.
What still breaks is the work this costs. Figure 1 (top) plays Dijkstra’s search one cell per frame: watch the red cells, the ones taken off the open list, grow as a ring around S, down to the bottom wall and left to the pole, where no route to the door goes.

Figure 1: The same search loop with three guesses h of the distance left, on the room grid from the start cell S to the goal cell G under the door, one cell taken off the open list per frame in all three panels (two per frame after frame “expansion 11”, when only Dijkstra still changes). Top: h = 0, which is Dijkstra’s algorithm. Middle: A* with the straight-line distance to G. Bottom: A* with the octile distance to G. Light red: cells taken off the open list; light green: cells on it; orange outline: the cell just taken off; grey: blocked cells. A* with the octile distance is done after 9 cells, with the straight line after 11, and each holds its last frame; Dijkstra spreads in every direction and is done after 54. All three routes (blue) are 3.414 m long; Dijkstra’s differs in shape because several routes tie at that length
Dijkstra takes 54 cells off its open list in all: every free cell nearer to S than 3.414 m, 53 of them, and then G (notebook). Dijkstra ranks cells only by the distance already driven, so it knows nothing about where the door is and spreads evenly in every direction (CS188 §1.4).
The other two panels of Figure 1 run the search this Note builds, A*: the same loop, with a guess of the distance left added to each cell’s score. With the straight-line distance as the guess (middle) it reaches G after 11 cells, with the octile distance of Section 2 (bottom) after 9, and both return the same 3.414 m. This Note adds the one thing Dijkstra lacks, a guess of the distance left, and makes it safe to use:

the guess itself, the heuristic (Section 2);
searching by the guess alone, which is fast but can go the wrong way (Section 3);
A*, which adds the guess to the distance driven (Section 4);
why A* still returns the shortest route when the guess never overestimates (Section 5), and the stronger rule it needs when it never revisits a cell (Section 6);
variants for less memory (Section 7), for searching from the door (Section 8), for several goals (Section 9), for less time (Section 10), for fewer cells on open grids (Section 11), and for routes that are not limited to 45° turns (Section 12).

2. A guess of the distance left: the heuristic


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Dijkstra cannot tell a cell near the door from a cell far from it. A cheap guess of the distance left from each cell, worked out as if there were no obstacles, gives it that sense of direction: from S the guess is 3.121 m, the true distance 3.414 m.


The idea. Dijkstra ranks the cells on its open list by the distance driven from S, so a cell 1 m behind the robot ranks with a cell 1 m towards the door. To prefer the second, the search needs, for each cell, some idea of how far the door still is. The idea has to be cheap: the exact distance left is what we are searching for.
A traveller does this with a map: before knowing the roads, the distance as the crow flies already tells which town is nearer. The robot can do the same on its grid: count the moves to G as if the table, the cabinet and the poles were not there.
The standard term. A function that guesses the cost still to go from a cell to the goal is a heuristic (G-2570)Heuristic h: A cheap guess of the cost still to go from a state to the goal, such as 3.121 m from the start cell to the door; a search uses it to prefer states that look nearer the goal. Explained in §2. A guess of the distance left: the heuristic., written h (CS188 §1.4; LaValle §2.2.2). Figure 2 writes the guess for our room in every free cell.
Make interactive
Figure 2: The heuristic h in every free cell of the left part of the room (x 0 to 5.5 m): the octile distance to G, in m, the length of the shortest 8-connected route if there were no obstacles. From S it is 3.121 m, the dotted route of 3 diagonal and 2 straight moves, which runs through the table’s cells; the dashed line is the straight-line distance, 2.915 m. The true shortest route from S is 3.414 m
The mechanism on our numbers. On an empty 8-connected grid the shortest route makes diagonal moves while both the column count and the row count still have to shrink, and straight moves for what is left (Patel, Heuristics). S is 3 columns left of G and 5 rows below it, so with:

\Delta x, the number of columns between the cell and G, 3 for S;
\Delta y, the number of rows between the cell and G, 5 for S;
m, the smaller of \Delta x and \Delta y, 3 for S;
M, the larger of them, 5 for S;
a, the length of a straight move, 0.5 m;
\ell, the length of a diagonal move, 0.707 m.

The route takes m diagonal moves, which cover the 3 columns and 3 of the rows, and then M - m straight moves for the 2 rows left:
h(S) = 3 \times 0.707 + 2 \times 0.5
= 2.121 + 1.0
= 3.121 \text{ m}
The same in symbols:
h = \ell \times m + a \times (M - m)
This heuristic is the octile distance (G-2571)Octile distance: The length of the shortest route between two cells of an 8-connected grid with no obstacles: diagonal moves while both the column and the row count shrink, then straight moves; with straight moves of length a and diagonals of length \ell it is \ell \min + a(\max - \min) of the column and row counts; a heuristic for 8-connected grids that never overestimates. Explained in §2. A guess of the distance left: the heuristic. (Patel, Heuristics). The octile distance is the exact answer to an easier problem, the same grid with every obstacle removed; dropping a rule of the real problem in this way is a common source of heuristics (CS188 §1.4).
A second heuristic is the straight line from the centre of S to the centre of G, the Euclidean distance (G-715)Euclidean distance: The straight-line distance between two points. Explained in: Handling Missing Data: KNN Imputer, §4.1 The Euclidean distance, which drops one more rule: that moves follow the grid. With 3 columns and 5 rows of 0.5 m:
\text{straight line} = 0.5 \times \sqrt{3^2 + 5^2}
= 0.5 \times \sqrt{34}
= 0.5 \times 5.83095
= 2.915 \text{ m}
Both heuristics cost a few multiplications per cell, and both fall short of the true 3.414 m, because the table makes the real route bend. The heuristic is ready; the next question is how the search should use it.
3. Following the guess alone: greedy best-first search


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Taking off the open list the cell whose heuristic h, the guess of the distance left, is smallest heads straight for the goal and looks at few cells, but it never counts the distance already driven, so it can return a long route: 9.536 m where 8.000 m exists.


The idea. The simplest use of the heuristic from Section 2: keep the same open list, but always take off the cell that looks nearest to the goal, the one with the smallest h. On the door trip this works: it reaches G after 7 cells with the 3.414 m route (notebook).
The standard term. Expanding, at every step, the open cell with the smallest heuristic value is greedy best-first search (G-2573)Greedy best-first search: A search that always expands the open state with the smallest heuristic value, ignoring the cost already paid; it heads straight for the goal and looks at few states, but can return a long route. Explained in §3. Following the guess alone: greedy best-first search. (CS188 §1.4). “Best-first” names any search that takes off the open list the cell that scores best; “greedy” says the score is the heuristic alone.
Where it goes wrong. The door trip is too short to show the flaw, so we give the robot a longer trip in the same room: from the bottom-left corner cell (x 0 to 0.5 m, y 0 to 0.5 m) to a cell at the right wall (x 6.5 to 7.0 m, y 1.5 to 2.0 m), behind the table. Figure 3 runs greedy best-first search on it: watch the red cells head up and to the right, straight at the goal, until the table’s left side stops them, and then slide down the table to the bottom of the room.

Figure 3: Greedy best-first search on the long trip, from S in the bottom-left corner cell to G at the right wall, one cell per frame: it always takes off the open list the cell with the smallest heuristic h, the octile distance to G (7.121 m at S), and never looks at the distance already driven. The search heads up and right, meets the table, and slides down its left side. Last frame: its route, 9.536 m after 21 cells (blue), and the shortest route, 8.000 m along the bottom wall (green, dashed)
Greedy best-first search returns 9.536 m after 21 cells; the shortest route, along the bottom wall, is 8.000 m (notebook). The climb towards the goal’s height looked good to the heuristic, and nothing in the score counted what the climb and the way back down cost:
\text{extra} = 9.536 - 8.000
= 1.536 \text{ m}
Greedy search can go straight to the goal or wander like a badly guided depth-first search, depending on the obstacles (CS188 §1.4). The fix is to score each cell by both what it has cost and what it still promises.
4. A*: cost so far plus the guess


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A* scores every cell on the open list by f = g + h: the length of the best route found so far from S to the cell, plus the heuristic, the guess of the length left. A* takes off the cell with the smallest f, so it heads for the door like greedy search but drops a route as soon as its distance driven makes it look worse than another.


Greedy search of Section 3 forgot the distance driven; Dijkstra forgot the distance left. A* adds the two. We walk it through on the door trip, where every step can be checked by hand (CMU 16-350, A*; Hart et al. 1968).
4.1 g, h and f on the first step
For every cell the search has reached, it keeps three numbers:

g, the length of the best route found so far from S to the cell, in m: the cost so far (G-2574)Cost so far g (g-value): The length of the best route found so far from the start to a state; A* lowers it whenever a shorter way into the state turns up. Explained in §4.1 g, h and f on the first step., also called the g-value;
h, the heuristic: the octile distance, a guess of the length left from the cell to G, in m (Section 2);
f, their sum, in m: the estimated total cost (G-2575)Estimated total cost f (f-value): The cost so far plus the heuristic, f = g + h: the length of the best route through a state if the guess were exact; A* expands the open state with the smallest f. Explained in §4.1 g, h and f on the first step., also called the f-value, the length of the best route through the cell if the heuristic were exact.

f = g + h
At the start only S is on the open list, with g = 0 and h = 3.121 m, so f = 3.121 m. A* takes S off and expands it, as in breadth-first search (G-2550)Breadth-first search (BFS): A search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §5. Breadth-first search: ring by ring: it puts each of its 8 neighbours on the open list, here with its own g, h and f. For the cell diagonally up and to the right of S, 2 columns left of G and 4 rows below it:
g = 0.707
h = 2 \times 0.707 + 2 \times 0.5
= 2.414
f = 0.707 + 2.414
= 3.121 \text{ m}
For the cell straight above S, 3 columns and 4 rows from G:
g = 0.5
h = 3 \times 0.707 + 1 \times 0.5
= 2.621
f = 0.5 + 2.621
= 3.121 \text{ m}

4.2 The smallest f first, ties to the smaller h
A* now takes off the open list the cell with the smallest f, as Dijkstra takes the smallest g. Two cells tie at 3.121 m, the cell up and to the right of S and the cell above S. A tie is broken by the smaller heuristic, which means the cell nearer to G by the heuristic (Patel, Heuristics): 2.414 m beats 2.621 m, so the cell up-right of S goes first (frame “2”).
Frames “2” to “4” show why the smallest f is a good choice. While the search heads straight for G, each move adds to g exactly what it takes off h, so f stays at 3.121 m. Moving up from the cell up-right of S:
g = 0.707 + 0.5 = 1.207
h = 2.414 - 0.5 = 1.914
f = 1.207 + 1.914 = 3.121 \text{ m}
At the cell below the table’s corner (frame “4”) the diagonal towards G would cut the corner of a blocked table cell, which is not allowed. The cell above it gets f = 3.414 m: the detour round the corner costs what the heuristic did not see,
3.414 - 3.121 = 0.293 \text{ m}
4.3 A shorter way in lowers g
The cells straight up from the cell up-right of S are used up: the next one has f = 3.414 m. So A* goes back to the other cell with f = 3.121 m, the one straight above S (frame “5”). From there it reaches the cell two above S again. That cell already had g = 1.414 m from the first time it was reached, by two diagonal moves; the new way in is two straight moves:
g_{\text{old}} = 0.707 + 0.707 = 1.414 \text{ m}
g_{\text{new}} = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0 \text{ m}
The new way is shorter, so A* lowers the cell’s g to 1.0 m and its f from 3.536 to 3.121 m (CMU 16-350, A*). Frame “6” does the same one cell higher: 1.914 m falls to 1.5 m. A cell on the open list keeps the best g found so far, never the first.
4.4 Parent arrows give the route
Now every f left is 3.414 m or more. Three cells tie at 3.414 m, and the smallest heuristic, 1.207 m, wins (frame “7”); then the cell left of G (frame “8”), then G itself (frame “9”). G comes off the open list with h = 0, so its f is its g: 3.414 m, the route length.
To find the route itself, each cell also stores the cell its best g came from: its parent (G-2576)Parent (back pointer): The vertex from which a search reached a vertex, stored with it during the search; following parents back from the goal gives the route. In A*, a cell’s parent changes whenever a shorter way in lowers its cost so far. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §4. Searching with a frontier and a visited list, the back pointer breadth-first search keeps too, here changed whenever g drops (CMU 16-350, A*). The last frame of Figure 4 draws the parents as arrows. Following them back from G to S gives the route: up-right from S, three cells up, past the table’s corner, and right into G.
4.5 The algorithm
The steps of Sections 4.1 to 4.4, with the open list kept as a priority queue (G-2568)Priority queue: A collection with two operations, insert an entry with a priority and remove the entry with the best priority (for Dijkstra’s algorithm, the smallest distance); it is what lets a search always pick its most promising vertex next. Explained in: Dijkstra’s Algorithm and Priority Queues, §5.1 Why a plain list is slow ordered by f and the closed list as the visited list (G-2548)Visited list (closed list): The vertices a search has already expanded; a search never expands them again, so it explores each vertex once (7 expansions on the waypoint graph instead of 40 paths). Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §4. Searching with a frontier and a visited list of cells already expanded (CMU 16-350, A*; LaValle §2.2.2):

Put S on the open list with g = 0 and f = h(S).
Take off the open list the cell with the smallest f (ties: the smallest h) and put it on the closed list.
If that cell is G, stop: follow the parents back to S.
Otherwise, for each neighbour that is free and not on the closed list, work out g through the current cell. If the neighbour is new, or this g is smaller than its stored g, store the new g, f and parent and put it on the open list.
Go to step 2.

The loop above is A* (G-2577)A search:* Dijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid). Explained in §4.5 The algorithm., “A star” (Hart et al. 1968): Dijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h instead of g. With h = 0 everywhere, f is g and A* is Dijkstra (LaValle §2.2.2; Patel, Heuristics).
Figure 1 compared exactly these two, top and bottom: 54 cells with h = 0 against 9 with the octile heuristic, for the same 3.414 m. A* returned the shortest route here, but nothing so far says it always will.
5. Why A* returns the shortest route: admissible heuristics


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

If the heuristic h is never more than the true distance left, f, the cost so far plus the heuristic, is a lower bound on any route through a cell, so the first route to G off the open list is the shortest. The heuristic is the one free choice in A*: among heuristics that never overestimate, a closer one takes fewer cells, 54, 11 and 9 for h = 0, the straight line and the octile distance, all with the 3.414 m route.


A* stopped at 3.414 m after only 9 of the 76 cells, without looking at most of the room. Section 5 checks why the cells it never expanded cannot hide a shorter route.
5.1 A guess that never overestimates
A trip by road is never shorter than the distance as the crow flies, so “crow-flight distance so far plus crow-flight distance left” can never overshoot the trip (Wikipedia, A* search algorithm). A* relies on the same property. A heuristic that is never more than the true cost left from any cell is an admissible heuristic (G-2578)Admissible heuristic: A heuristic that is never more than the true cost left from any state, h \le h^\ast; it makes f a lower bound on every route through a state, so the first route A* takes off the open list is the shortest. Explained in §5.1 A guess that never overestimates. (CS188 §1.4). With:

h(n), the heuristic at a cell n, in m (3.121 m at S);
h^\ast(n), the true shortest distance left from n to G, in m (3.414 m at S).

The rule is, for every cell:
h(n) \le h^\ast(n)
The octile heuristic is admissible because it is the length of the shortest route in the room with its obstacles removed (Section 2), and putting obstacles back can only remove moves, never add a shorter one (LaValle §2.2.2). Figure 5 checks this on every free cell: the true distances come from one Dijkstra run backwards from G, and every dot lies on or below the line where guess and truth are equal.

5.2 Why the first route out is the shortest
When G comes off the open list, every other route from S to G is still unfinished. Any such route starts in a closed cell, S, and must leave the closed cells somewhere: the first cell it reaches outside them is on the open list. Take the cell left of S, which is on the open list when G comes off (Figure 4, frame “9”), with:

n, that open cell;
g(n), its cost so far, 0.5 m, one straight move from S, already the shortest way to it;
h(n), its heuristic, 3.328 m;
f(n), its estimated total cost, 3.828 m;
L(n), the length of the shortest route from S to G through n, in m, unknown;
g(G), the length A* returns, 3.414 m; since h(G) = 0, it is also f(G).

L(n) = 0.5 + h^\ast(n)
\ge 0.5 + 3.328
= 3.828
\ge 3.414
= g(G)
The same steps in symbols:
L(n) = g(n) + h^\ast(n)
\ge g(n) + h(n)
= f(n)
\ge f(G)
= g(G)
The second line is the admissible rule; the fourth holds because A* took G off before n, so f(G) was the smallest f on the open list. Every open cell gives the same chain, so no route is shorter than the one A* returned (CS188 §1.4). The first line needs g(n) to be the shortest way to n; it is here, and Section 6 shows when the closed list breaks it.
The chain also shows what a heuristic that overestimates does. If h could be larger than h^\ast, the second line would fail, f(n) could exceed the length of the best route through n, and A* could take G off before ever expanding n: it might return a longer route, though faster (Patel, Heuristics). Section 10 uses that trade on purpose.
5.3 A closer guess takes fewer cells
The loop of Section 4.5 never changes; the heuristic h is the one part we choose, and it decides how much the loop searches. Any admissible heuristic keeps the answer right; the closer it is to the true distance left, the fewer cells A* takes off the open list. An admissible heuristic that is never smaller than another, cell by cell, dominates it (G-2579)Dominance (of heuristics): One admissible heuristic dominates another when it is at least as large at every state; being closer to the true cost, it makes A* expand fewer states (the octile distance dominates the straight line). Explained in §5.3 A closer guess takes fewer cells. (CS188 §1.4): the octile distance dominates the straight line, which dominates 0. A cell is taken off the open list only if its f is at most the route’s length (Hart et al. 1968), and a larger admissible heuristic pushes more cells’ f above it, so fewer cells look as promising as the real route. 6. When admissible is not enough: consistent heuristics


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A* never expands a cell twice, so a cell closed by a long way in keeps that wrong cost so far g. A heuristic can be admissible and still let that happen. The fix is a consistent heuristic: along any move it never falls by more than the move’s length, and then every cell leaves the open list with its shortest g.


Section 5.2 needed the cost so far g of each open cell to be the shortest way in. On the grid that held, because the octile heuristic changes by no more than the move between two neighbouring cells; Section 6.2 shows why that matters. Here is a heuristic that is admissible and still breaks it.
6.1 The closed list throws away a shorter way in
A trace by hand is easier on a few points than on 76 cells, so we use a small roadmap in the same room: five points joined by straight lines through free floor, with lengths in metres. S is the robot at (2.0, 1.0) m, G the doorway’s centre at (3.6, 4.0) m, and A, B and C are points of free floor (Figure 6). The shortest route is S-A-C-G:
\text{S-A-C-G} = 1.581 + 0.906 + 1.166
= 3.653 \text{ m}
The heuristic is 0 at every point except A, where the robot remembers the exact distance left from an earlier trip:
h(A) = 0.906 + 1.166
= 2.072 \text{ m}
No value of the heuristic is above the true distance left, so the heuristic is admissible. Figure 6 runs A* on it; watch frames “run 1: take C off” and “run 1: take A off”.

6.2 The fix: a guess that never drops faster than the distance
The trouble is the jump in the heuristic between A and C: over an edge of 0.906 m, h falls from 2.072 m to 0. A real distance left cannot fall by more than the distance moved, so a heuristic that does breaks the picture A* relies on. With:

n, a cell or point;
n', a neighbour of it, one move away;
c, the length of the move from n to n', in m.

The rule is, for every move:
h(n) \le c + h(n')

Explained in §6.2 The fix: a guess that never drops faster than the distance., also called a monotone heuristic (CMU 16-350, A*; Wikipedia, A* search algorithm). The rule is a triangle inequality: going from n to G directly is estimated no longer than going by way of n'. Figure 7 checks one move of each example.

6.3 Why consistency keeps g right
The consistent rule makes f never fall along a route. Take a move from the cell below the table’s corner, n, to the cell above it, n', with:

g(n), the cost so far at n, 1.707 m;
h(n), its heuristic, 1.414 m, so f(n) = 3.121 m;
c, the move, 0.5 m;
h(n'), the heuristic at n', 1.207 m.

f(n') = 1.707 + 0.5 + 1.207
= 3.414
\ge 1.707 + 1.414
= 3.121
= f(n)
The same steps in symbols:
f(n') = g(n) + c + h(n')
\ge g(n) + h(n)
= f(n)
The second line is the consistent rule with g(n) added to both sides. So the f values along any route never decrease, and A* takes cells off the open list in order of f. A cell reached first by a long way, as C by way of B, has a larger f than every cell on its short way in, so those cells come off first and lower its g before it is closed (CMU 16-350, A*; Wikipedia, A* search algorithm).
On the roadmap, run 1’s f falls from 3.653 at A to 2.487 at C by way of A: that fall is what let C close early.
A second fix keeps any admissible heuristic: reopen a closed cell when a shorter way into it turns up, at the price of expanding some cells more than once (CS188 §1.4). The octile heuristic is consistent, so on the grid A* expands each cell once and returns the shortest route. What it still costs is memory: it keeps every cell it has reached.
7. Saving memory: iterative deepening and IDA*


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A* stores every cell it has reached; a depth-first search stores only its current route. Iterative deepening repeats a depth-first search with a growing limit; IDA* puts the limit on f, the cost so far plus the heuristic, so it returns the shortest route while storing at most one route: on the door trip, 17 visits with at most 7 cells in memory.


When A* stopped on the door trip it held 23 cells: 9 on the closed list and 14 on the open list (notebook). The room is small, but a planner over position and heading, or over the joints of an arm, has far more states, and A*‘s lists grow with the number of states it reaches (CMU 16-350, heuristics).
The idea. Depth-first search (G-2552)Depth-first search (DFS): A search whose frontier is a stack, so it always extends the newest path and dives deep before backing up; it backs up to its last untried choice at dead ends and finds a route, but which one, and how long, depends on the order the moves are tried (22 moves where breadth-first search found 8). Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §6. Depth-first search: dive, then back up, the search that dives along one route and backs up at dead ends, stores only the route it is on: memory that grows with the length of a route, not with the number of cells (LaValle §2.2.2). But it returns whatever route it finds first. The fix is to give the dive a limit and repeat it with a larger limit until a route fits.
The standard term. Depth-first search with a limit on the number of moves, run with the limits 0, 1, 2 and so on until it reaches the goal, is iterative deepening (G-2581)Iterative deepening (DFID): Depth-first search with a limit on the number of moves, repeated with the limits 0, 1, 2 and so on until the goal is reached; it finds the fewest moves, like breadth-first search, while storing only one route, like depth-first search. Explained in §7. Saving memory: iterative deepening and IDA., also called depth-first iterative deepening (DFID) (LaValle §2.2.2; Korf 1985). Iterative deepening finds the route with the fewest moves, like breadth-first search, with the memory of depth-first search. IDA*. Put the limit on the estimated total cost f = g + h, the cost so far plus the heuristic (Section 4.1), instead of on the number of moves. Round 1 dives from S and drops any branch whose f passes the limit, which starts at h(S) = 3.121 m. If no route fits, the next round’s limit is the smallest f that passed: no route can be shorter, since f never overestimates.
Depth-first search with a limit on f is IDA* (G-2582)IDA (iterative-deepening A):** Iterative deepening with the limit on f = g + h instead of on moves, each new limit being the smallest f that passed the last; it returns the shortest route with an admissible heuristic while storing only the current route. 8. Searching from the door: backward and bidirectional search


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A search can run from the goal back to the start, or from both ends until they meet. From the door, which stands against the wall, Dijkstra needs 31 cells instead of 54; from both ends, 38. Two searches that meet must still compare every cell both have reached, because the cell where they meet need not lie on the shortest route.


Every search so far started at S. But the door never moves while robots, and the same robot later, start from many places; and the door’s side of the room is narrow, against the top wall.
8.1 Backward search
The idea. Run the search from G, following each move backwards, until it reaches S. Our moves cost the same in both directions, so the backward search uses the same moves (LaValle §2.2.3). Its cost so far g at a cell is then the distance left from that cell to G, the true distance left h^\ast of Section 5.1.
Run to the end, one backward search gives every cell’s distance to the door at once: a perfect heuristic for later searches, and the route for any start (CMU 16-350, heuristics). Many robots sharing one destination can use one search from the destination instead of one A* each (Patel, Variants).
The standard term. Searching from the goal towards the start, with every move reversed, is backward search (G-2583)Backward search: A search that starts at the goal and follows every move backwards until it reaches the start; it is cheaper when the goal’s side branches less, and run to the end it gives every state’s cost to the goal. Explained in §8.1 Backward search. (LaValle §2.2.3). Figure 9 (top) runs Dijkstra backwards from G: it reaches S after 31 cells, against 54 forwards (notebook).
Only 30 free cells lie within 3.414 m of G, against 53 within 3.414 m of S, because the door stands against the wall and much of the circle round it lies outside the room. A backward search pays when the goal’s side branches less than the start’s (LaValle §2.2.3).

8.2 Bidirectional search
The idea. Grow two searches at once, one from S and one from G, a step of each in turn; a route exists as soon as a cell has been reached by both. Each search then has to cover only about half the distance.
The standard term. Running a forward search from the start and a backward search from the goal until they meet is bidirectional search (G-2584)Bidirectional search: A forward search from the start and a backward search from the goal run in turn until some state has been expanded by both; the route is the smallest sum of the two costs over all states both reached, since the meeting state can be off the shortest route. Explained in §8.2 Bidirectional search. (LaValle §2.2.3; MIT 6.006 L18 notes). Figure 9 (bottom) alternates one Dijkstra step from S and one from G: the red ring round S and the blue ring round G grow until a cell has come off both open lists, after 38 cells, 19 from each side.
The 38 are fewer than the 54 of the forward search, but more than the backward search alone: in our room, the door’s narrow side is the cheaper one to search from. In many larger problems bidirectional search cuts the exploration sharply (LaValle §2.2.3).
8.3 When to stop, and where the route is
The two searches stop when some cell, call it w, has come off both open lists (MIT 6.006 L18 notes). The route through w seems the obvious answer, but w need not lie on the shortest route. On the door trip the meeting cell happens to lie on a shortest route, so Figure 10 shows the trap on a shorter trip: from R, the cell two above S, to G.

                  Key point 
                  
                

When any of several goals will do, join each goal to one added vertex, the virtual goal, and run A* to it once, with the smallest of the guesses to the goals: for three charging docks this takes 12 cells instead of 30 for three separate runs, and ends at the dock nearest by route, 3.207 m away, which is not the dock nearest in a straight line. A goal that moves becomes many goals, one per cell and time: searching over (cell, time), the robot meets a walking person at 5.414 s.

9.1 The virtual goal
The idea. The three runs search the same room three times; one search can find the nearest dock instead. Add one new vertex V and join each dock to it by an edge of 0 m (CMU 16-350, A*). V is not a place in the room; reaching it stands for “docked”. Every route to V passes through one dock and costs exactly as much as the route to that dock, so the shortest route to V ends at the dock nearest by route (Patel, Heuristics).
The guess. A* to V needs a heuristic: a guess of the distance left to V, which is the distance to whichever dock is nearest. The guess is the smallest of the octile distances of Section 2 to the three docks (Patel, Heuristics). D1 is 4 columns and 5 rows from S, D2 is 6 columns and 1 row, so with:

h_{\text{G}}, h_{\text{D1}}, h_{\text{D2}}, the octile distances from a cell to G, D1 and D2, in m;
h, the heuristic of the search to V at that cell, in m.

h_{\text{G}}(S) = 3.121 \text{ m}
h_{\text{D1}}(S) = 4 \times 0.707 + 1 \times 0.5
= 3.328 \text{ m}
h_{\text{D2}}(S) = 1 \times 0.707 + 5 \times 0.5
= 3.207 \text{ m}
h(S) = \min(3.121, 3.328, 3.207)
= 3.121 \text{ m}
The same in symbols:
h = \min(h_{\text{G}}, h_{\text{D1}}, h_{\text{D2}})
The guess never overestimates: the shortest route to V ends at some dock, its length is at least the octile distance to that dock, and that distance is at least the smallest of the three.
The standard term. A* run to an added vertex joined to every acceptable goal is multi-goal A* (G-2585)Multi-goal A:* A* run to an added vertex joined to every acceptable goal, so one search finds the cheapest of several goals, such as the nearest of three charging docks by route or the first reachable meeting point with a moving person. Explained in §9.1 The virtual goal., and the added vertex is a virtual goal (G-2586)Virtual goal (imaginary goal): An extra vertex added to a graph and joined to each real goal by an edge of 0 (or of that goal’s extra cost); the shortest route to it ends at the best real goal, which turns a search for several goals into a search for one. Explained in §9.1 The virtual goal., also called an imaginary goal (CMU 16-350, A*). A backward search from V is a backward search from all goals at once (LaValle §2.2.3).
The run. 9.2 A moving goal
Suppose instead the robot must meet a person who walks under the top wall, along a path the robot knows: the person starts in the cell x 5.0 to 5.5 m and moves one cell (0.5 m) to the left every second, so the person is in the first cell from 0 to 1 s, in the next from 1 to 2 s, and so on. A cell of that walk is a goal only while the person is in it, so the cell alone cannot say whether the robot has arrived in time. The search state (G-2562)Search state: What a search keeps for each vertex: the quantities that decide which moves are allowed and what they cost, and nothing more, such as (cell, charge left) for a robot with a battery; leaving one out breaks the Markov property and can hide routes. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §10. Choosing the search state: the Markov rule, everything the next moves depend on, must hold the time as well as the cell (LaValle §7.1.1). Each pair of a cell and a time at which the person is in that cell joins the virtual goal V: these are the possible intercept points (CMU 16-350, A*).
The moves. The robot drives at 0.5 m/s. From a state (cell, time) it can:

move straight, 0.5 m, which adds 1 s;
move diagonally, 0.707 m, which adds 1.414 s;
wait one second in its cell, which adds 1 s.

Time only moves forward, so no move leads back to an earlier time (LaValle §7.1.1). A route’s cost is its time, so the cheapest route to V is the earliest meeting.
The guess. The cost is now time, so the cost so far, the guess and their sum are in seconds. With:

g, the cost so far of a state: the time at which the robot gets there, in s;
d, the octile distance from the state’s cell to the nearest cell of the person’s walk, in m (2.5 m from S, straight up);
v, the robot’s speed, 0.5 m/s;
h, the guess of the time left, in s;
f, their sum, the estimated total cost, in s.

h(S) = 2.5 / 0.5
= 5 \text{ s}
The same in symbols:
h = d / v
The guess never overestimates: every meeting happens in a cell of the walk, and the robot cannot get there faster.
The run. A* over (cell, time) takes 8 states off the open list, then V (notebook). The first 6 are the straight line up from S, at 0 to 5 s, each with f of 5 s: driving straight at the top wall adds to g exactly what it takes off h. At 5 s the robot would be in the cell x 2.0 to 2.5 m under the wall, but the person is then in the cell to its right. The cheapest states left have f of 5.414 s, and ties go to the smaller guess (Section 4.2), so the first two are the diagonals from the cell below into the top row: into x 1.5 to 2.0 m, where nobody is, and into x 2.5 to 3.0 m, where the person is from 5 to 6 s. L = 4 \times 0.5 + 0.707
= 2.707 \text{ m}
T = 2.707 / 0.5
= 5.414 \text{ s}

10. Trading length for time: weighted A* and anytime A*


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Multiplying the heuristic by a weight \varepsilon above 1 makes A* rush towards the goal: fewer cells, and a route at most \varepsilon times the shortest. Anytime A* runs weighted A* with falling weights and always has a route ready: on the long trip, 9.243 m at once, then 8.414 m, then the shortest, 8.000 m.


A robot must often start moving before an exact search finishes, and a slightly longer route found at once is better than the best route found too late (CMU 16-350, anytime). The door trip is too easy to show the trade: every weight there returns the same 3.414 m. So we use the long trip of Section 3, where A* takes 43 cells to find 8.000 m.
10.1 Weighted A*
The idea. Between Dijkstra, which ignores the heuristic, and greedy search, which follows nothing else, lies a whole range: count the heuristic more than the distance driven. With:

g, h, the cost so far and the heuristic of Section 4.1, in m.

A* takes off the open list the cell with the smallest
f = g + \varepsilon \times h
which is weighted A* (G-2587)Weighted A:* A* that sorts by f = g + \varepsilon h with a weight \varepsilon above 1, counting the guess more than the cost so far; it expands fewer states and returns a route at most \varepsilon times the shortest. Explained in §10.1 Weighted A. (CMU 16-350, heuristics; Pohl 1970). A large \varepsilon behaves like greedy search; \varepsilon = 1 is A* (CMU 16-350, heuristics). 10.2 Anytime A* and ARA*
The idea. Run weighted A* with a large \varepsilon to get a route at once, and then again with smaller and smaller \varepsilon, each run giving a better route, until \varepsilon = 1 gives the shortest. The robot can stop the planner whenever it must move and use the best route so far (CMU 16-350, anytime).

11. Skipping equal routes: jump point search


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

On a grid where every move of one kind costs the same, many routes tie, and A* puts cells of all of them on its open list. Jump point search scans along straight lines and diagonals and puts on the open list only the cells where a route may have to turn: on the door trip, 7 cells ever enter its open list, against 23 for A*, for the same 3.414 m route.


In Figure 1, Dijkstra and A* returned two different routes of the same 3.414 m. On a grid with no obstacles in the way, the number of such equal routes between two cells grows fast, and A* treats each one as a separate possibility, putting its cells on the open list and keeping their numbers.
The idea. Equal routes differ only in the order of the same moves, such as up then up-right against up-right then up (zerowidth JPS). So from a cell, keep going in one direction for as long as nothing could make a turn necessary, without putting the cells passed on the open list. Stop only at the goal, or next to an obstacle’s corner, where a cell beside the line has just opened up and a route may have to turn into it.
The standard terms. A neighbour that the cell before could normally reach by an equally short route of its own, but which an obstacle beside the line leaves reachable by a shortest route only by turning at the current cell, is a forced neighbour (G-2592)Forced neighbour: A neighbour that the cell before could normally reach by an equally short route of its own, but which an obstacle beside the line of travel leaves reachable by a shortest route only by turning at the current cell; it makes that cell a jump point. Explained in §11. Skipping equal routes: jump point search.: the search is forced to look at it there.
A cell where a scan stops, because it is the goal or has a forced neighbour, is a jump point (G-2593)Jump point: A cell where a scan of jump point search stops because it is the goal or has a forced neighbour, a place where a route may have to turn; only jump points go on the open list. Explained in §11. Skipping equal routes: jump point search., and A* that puts only jump points on its open list is jump point search (G-2594)Jump point search (JPS): A* for grids with equal move costs that scans along straight lines and diagonals and puts only jump points on the open list; it skips equal routes that differ only in the order of their moves, and returns the same shortest route with far fewer open-list operations. Explained in §11. Skipping equal routes: jump point search., JPS (Harabor and Grastien 2011; zerowidth JPS).
A diagonal scan checks a straight scan in both of its directions at every step, and stops where one of them finds a jump point (zerowidth JPS). Our grid forbids cutting corners, so we use the version for that rule (Harabor and Grastien 2012). Figure 14 runs it on the door trip.

The scans still look at cells, but looking costs far less than putting a cell on the open list and taking it off again, so JPS is faster without giving up the shortest route, on grids where every straight move and every diagonal move costs the same (Harabor and Grastien 2011; zerowidth JPS).
