RO/navigation/04-graph-search-and-config.title: Obstacles in C-space
RO/navigation/04-graph-search-and-config.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Vector magnitude, distance and scalar operationsExplained in: Magnitude, Distance and Scalar Operations on Vectors, §2. Magnitude: the distance from the origin; Maps and landmarksMap: A robot’s list of the objects in its surroundings that matter, with their positions and properties, such as the pink pole at (1, 3); readings only give positions relative to the robot, and the map turns them into a pose. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §2.1 What a map is for; Configuration spaceConfiguration space (C-space): The set of all configurations of a robot, one point per placement of the whole robot, such as a box of (x, y, \theta) whose top and bottom faces are the same headings for a floor robot; motion planning looks for paths through it. Explained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §2.2 The configuration space of the floor robot.
Leads to: Collision detectionCollision detection: Deciding, yes or no, whether two bodies overlap, such as the robot’s disk and the table; planners call it thousands of times instead of building the obstacle region. Explained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §2.2 Broad phase and narrow phase; Distance queries and GJKExplained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §5.2 The Minkowski difference and GJK.
Compare with: Breadth-first searchBreadth-first search (BFS): A search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §5. Breadth-first search: ring by ring.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A placement of the robot is free only if its whole body misses every obstacle, not just its centre. Drawing each obstacle in C-space as the set of placements that touch it (for a round robot, the obstacle grown by the robot’s radius) turns “is the robot clear?” into “is this point outside the grown obstacles?“.


Make interactive
Figure 1: Left: the room with the robot’s disk footprint, 0.25 m in radius, at the start (2, 1) and at a second placement whose centre is (3.5, 3.2); the doorway in the top wall is 1.2 m wide. Right: a zoom on the table’s corner (3.5, 3.0): the centre is 0.2 m above the corner, outside the table, but the disk reaches 0.25 m and overlaps the table by 0.05 m (red)
So far the robot can plan a route on the room’s grid: breadth-first searchBreadth-first search (BFS): A search whose frontier is a queue, so it expands vertices in rings of equal moves from the start; the first route it finds has the fewest moves, which is the shortest only when every move costs the same. Explained in: Graphs and Uninformed Search, §5. Breadth-first search: ring by ring reaches the cell under the door in 8 moves, and A*Explained in: A* and Heuristics, §4. A: cost so far plus the guess finds a 3.414 m route with diagonal moves. The grid routes move a point. The configuration space (G-2287)Configuration space (C-space): The set of all configurations of a robot, one point per placement of the whole robot, such as a box of (x, y, \theta) whose top and bottom faces are the same headings for a floor robot; motion planning looks for paths through it. Explained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §2.2 The configuration space of the floor robot, C-space for short, makes the whole robot a point too: each placement (x, y, \theta), position and heading, is one point, and the basic motion planning problemBasic motion planning problem (piano mover’s problem): Given a robot, its obstacles, a start configuration and a goal configuration, find a continuous path in C-space between them through configurations where the robot touches no obstacle, or report that none exists; it states every collision-free motion task as one search through C-space. Explained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §6. The basic motion planning problem is to find a path of free points from the start, (2 m, 1 m) facing 30°, to the doorway centre, (3.6 m, 4.0 m).
What still breaks is the word “free”. The map of the room marks where the obstacles are, but the robot is not a point. Its footprint, the floor it covers, is a disk of radius 0.25 m centred on the middle of its axle (Figure 1):

with its centre at (3.5, 3.2), the robot stands 0.2 m above the table’s corner (3.5, 3.0); the centre is outside the table, yet the disk reaches 0.25 m and overlaps the table by 0.05 m;
the doorway is 1.2 m wide, but a robot 0.5 m wide cannot put its centre close to either side of it;
if the robot carries a board 1.4 m long, which way it faces decides whether the board fits through the 1.2 m doorway at all.

The opening question of this Note: which placements (x, y, \theta) are free, so that a planner can search C-space for a route to the door? We answer it in steps:

the placements that touch an obstacle, drawn in C-space, and the free placements that remain, for the round robot (Section 2);
a rule that works for any shape, such as the board, and what turning does to it (Section 3);
whether a path can exist at all: the separate pieces of free space (Section 4).

2. The obstacle region and free space


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

The obstacle region (G-2650)Obstacle region (C-obstacle): The set of all configurations at which the robot’s body touches or overlaps an obstacle, C_{\text{obs}}; drawing it in C-space lets a planner test a placement as one point, such as the disk robot’s centre (3.5, 3.2), which lies in it 0.2 m from the table. Explained in §2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle. is every placement at which the robot touches an obstacle; free space (G-2651)Free space: All configurations at which the robot touches no obstacle, C_{\text{free}}, the C-space without the obstacle region; a planner looks for a path that stays inside it. Explained in §2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle. is all the others. For the disk robot, a placement touches an obstacle exactly when its centre is within 0.25 m of it, so the obstacle region is every obstacle grown by 0.25 m.


2.1 Why the centre alone cannot say what is free
The first part of the opening problem is the placement with its centre at (3.5, 3.2). Its centre is outside the table, so a planner that tests only the centre calls it free. Figure 1 shows that it is not: the disk reaches below the centre to y = 2.95, and the table’s corner is at y = 3.0. With:

the centre’s height, 3.2 m;
the robot’s radius, 0.25 m;
the corner’s height, 3.0 m.

The lowest point of the disk, straight below the centre:
3.2 - 0.25 = 2.95 \text{ m}
The disk’s lowest point lies below the corner, by:
3.0 - 2.95 = 0.05 \text{ m}
So whether a placement is free depends on every floor point the robot covers, not on one point. Testing the whole disk against every obstacle for every placement a planner tries is the slow way; the rest of this section moves the test to the centre, where a planner can make it in one step.
2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle
To move the test to the centre, picture the robot sliding round the table while it keeps touching it, like a coin pushed round the edge of a book. Its centre traces a closed curve round the table (Figure 2). Every centre inside that curve puts the disk on the table; every centre outside leaves a gap. So the curve splits the placements in two, and we can draw the split once, in C-space, instead of testing the disk again and again.
Figure 2 plays the slide, counter-clockwise from under the table’s bottom edge. Watch the stages named in its titles. “Along an edge”: the centre runs parallel to the edge, 0.25 m out. “At a corner”: the centre swings round the corner on an arc of radius 0.25 m. The last stage, “the centre (3.5, 3.2) lies inside the grown table”, fills the curve and marks the placement of Figure 1, which falls inside.

Figure 2: Animation: the robot’s 0.25 m disk footprint slides counter-clockwise round the table, always touching it; a black line joins its centre to the touching point. Along an edge the centre runs parallel to the edge, 0.25 m out; at a corner it swings round on an arc of radius 0.25 m. The orange trace of the centre closes into the boundary of the grown table, which the last frames fill (orange) and in which they mark the centre (3.5, 3.2), 0.2 m from the corner, in collision
The standard terms (LaValle §4.3.1; Hauser ch.9):

The set of floor points the robot covers when it is placed at a configuration (a placement) is its footprint at that configuration (G-2286)Configuration: The list of numbers that fixes the position of every point of a robot, such as q = (x, y, \theta) = (2, 1, 0.524) for a floor robot or the joint angles (\theta_1, \theta_2) of a 2R arm; with it a planner treats the whole robot as one point. Explained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §2.1 The configuration: numbers that place every point.
The set of all configurations at which the footprint touches or overlaps an obstacle is the obstacle region (G-2650)Obstacle region (C-obstacle): The set of all configurations at which the robot’s body touches or overlaps an obstacle, C_{\text{obs}}; drawing it in C-space lets a planner test a placement as one point, such as the disk robot’s centre (3.5, 3.2), which lies in it 0.2 m from the table. Explained in §2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle., also called the C-obstacle, or C-space obstacle.
Everything else in C-space is free space (G-2651)Free space: All configurations at which the robot touches no obstacle, C_{\text{free}}, the C-space without the obstacle region; a planner looks for a path that stays inside it. Explained in §2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle.: the configurations at which the robot touches nothing.

The obstacle region of the table, the filled shape in the last frame of Figure 2, is the table’s C-obstacle. The configuration whose centre is (3.5, 3.2) lies in it; the start, (2, 1), does not.
The formal version needs set notation, which we read on small instances:

q is a configuration, such as the start, q = (2 \text{ m}, 1 \text{ m}, 30^\circ);
C is the C-space, the set of all configurations;
A(q) is the robot’s footprint at q, a set of floor points: at the start, every point within 0.25 m of (2, 1);
O is the obstacles, the set of floor points covered by the table, the cabinet, the poles and the walls;
\cap gives the intersection (G-967)Intersection (A ∩ B): The set of elements that are in both A and B, such as the points inside both of two half-planes; for events, the event that both A and B happen. Explained in: Naive Bayes Foundations: Conditional Probability, §2. The definition, the points in both sets, and \emptyset is the empty set, so A(q) \cap O \ne \emptyset reads “the robot and the obstacles share at least one point”;
\setminus removes one set from another: C \setminus C_{\text{obs}} is C without the obstacle region;
\in reads “is in”: q \in C says that q is one of the configurations in C;
in the braces, the bar reads “such that”.

C_{\text{obs}} = \lbrace q \in C \mid A(q) \cap O \ne \emptyset \rbrace
C_{\text{free}} = C \setminus C_{\text{obs}}
(LaValle §4.3.1, eq. 4.34; Hauser ch.9). A planner now asks one question per configuration: is q in C_{\text{obs}}? For the disk, the slide of Figure 2 already gave the answer’s shape; the next step gives its rule.
2.3 Growing the obstacles by the robot’s radius


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

For a disk robot, the obstacle region of each obstacle is a grown obstacle (G-2652)Grown obstacle (inflated obstacle): An obstacle with every point within the robot’s radius added, its edges pushed out and its corners rounded; for a disk robot it is exactly the obstacle region, so the robot can be treated as a point (the table, 3.625 m², grows to 5.747 m² for a 0.25 m radius). Explained in §2.3 Growing the obstacles by the robot’s radius.: the obstacle with its edges pushed out by the radius, 0.25 m, and its corners rounded with arcs of radius 0.25 m. The grown table covers 5.747 m² against the table’s 3.625 m².


Figure 2 found the table’s obstacle region by sliding the disk round it. A planner needs a rule it can compute for every obstacle of the room, and the disk gives a simple one.
Why the rule holds. The disk covers every floor point within 0.25 m of its centre. The disk touches an obstacle exactly when some obstacle point lies within 0.25 m of the centre: when the centre’s Euclidean distance (G-715)Euclidean distance: The straight-line distance between two points. Explained in: Handling Missing Data: KNN Imputer, §4.1 The Euclidean distance, the straight-line distance, to the nearest obstacle point is at most 0.25 m. So for the disk (Hauser ch.9, “Planar translating disks”):

r is the robot’s radius, 0.25 m;
\text{dist}(q, O) is the distance from the centre of configuration q to the nearest point of the obstacles O, in m: 0.2 m for the centre (3.5, 3.2).

C_{\text{obs}} = \lbrace q \mid \text{dist}(q, O) \le r \rbrace
The configuration of Figure 1 passes the test:
\text{dist} = 0.2 \le 0.25
so it is in the obstacle region, as the disk’s 0.05 m overlap showed. An obstacle grown this way, every point within r of it added, is a grown obstacle (G-2652)Grown obstacle (inflated obstacle): An obstacle with every point within the robot’s radius added, its edges pushed out and its corners rounded; for a disk robot it is exactly the obstacle region, so the robot can be treated as a point (the table, 3.625 m², grows to 5.747 m² for a 0.25 m radius). Explained in §2.3 Growing the obstacles by the robot’s radius., also called an inflated obstacle. The robot has become a point, and the obstacles have grown by its size.
Why lines and arcs. Along an edge, the nearest obstacle point is on that edge, so the centres at distance 0.25 m form a line parallel to the edge. Round a corner, the nearest point is the corner itself, so they form an arc of a circle of radius 0.25 m about the corner (Hauser ch.9). Each arc spans the angle by which the table’s outline turns at that corner. At the corner (3.5, 3.0) the two edges meet at a right angle, so its arc is a quarter circle. A centre straight above that corner, like the one of Figure 1, has the corner as its nearest table point, 0.2 m away.
A check: the grown table’s area. The growth adds a strip along every edge and a wedge of a circle at every corner. The table’s numbers (notebook):

the table’s area, 3.625 m²;
the table’s perimeter, the four edges added, 7.704 m;
the turns of its outline at its four corners: 104.0°, 71.6°, 94.4° and 90.0°.

Walking round a convex outline, we turn at each corner and finish facing the way we started, so the turns add up to one full turn:
104.0 + 71.6 + 94.4 + 90.0 = 360^\circ
The four corner wedges therefore make one whole circle of radius 0.25 m. The strips are each edge’s length times 0.25 m. Adding the parts:
\text{grown area} = 3.625 + 7.704 \times 0.25
+ \pi \times 0.25^2
= 3.625 + 1.926 + 0.196
= 5.747 \text{ m}^2
The same steps in symbols:

s is the obstacle’s area, in m²;
p is its perimeter, in m;
r is the robot’s radius, in m.

\text{grown area} = s + p\thinspace r + \pi r^2
The library that grows shapes in the notebook (shapely) measures the same 5.747 m². So the table’s obstacle region is 2.122 m² larger than the table:
5.747 - 3.625 = 2.122 \text{ m}^2
Every one of those extra square metres is floor that looks free on the map but where the robot’s centre cannot go. The table is one obstacle; the room has four more kinds.
2.4 The room in C-space, and the drive to the door


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Grow every obstacle of the room by 0.25 m, walls included, and what stays white is the free space of the disk robot. The doorway leaves 0.7 m for the centre, and the straight 3.4 m drive from the start to the doorway centre clears the grown table by 0.132 m.


The second part of the opening problem is the doorway. Growing every obstacle answers it and the first part at once. Figure 3 grows the whole room (Hauser ch.9):

the walls move 0.25 m into the room, because the centre must stay 0.25 m from each wall;
each pole, 0.1 m in radius, becomes a disk 0.35 m in radius;
the cabinet’s L grows along its outline;
the door jambs, the wall ends at (3.0, 4.0) and (4.2, 4.0), grow into quarter-disks of radius 0.25 m.

Make interactive
Figure 3: The obstacle region of the room for the disk robot: every obstacle grown by 0.25 m (orange), the walls moved 0.25 m inwards, the poles grown to 0.35 m disks, the door jambs grown into quarter-disks. White is the free space. The centre (3.5, 3.2) (red) is inside the grown table; the start (2, 1) and the doorway centre (3.6, 4.0) are free; only 0.7 m of the 1.2 m doorway is free for the centre
In Figure 3, white is free space and orange is the obstacle region; a configuration is free when its centre is on white. The doorway’s free stretch lies between the two grown jambs:
3.0 + 0.25 = 3.25 \text{ m}
4.2 - 0.25 = 3.95 \text{ m}
3.95 - 3.25 = 0.7 \text{ m}
So of the 1.2 m doorway, 0.7 m is open to the centre, which settles the second part of the opening problem.
The drive in both pictures. Now the robot can check a whole route. The simplest is the straight drive from the start (2, 1) to the doorway centre (3.6, 4.0): the robot turns on the spot to face along it and drives forward. The drive runs 1.6 m along x and 3.0 m along y:
3.6 - 2.0 = 1.6 \text{ m}
4.0 - 1.0 = 3.0 \text{ m}
\text{length} = \sqrt{1.6^2 + 3.0^2} = 3.4 \text{ m}
\text{heading} = \text{atan2}(3.0,\ 1.6) = 61.9^\circ
where atan2 (G-2325)atan2: A function atan2(rise, run) that returns the direction of a line over the full circle from its rise and run given separately; needed because the plain inverse tangent of the ratio cannot tell opposite directions apart. Explained in: Probabilistic Motion Models: Velocity and Odometry, §4.2 Turn, drive, turn turns the rise, 3.0 m, and the run, 1.6 m, into the direction of the drive.
Figure 4 plays the drive in two pictures side by side, the way it is usually drawn (MR 10.2). Left, the room: the robot turns, then drives. Right, C-space seen from above: the same drive is a point moving through the white free space. Watch the frame “closest to the table”: the robot’s centre passes 0.382 m from the table’s corner, and the point passes 0.132 m from the grown table. The two numbers are one fact in two pictures:
0.382 - 0.25 = 0.132 \text{ m}

Figure 4: Animation in two panels. Left, the room: the robot (disk footprint, radius 0.25 m) at the start (2, 1) facing 30 degrees turns on the spot to 61.9 degrees, then drives straight 3.4 m to the doorway centre (3.6, 4.0); its path so far is green. Right, C-space seen from above: the obstacles grown by 0.25 m (orange) and the robot as a point moving along the same line; during the turn the point stays put. Frame “closest to the table”: after 2.471 m the centre is 0.382 m from the table’s corner, and the point is 0.132 m from the grown table. The last frame shows the whole drive inside free space
The disk is round, so turning on the spot changes nothing it covers: in Figure 4 the point stands still while the robot turns. Every heading gives the same picture, so the C-space slice drawn on the right is the whole story for the disk. The straight drive stays in free space all the way, so the disk robot can drive straight to the door with 0.132 m to spare. The rule that gave this answer, “grow by the radius”, used one fact about the disk: it looks the same from every side. The board of the opening problem does not.
3. The Minkowski sum: obstacles for any robot shape


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

For a robot of any shape that moves without turning, the obstacle region (the placements that touch an obstacle) is the Minkowski sum (G-2653)Minkowski sum: The set of all sums of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \oplus B, like sweeping one shape over the other; the obstacle region of a robot that keeps its heading is the obstacle’s Minkowski sum with the robot reflected through its centre. Explained in §3.2 Minkowski sum and difference. of the obstacle and the robot’s shape reflected through its centre: every obstacle point minus every robot point. For two convex polygons it is a convex polygon with at most as many corners as both together.


3.1 Why a board breaks the disk rule
The third part of the opening problem: the robot carries a board 1.4 m long and 0.3 m wide, centred over the middle of its axle and lying along its heading. The board is what now touches the obstacles, so its outline is the footprint; the 0.25 m disk lies inside it. The board is a new example for one reason: it is not round, so the direction the robot faces matters.
Facing along the wall, at heading 0°, the board lies across the doorway with its full 1.4 m:
1.2 - 1.4 = -0.2 \text{ m}
The board is 0.2 m too long to fit. Facing the door, at 90°, only its 0.3 m width crosses:
1.2 - 0.3 = 0.9 \text{ m}
So “grow every obstacle by one radius” cannot work: the board reaches 0.7 m ahead of its centre but only 0.15 m to the side. We need a rule that builds the obstacle region from any shape, then we can turn the shape.
3.2 Minkowski sum and difference
The rule starts from one placement on the edge of the board’s obstacle region.
Where the board touches. Fix the heading at 0° and slide the board towards the table until its front end touches the table’s bottom-left corner (the first frame of Figure 5). The configuration gives the position of one chosen point of the robot, the middle of its axle, which is also the board’s centre. Each point of the board sits at a fixed offset from that centre: the middle of the front end is 0.7 m ahead. The touching point is that offset added to the centre, and it equals the corner. With the numbers, the centre q is:
q + (0.7,\ 0) = (3.0,\ 1.0)
q = (3.0,\ 1.0) - (0.7,\ 0)
q = (2.3,\ 1.0)
The same steps in symbols, with:

q is the position of the centre, (2.3, 1.0) here;
a is the offset of a point of the robot from the centre, (0.7, 0) for the middle of the front end;
o is the obstacle point it touches, the corner (3.0, 1.0);
A is the robot’s shape as a set of offsets, the board at heading 0°;
O is the obstacle as a set of points, the table.

q + a = o
q = o - a
Touching means some robot point lands on some obstacle point, so the centre is the obstacle point minus the robot point’s offset. Collecting every such centre over every obstacle point and every robot offset gives the obstacle region of the robot moving without turning:
C_{\text{obs}} = \lbrace o - a \mid o \in O,\ a \in A \rbrace
= O \ominus A
(LaValle §4.3.2, eq. 4.37; Hauser ch.9; KAIST C-space slides). Taking every difference of points of two sets is the Minkowski difference (G-2654)Minkowski difference: The set of all differences of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \ominus B, which equals A \oplus (-B); obstacle minus robot gives the obstacle region, and two convex bodies overlap exactly when their difference contains the origin. Explained in §3.2 Minkowski sum and difference., written \ominus. Taking every sum instead is the Minkowski sum (G-2653)Minkowski sum: The set of all sums of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \oplus B, like sweeping one shape over the other; the obstacle region of a robot that keeps its heading is the obstacle’s Minkowski sum with the robot reflected through its centre. Explained in §3.2 Minkowski sum and difference., written \oplus, “add every point of one shape to every point of the other”. Subtracting a is adding -a, the offset turned through 180° about the centre. So with -A, the robot reflected through its centre:
O \ominus A = O \oplus (-A)
(LaValle §4.3.2). The board and the disk are both symmetric about their centre: each offset a has a partner -a on the far side (the front end’s middle (0.7, 0) and the back end’s middle (−0.7, 0)). So for them the reflected shape is the shape itself, and the obstacle region is the obstacle plus the robot. For the disk, adding a 0.25 m disk to every table point gives every point within 0.25 m of the table: the grown table of Section 2.3 is a Minkowski sum.
Building it. “Add every point of one shape to every point of the other” is a picture of sweeping one shape over the other (Hauser ch.9, “Minkowski sums and differences”): place a copy of the reflected board, centred, on every point of the table, and the copies cover the obstacle region. Figure 5 builds it in that order. Watch the stages named in its titles: the board touching the corner; a reflected board centred on each table corner in turn; copies along the edges; copies everywhere, which sweep out a region; and, in the last frame, its outline.

Figure 5: Animation: the board’s obstacle region at heading 0 as a Minkowski sum. First the board (1.4 m by 0.3 m, brown) with its front end on the table’s corner (3.0, 1.0): its centre q is at (2.3, 1.0). Then copies of the reflected board are centred on the table’s four corners, then along its edges, then inside it; together they sweep out a region. The last frames outline it (orange): a convex polygon with 7 corners, on whose left edge the centre (2.3, 1.0) lies
The last frame of Figure 5 has 7 corners. Every corner of the outline is a table corner plus a board corner, and every edge of the outline is a table edge or a board edge moved into place (LaValle §4.3.2, “A polygonal C-space obstacle”; KAIST C-space slides). So for two convex (G-479)Convex set: A set that contains the whole segment between any two of its points. Explained in: Convex Sets, Convex Functions and Convex Optimisation, §2.1 Walking along the segment polygons, sets that contain the segment between any two of their points, the Minkowski sum is convex and has at most as many corners as both together (Hauser ch.9; KAIST C-space slides):
4 + 4 = 8 \text{ corners at most}
At heading 0° the table’s bottom edge and the board’s long edges are all horizontal, so two edges line up into one and 7 corners remain; at 30° there are 8 (notebook). A recipe a computer can follow (Hauser ch.9): add each of the 4 board corners (reflected) to each of the 4 table corners, 16 points, and take their convex hull (G-477)Convex hull: The smallest region with straight edges that contains a set of points; every weighted average of the points lies inside it. Explained in: Self-Attention, Geometrically, §7.1 The output sits between the value vectors, the smallest region with straight edges that contains them. The cabinet, a union of two rectangles, gets one Minkowski sum per rectangle, joined (LaValle §4.3.2). So one rule now covers any shape that keeps its heading; the board, though, turns with the robot.
3.3 Turning: a different slice for every heading


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Each heading gives its own obstacle region in the plane, a slice of C-space; stacked by heading they make the obstacle region in (x, y, \theta). For the board the slices change shape: the doorway is closed to the centre at 0° and open over 0.90 m at 90°.


The board’s obstacle region of Figure 5 was for heading 0° only. Turn the robot to 30° and the board points a different way, so the reflected board in the Minkowski sum turns too, and the obstacle region changes shape. The obstacle region for all configurations (x, y, \theta) is three-dimensional; holding the heading fixed cuts it into a flat slice: the set of positions (x, y) that are free, or not, at that one heading (KAIST C-space slides; Hauser ch.9, “C-obstacles for rotational motion”).
Figure 6 plays the slices of the whole room for the robot with the board, one heading per frame, from 0° to 180° in steps of 10°. The small panel shows which way the board points. Watch the orange obstacle region swell along the board’s direction as it turns, and watch the green bar in the doorway: the doorway’s free stretch for the centre.

Figure 6: Animation: the obstacle region of the room (orange) for the robot carrying the 1.4 m by 0.3 m board, one heading per frame from 0 to 180 degrees in steps of 10 degrees; white is free; a small panel shows the board’s heading. The orange region stretches along the board’s direction. The doorway’s free stretch for the centre (green bar): closed at 0 degrees, 0.22 m at 30, 0.55 m at 60, 0.90 m at 90, then closing again; the slice at 180 degrees is the same as at 0
The doorway’s free stretch at each heading (notebook):





















Heading0°20°30°60°90°Free stretch of the doorway00.05 m0.22 m0.55 m0.90 m
At 0° the doorway is shut, as the 0.2 m shortfall of Section 3.1 said; it opens at about 18° and is widest, 0.90 m, when the board faces the door. At 180° the board covers the same floor as at 0°, so the slice is the same: the board’s obstacle region repeats every half turn.
Figure 7 stacks the slices with the heading as the height, for the table alone. For the board, the slices turn and change shape as the heading rises, so the obstacle region is a twisted column. For the disk, every slice is the same grown table, so the column is straight. Both columns run from 0° to 360°, and in C-space the top and the bottom are the same heading (360° is 0°), so each column’s top joins its bottom: one region, not two ends (MR 10.2).
Make interactive
Figure 7: Slices stacked by heading. Left: the table’s obstacle region for the board, one orange outline every 10 degrees of heading from 0 to 360 (thicker every 90 degrees); the outlines turn and change shape, making a twisted column. Right: the same for the disk robot; every outline is the table grown by 0.25 m, making a straight column. The table itself is drawn in blue at the bottom and the top
So for the board, whether a position is free depends on the heading: the centre (3.6, 4.0) in the doorway is in the obstacle region at 0° and free at 90°. The robot carrying the board must face the door to pass. Free space has become a three-dimensional shape that may be cut into separate pieces, which decides whether any route exists.
4. Connected components of free space


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Free space, the placements that touch nothing, can fall into separate pieces, its connected components (G-2656)Connected component (of free space): A piece of free space within which the robot can move from any configuration to any other without touching an obstacle; a path between two configurations exists only if both lie in the same component. Explained in §4.1 One piece or several., and a path between two configurations exists only if both lie in the same piece. For the disk the room’s free space is one piece; for the board single slices split into 2 to 4 pieces, but turning joins them all into one.


4.1 One piece or several
The opening question asks for free placements so that a planner can search for a route. Before any search, one question settles whether a route can exist: can the robot get from the start to the door without leaving free space?
Free space can fall into pieces that free paths cannot join. Within one piece, the robot can move from any configuration to any other without touching an obstacle; between two pieces, every path crosses the obstacle region. Each such piece is a connected component (G-2656)Connected component (of free space): A piece of free space within which the robot can move from any configuration to any other without touching an obstacle; a path between two configurations exists only if both lie in the same component. Explained in §4.1 One piece or several. of free space, and a path between two configurations exists only if both lie in the same component (MR 10.2).
The disk robot. In Figure 3 the white free space is one piece: every gap between grown obstacles stays open. The narrowest is between the green pole and the bottom wall:

the pole’s centre is 0.8 m above the wall;
the pole’s radius is 0.1 m;
the robot is 0.5 m wide.

The gap under the pole, and what is left of it once the robot is in it:
0.8 - 0.1 = 0.7 \text{ m}
0.7 - 0.5 = 0.2 \text{ m}
The notebook counts the pieces of the free space on a grid of 0.01 m and finds one. So the start and the door are in the same component, which is why the drive of Figure 4 could exist.
4.2 Turning joins the pieces
The board, one heading at a time. The disk’s free space is one piece; the board’s is not, at a fixed heading. Figure 8 colours the free pieces of two slices, one colour per piece. At heading 0° the free space has 2 pieces: a large one and a small one of 0.39 m² right of the table, above the green pole. At heading 90° there are 3:

a large piece that holds both the start (2, 1) and the doorway centre (3.6, 4.0);
a piece round the green pole, which holds the point (6.6, 1.3);
a sliver of 0.004 m² between the table and the cabinet.

At 60° there are 4 (notebook).
Make interactive
Figure 8: Connected components of free space in two slices for the robot carrying the board; each colour is one piece of free centres, orange is the obstacle region. Heading 0 degrees: 2 pieces. Heading 90 degrees: 3 pieces; the start (2, 1) and the doorway centre (3.6, 4.0) share the large green piece, the point (6.6, 1.3) is in the blue piece round the green pole, and a sliver of 0.004 square metres sits between the table and the cabinet
A robot at (6.6, 1.3) facing the door, if it kept that heading, could never reach the door: its piece of the 90° slice does not include the doorway. The robot can turn, though, and a turn moves it up or down through the stack of Figure 7 into another slice, where the pieces lie differently. The notebook joins all the slices from 0° to 179°, every 1°, with the heading wrapping round, and counts the pieces of free space in (x, y, \theta): one. The pieces of each slice are cross-sections of that one region, cut at one heading, as an obstacle drawn on the 2R arm’s square C-spaceExplained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §5.1 Cutting the torus into a square can look like three pieces until we remember that its opposite edges are glued (MR 10.2).
So for the board too a path exists from the start to the door. The robot can turn on the spot at the start from 30° to 90°, which stays free at every heading in between (notebook), and the large piece of the 90° slice then holds both ends. A path in C-space may also move sideways, which a differential-drive robot cannot do directly (no sideways motionExplained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §6.1 The rule: no sideways motion); turning such a path into wheel commands is a later topic.
4.3 Why planners do not build the obstacle region
The obstacle regions of this Note were cheap to build: a disk and a board against a few convex shapes in a 3D C-space. Real robots break all three conditions:

the robot and the obstacles are not convex; a Minkowski sum of two non-convex shapes is the union of the sums of their convex pieces and can have many more corners (Hauser ch.9);
in 3D, two objects of 444 and 1,134 triangles give a Minkowski sum made of 66,667 pieces (KAIST C-space slides 15 and 16);
an arm with six joints has a six-dimensional C-space, in which no picture or stack of slices can hold the obstacle region.

So building the obstacle region exactly is impractical (MR 10.2; KAIST C-space slides). Most planners never build it. Instead, a planner asks a subroutine one question at a time: is this configuration free, and is this short path segment free (MR 10.2; Hauser ch.10, “Implicit C-obstacle representation”)? Answering those questions fast, for thousands of configurations, is collision checkingExplained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §2. Collision detection: broad phase and narrow phase.
5. Summary








































IdeaWhat it isOn our roomObstacle regionconfigurations at which the robot touches an obstaclecentre (3.5, 3.2) is in it, 0.2 m from the tableFree spaceall other configurationswhite in Figure 3Grown obstaclefor a disk robot, the obstacle plus every point within the radiustable 3.625 m² grows to 5.747 m²Minkowski sumevery point of one shape plus every point of the otherthe board’s region at 0°: 7 corners, at most 4 + 4Slicethe obstacle region at one headingthe doorway is closed to the centre at 0°, open over 0.90 m at 90°Connected componenta piece of free space that free paths can crossdisk: 1; board: 2 to 4 per slice, 1 in all

For the disk robot a configuration is free when its centre lies outside every obstacle grown by 0.25 m: the centre (3.5, 3.2) is 0.2 m from the table, so it is in collision, the doorway leaves 0.7 m for the centre, and the straight 3.4 m drive to the doorway centre clears the grown table by 0.132 m, because the disk touches an obstacle exactly when its centre is within 0.25 m of it. The robot carrying the 1.4 m board must face the door, because the doorway is closed to its centre at 0° and open over 0.90 m at 90°.
The obstacle region (G-2650)Obstacle region (C-obstacle): The set of all configurations at which the robot’s body touches or overlaps an obstacle, C_{\text{obs}}; drawing it in C-space lets a planner test a placement as one point, such as the disk robot’s centre (3.5, 3.2), which lies in it 0.2 m from the table. Explained in §2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle. is drawn once in C-space, so a planner can test a configuration as a point instead of testing the whole robot against every obstacle.
Growing a convex obstacle pushes its edges out and rounds its corners, so its area grows by perimeter times radius plus one circle, because the corner turns of a convex outline add up to 360°.
The Minkowski difference (G-2654)Minkowski difference: The set of all differences of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \ominus B, which equals A \oplus (-B); obstacle minus robot gives the obstacle region, and two convex bodies overlap exactly when their difference contains the origin. Explained in §3.2 Minkowski sum and difference. O \ominus A, every obstacle point minus every robot offset, is the obstacle region of a robot that keeps its heading, because a robot point a lands on an obstacle point o exactly when the centre is at o - a; for robots symmetric about their centre, such as the disk and the board, it is the Minkowski sum (G-2653)Minkowski sum: The set of all sums of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \oplus B, like sweeping one shape over the other; the obstacle region of a robot that keeps its heading is the obstacle’s Minkowski sum with the robot reflected through its centre. Explained in §3.2 Minkowski sum and difference. of the obstacle and the robot.
Two convex polygons give a convex sum with at most as many corners as both together, so the sum is quick to build from the corner sums and their convex hull.
For a robot that is not round, each heading has its own slice of C-space, so the board must face the door: the doorway is shut to its centre at 0° and open over 0.90 m at 90°.
A path exists only within one connected component (G-2656)Connected component (of free space): A piece of free space within which the robot can move from any configuration to any other without touching an obstacle; a path between two configurations exists only if both lie in the same component. Explained in §4.1 One piece or several. of free space, so counting pieces tells before any search whether the door can be reached; turning joins the board’s 2 to 4 pieces per slice into one.

The robot can now tell, for any configuration, whether its body is clear of the room, and the disk robot has a free straight drive to the door. Still missing: building the obstacle region exactly costs too much for real robots, so planners test one configuration or one segment at a time, and they need those tests to be fast and their distances to treat headings correctly. Collision checking and nearest neighbours in C-spaceExplained in: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space, §1. Overview builds those tests.

RO/navigation/04-graph-search-and-config.title: Collision Checking and Nearest Neighbours in C-space
RO/navigation/04-graph-search-and-config.content:
Where this fits 
                  
                


Builds on: Vector magnitude, distance and scalar operationsExplained in: Magnitude, Distance and Scalar Operations on Vectors, §2. Magnitude: the distance from the origin; Dot productDot product: Multiplying two vectors entry by entry and adding the products, u^{\mathsf T}x, which gives one number. It is large when the vectors point the same way, so it measures similarity and gives projections. Explained in: Dot Product and Cosine Similarity, §3. Computing the dot product; Uniform distributionUniform distribution: A distribution in which every outcome in a range is equally likely. Explained in: Uniform and Log-normal Distributions, §2. The uniform distribution; K-nearest neighboursK-nearest neighbours (KNN): Predicting from the answers of the k closest stored points. Explained in: K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN), §2. How KNN predicts; Minkowski sumMinkowski sum: The set of all sums of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \oplus B, like sweeping one shape over the other; the obstacle region of a robot that keeps its heading is the obstacle’s Minkowski sum with the robot reflected through its centre. Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §3.2 Minkowski sum and difference; Obstacle region and free spaceFree space: All configurations at which the robot touches no obstacle, C_{\text{free}}, the C-space without the obstacle region; a planner looks for a path that stays inside it. Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle.




1. Overview


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A planner that never builds the obstacle region asks three questions thousands of times: is this configuration free, is this straight segment free, and which stored configuration is nearest? Cheap box tests first, a tree of boxes, well-ordered checks along a segment and a distance that knows headings wrap answer them fast and correctly.


Make interactive
Figure 1: Left: the room with three test points. The robot’s disk centred at (3.5, 3.2) (red) overlaps the table. The segment from a = (2, 2) to b = (4, 3.6) has free ends and a free middle (green), yet the point (3.5, 3.2) on it is in collision. Right: a heading dial with a query at 350 degrees and stored headings at 15 and 320 degrees; round the circle 15 is 25 degrees from 350, while plain subtraction says 335
So far the robot knows which of its placements are free. The obstacle region (G-2650)Obstacle region (C-obstacle): The set of all configurations at which the robot’s body touches or overlaps an obstacle, C_{\text{obs}}; drawing it in C-space lets a planner test a placement as one point, such as the disk robot’s centre (3.5, 3.2), which lies in it 0.2 m from the table. Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacle, the set of configurations at which the robot’s body touches an obstacle, is the room’s obstacles grown by the robot’s 0.25 m radius. In it, the robot’s disk with its centre at (3.5, 3.2) touches the table, and the straight drive from the start (2, 1) to the doorway centre (3.6, 4.0) is free. But building that region exactlyExplained in: Obstacles in C-space, §4.3 Why planners do not build the obstacle region is impractical for real robots, so planners ask one question at a time instead (MR 10.2; Hauser ch.10). Three questions come back thousands of times, and on our room each has a trap (Figure 1):

Is this configuration free? Testing the robot exactly against every obstacle for every configuration is slow: with 10,000 bodies there are 49,995,000 pairs to test (Müller SAP slides).
Is this straight segment free? A segment holds infinitely many configurations. The segment from (2, 2) to (4, 3.6) is free at both ends and in the middle, yet the robot at (3.5, 3.2), three quarters of the way along, hits the table.
Which stored configuration is nearest? Headings wrap round: a stored heading of 15° is 25° from a query at 350°, but plain subtraction says 335°, so a plain search returns the wrong neighbour.

This Note builds the tools that answer them, on the same room and the same 0.25 m disk:

cheap box tests before exact ones (Section 2), a tree of boxes (Section 3) and links of one robot that may hit each other (Section 4);
how far a robot is from an obstacle (Section 5) and how to check a whole segment (Section 6);
a distance for configurations with headings (Section 7), a nearest-neighbour search that knows headings wrap (Section 8), and random configurations that favour no direction (Section 9).

2. Collision detection: broad phase and narrow phase


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Collision detection (G-2665)Collision detection: Deciding, yes or no, whether two bodies overlap, such as the robot’s disk and the table; planners call it thousands of times instead of building the obstacle region. Explained in §2.1 The yes-or-no question and what it costs. answers “do these two bodies overlap?” in two steps: the broad phase (G-2666)Broad phase: The first, cheap step of collision detection: wrap each body in a simple shape such as a box and keep only the pairs whose shapes overlap, so the costly exact test runs on few pairs. Explained in §2.2 Broad phase and narrow phase. throws out pairs whose simple boxes do not overlap, and the narrow phase (G-2667)Narrow phase: The second step of collision detection: the exact overlap test on the pairs the broad phase kept, such as the distance from the robot’s centre to the table compared with its 0.25 m radius. Explained in §2.2 Broad phase and narrow phase. tests the few pairs left exactly. Sweep and prune finds the overlapping boxes by sorting them along one axis.


2.1 The yes-or-no question and what it costs
The first question of the opening problem: is the configuration with centre (3.5, 3.2) free? Answering it means collision detection (G-2665)Collision detection: Deciding, yes or no, whether two bodies overlap, such as the robot’s disk and the table; planners call it thousands of times instead of building the obstacle region. Explained in §2.1 The yes-or-no question and what it costs.: deciding, yes or no, whether two bodies overlap (Hauser ch.7, “Proximity queries”). Besides the walls, the robot can overlap four pieces of furniture in our room (the table, the cabinet and the two poles), so one configuration needs four exact tests for them, and a planner runs thousands of configurations. The exact test is the costly part: for the disk against the table it means the distance from the centre to a polygon; for detailed bodies, made of thousands of triangles like triangle meshes (G-2338)Triangle mesh: A set of triangles, each given by three corner points in space, that together cover an object’s surface (a table as 12 triangles on 8 corners); fast to draw in 3D, but it does not say what is inside. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §5.1 Triangle meshes, many more steps.
With n bodies there are this many pairs, because each body pairs with every other body and each pair is counted twice:

n is the number of bodies: 5 in our room (the robot and the four pieces of furniture).

\text{pairs} = \frac{n(n - 1)}{2}
= \frac{5 \times 4}{2} = 10
For a scene of 10,000 bodies, the same count gives 49,995,000 pairs (Müller SAP slides). Most of those pairs are far apart and could be ruled out at a glance. The question is how to glance cheaply.
2.2 Broad phase and narrow phase


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

Wrap each body in its smallest box with sides along x and y. Two bodies can only touch if their boxes overlap, and two boxes are compared with four number comparisons.


A box round a body is a quick stand-in for it: if two boxes do not overlap, the bodies inside cannot overlap either. Comparing two boxes takes four comparisons of numbers, far fewer steps than an exact test. So collision detection runs in two phases (Müller SAP slides; LaValle §5.3.1):

the broad phase (G-2666)Broad phase: The first, cheap step of collision detection: wrap each body in a simple shape such as a box and keep only the pairs whose shapes overlap, so the costly exact test runs on few pairs. Explained in §2.2 Broad phase and narrow phase.: wrap every body in a simple shape and keep only the pairs whose shapes overlap;
the narrow phase (G-2667)Narrow phase: The second step of collision detection: the exact overlap test on the pairs the broad phase kept, such as the distance from the robot’s centre to the table compared with its 0.25 m radius. Explained in §2.2 Broad phase and narrow phase.: test the kept pairs exactly.

A simple shape that encloses a body for such a quick test is a bounding volume (G-2668)Bounding volume: A simple shape that encloses a body, such as a sphere or a box; if two bounding volumes do not overlap, neither do the bodies, so it gives a quick test before an exact one. Explained in §2.2 Broad phase and narrow phase.: a sphere, a box, or a box turned with the body (Hauser ch.7). The commonest is the smallest box with sides along the x and y axes that holds the body, which we call the body’s box. Two such boxes overlap exactly when their x-intervals overlap and their y-intervals overlap (Hauser ch.7).

2.3 Sweep and prune
Testing the robot’s box against every other box is still a test per pair, 10 for our 5 bodies. Sweep and prune (G-2670)Sweep and prune: A broad phase that sorts the boxes by their left edge and sweeps along x, comparing each box only with the boxes it overlaps along x; it cuts the pairs tested, though long boxes that span the axis defeat it. Explained in §2.3 Sweep and prune. cuts that number by sorting (Müller SAP slides):

sort the boxes by their left edge;
sweep a vertical line from left to right: a box joins the list of active boxes when the line reaches its left edge and leaves at its right edge;
a box that joins is compared only with the boxes already active, the ones it overlaps along x;
for those pairs, a full box test checks y as well; a pair that passes goes to the narrow phase.

Sorting puts the boxes that might overlap next to each other, so each box looks only at its neighbours along x. The sort takes far fewer steps than testing all pairs (Müller SAP slides). With:

n the number of bodies, each in its box, now 10,000;
\log_2 n the number of times n can be halved before reaching 1, 13.3 for 10,000.

\text{sort steps} \approx n \log_2 n
\log_2 10{,}000 = 13.3
10{,}000 \times 13.3 = 133{,}000
The sort’s 133,000 steps are far below the 49,995,000 pairs, though how many pairs the sweep then compares depends on how the boxes lie (Müller SAP slides). Sweep and prune looks along one axis only, and a long wall’s box overlaps almost every other box along that axis.
3. Bounding-volume hierarchies


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A bounding-volume hierarchy (G-2671)Bounding-volume hierarchy (BVH): A tree of nested bounding volumes, each holding its two children’s down to one per body; a query skips every body inside a box that misses, so it needs about \log_2 n box tests for n bodies (9 among the room’s 25). Explained in §3.1 Why a tree of boxes. is a tree of boxes: each box holds two smaller ones, down to one box per body. A query opens a box only if it overlaps the robot’s box, so for n bodies it reaches the few near the robot after about \log_2 n levels: 9 box tests among the room’s 25 bodies.


3.1 Why a tree of boxes
The walls were left out of the sweep. Put them in, and each wall’s box stretches along a whole side of the room, overlapping almost every box along x, so sorting along one axis separates little (Müller BVH slides). With many bodies spread in two or three dimensions the problem grows: for 100 × 100 objects in a plane, sweep and prune still tests about 100 objects for each one (Müller BVH slides).
The fix is to group nearby bodies, and groups of groups, each group in one box. A query starts at the box that holds everything; if the robot’s box misses a group’s box, every body inside is ruled out at once. A tree of nested bounding volumes, each holding the boxes of its two children down to one box per body, is a bounding-volume hierarchy (G-2671)Bounding-volume hierarchy (BVH): A tree of nested bounding volumes, each holding its two children’s down to one per body; a query skips every body inside a box that misses, so it needs about \log_2 n box tests for n bodies (9 among the room’s 25). Explained in §3.1 Why a tree of boxes., BVH for short (Hauser ch.7; Müller BVH slides).
So that each wall takes up only a small box, we store it as panels about 1 m long, as a triangle mesh (G-2338)Triangle mesh: A set of triangles, each given by three corner points in space, that together cover an object’s surface (a table as 12 triangles on 8 corners); fast to draw in 3D, but it does not say what is inside. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §5.1 Triangle meshes stores a surface in small pieces: 7 panels along the bottom, 4 up each side and 3 on each side of the doorway, 21 in all. With the 4 pieces of furniture, the room has 25 bodies.
3.2 Building and searching the tree
The tree is built from the top down (Müller BVH slides; Hauser ch.7):

one box round all 25 bodies is the root;
sort the bodies of a box by the centres of their boxes along x and split them into two halves of equal count (13 and 12 here); each half gets its own box;
repeat inside each half, sorting along y, then x again, and so on, until each box holds one body.

A query for the robot’s box descends from the root (Hauser ch.7, “BVH queries”):

test the box of the current node against the robot’s box;
if they miss, skip the node and everything inside it;
if they overlap and the node holds one body, pass that body to the narrow phase; otherwise test both children.

Figure 3 builds the tree level by level, then runs the query for the robot at (3.5, 3.2). Watch the room on the left and the tree on the right: a red box is a miss, and every body under it is skipped without a test. The stage “query, test 4” is the first miss: the box of the room’s lower-left walls, which the robot’s box does not reach. The last frame shows the 9 tests that leave one body, the table.

Brute force would test 25 boxes
The query needed 9 box tests instead of 25 (notebook). From the start (2, 1), where nothing is close, it needs 11, and over 2,000 random centres in the room it averages 12.0. The tree has 5 levels below the root, because halving 25 bodies 4 times still leaves boxes with two bodies, and 5 times leaves one:
2^4 = 16 < 25 \le 32 = 2^5
In general, for a balanced tree:

n is the number of bodies, such as 32;
L is the number of levels below the root, 5 for 32 bodies.

n = 2^L
L = \log_2 n
so a query that goes down one branch makes about \log_2 n box tests (Müller BVH slides). With 10,000 objects in a plane that is about 13 tests per object, against about 100 for sweep and prune and 10,000 for brute force (13.3 from Section 2.3); with 1,000,000 objects in 3D, about 20 against about 10,000 and 1,000,000 (Müller BVH slides):
\log_2 1{,}000{,}000 = 19.9
The count grows when the robot is close to many bodies at once, since then several branches must be opened (Hauser ch.7, “Performance”). A BVH is built once for bodies that do not move and reused for every query, which is why planners use it for the room’s furniture and walls. The robot itself, though, may be more than one body.
4. Self-collision


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A robot made of several links can hit itself. A self-collision (G-2672)Self-collision: Two links of the same robot overlapping, such as an arm’s third link folding back across its first; a configuration with a self-collision is not free, so planners test the robot’s own link pairs too. Explained in §4. Self-collision. check tests the pairs of links that can meet; links joined by a joint touch all the time and are left out.


The first question, is this configuration free, has one more part for robots with several links. Our disk robot is one rigid body, so it cannot hit itself. An arm can: its links move relative to each other, and a far link can fold back onto a near one. We switch to a new example for this one section: a planar arm with three links, 1.0 m, 0.8 m and 0.6 m long, drawn as line segments, like the 2R armExplained in: Configuration Space and Degrees of Freedom, §3.2 Degrees of freedom of a robot made of links, the arm with two joints on the robot’s top plate, with a third link added. Its configuration is three joint angles, each measured from the direction of the link before it.
Figure 4 shows two configurations. At joint angles (0°, 90°, 90°) the arm folds into a hook and link 3 stays clear of link 1. At (0°, 150°, 150°) link 3 folds back across link 1, crossing it at (0.54, 0): a self-collision (G-2672)Self-collision: Two links of the same robot overlapping, such as an arm’s third link folding back across its first; a configuration with a self-collision is not free, so planners test the robot’s own link pairs too. Explained in §4. Self-collision., the robot’s own links overlapping (LaValle §4.3.1, “Obstacle region for multiple bodies”).
Make interactive

Right: joint angles (0, 150, 150) degrees; link 3 folds back across link 1 and crosses it at (0.54, 0), marked red: a self-collision
Which pairs to test. The pairs to test are the pairs of links that must not overlap (LaValle §4.3.1). Links next to each other share a joint, so they touch all the time and are left out (LaValle §4.3.1). For a chain of m links, the count of pairs is the one we used for bodies:
\text{all pairs} = \frac{m(m - 1)}{2}
\text{pairs joined by a joint} = m - 1
For our arm, with 3 links:
\frac{3 \times 2}{2} - 2 = 1 \text{ pair: links 1 and 3}
For an arm with 7 links:
\frac{7 \times 6}{2} - 6 = 15 \text{ pairs}
Some of the remaining pairs can never meet whatever the joint angles, and some always overlap; testing them wastes time. So robot software such as MoveIt’s Setup Assistant samples 10,000 random configurations by default and turns off checking for the pairs that are never in collision, always in collision, in collision in the robot’s default pose, or joined by a joint (MoveIt docs). For our arm, links 1 and 3 cross in 735 of 10,000 random configurations, 7.35 percent (notebook), so the pair stays on the list.
The self-collision pairs join the broad phase and the narrow phase like any other pair: a configuration is free only if no link hits an obstacle and no pair on the list overlaps (LaValle §4.3.1, eq. 4.36). Every check so far answers yes or no; a planner often needs to know by how much.
5. Distance queries


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A distance query (G-2674)Distance query: A geometric query that returns the shortest distance between two bodies, 0 if they overlap; it tells a planner how much room the robot has, not only whether it is free. Explained in §5.1 How far, not only whether. returns how far apart two bodies are, not only whether they touch. For two convex bodies it equals the distance from the origin to their Minkowski difference, which the GJK algorithm (G-2678)GJK algorithm: The Gilbert-Johnson-Keerthi algorithm: it decides whether two convex shapes overlap, or how far apart they are, by searching their Minkowski difference for the origin using each shape’s farthest point in chosen directions, without building the difference. Explained in §5.2 The Minkowski difference and GJK. finds from the shapes’ farthest points in chosen directions, without building the difference.


5.1 How far, not only whether
The second question, whole segments, needs more than yes or no. At the start (2, 1) the robot is free, but how much room does it have? A planner uses the answer to move fast where there is room and carefully near obstacles, and Section 6 uses it to clear whole segments at once. A distance query (G-2674)Distance query: A geometric query that returns the shortest distance between two bodies, 0 if they overlap; it tells a planner how much room the robot has, not only whether it is free. Explained in §5.1 How far, not only whether. returns the shortest distance between two bodies, 0 if they overlap (Hauser ch.7, “Proximity queries”). The distance from the robot’s body to the nearest obstacle is its clearance, the room it has to move.
Figure 5 (left) answers it for the start. The robot’s centre is 1.0 m from the table’s corner (3.0, 1.0) and 1.0 m above the bottom wall, and the body reaches 0.25 m of that:
1.0 - 0.25 = 0.75 \text{ m}
So the clearance at the start is 0.75 m, to the table and to the bottom wall alike (notebook). Seen in C-space, the clearance is the distance from the centre to the nearest grown obstacle (G-2652)Grown obstacle (inflated obstacle): An obstacle with every point within the robot’s radius added, its edges pushed out and its corners rounded; for a disk robot it is exactly the obstacle region, so the robot can be treated as a point (the table, 3.625 m², grows to 5.747 m² for a 0.25 m radius). Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §2.3 Growing the obstacles by the robot’s radius. When two bodies overlap, a distance query can say instead how deep the overlap is: at (3.5, 3.2) the disk reaches 0.05 m into the table (Hauser ch.7).
5.2 The Minkowski difference and GJK

For a disk the distance was one subtraction. For two bodies of any convex shape, the Minkowski difference (G-2654)Minkowski difference: The set of all differences of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \ominus B, which equals A \oplus (-B); obstacle minus robot gives the obstacle region, and two convex bodies overlap exactly when their difference contains the origin. Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §3.2 Minkowski sum and difference, every point of one shape minus every point of the other, gives a single rule. Take every point of the robot minus every point of the table:

if the two share a point, some difference is (0, 0), so the difference contains the origin and the bodies overlap;
otherwise the distance between the bodies is the smallest length of a difference, which is the distance from the origin to the Minkowski difference (dyn4j GJK distance).

In Figure 5 (right), the orange shape is the robot at (2, 1) minus the table. The shape does not contain the origin, and its nearest point to the origin is (−0.75, 0): 0.75 m, the clearance found above.
Farthest points. Building the whole difference costs as much as building the obstacle regionExplained in: Obstacles in C-space, §4.3 Why planners do not build the obstacle region. The GJK algorithm (G-2678)GJK algorithm: The Gilbert-Johnson-Keerthi algorithm: it decides whether two convex shapes overlap, or how far apart they are, by searching their Minkowski difference for the origin using each shape’s farthest point in chosen directions, without building the difference. Explained in §5.2 The Minkowski difference and GJK., named after Gilbert, Johnson and Keerthi, never builds it (dyn4j GJK). GJK works with one point at a time: the point of a shape farthest in a chosen direction, found as the point with the largest dot product (G-634)Dot product: Multiplying two vectors entry by entry and adding the products, u^{\mathsf T}x, which gives one number. It is large when the vectors point the same way, so it measures similarity and gives projections. Explained in: Dot Product and Cosine Similarity, §3. Computing the dot product with that direction, each coordinate times the direction’s, added (dyn4j GJK). With:

v the chosen direction, (1, 0), from the robot towards the table;
-v the opposite direction, (-1, 0).

The dot products of the table’s four corners (3, 1), (5, 1), (5.5, 2.5) and (3.5, 3) with -v are:
-3.0,\ -5.0,\ -5.5,\ -3.5
The largest is −3.0, so the table’s farthest point in the direction -v is the corner (3.0, 1.0). The robot’s farthest point in the direction v is its rim point straight ahead of the centre:
(2 + 0.25,\ 1) = (2.25,\ 1)
The farthest point of the difference in the direction v is the robot’s farthest point in v minus the table’s farthest point in -v (dyn4j GJK), because the dot product of a difference with v is the robot point’s dot product minus the table point’s, which is largest when the first is largest and the second smallest:
(2.25,\ 1) - (3.0,\ 1.0) = (-0.75,\ 0)
The point (−0.75, 0) is already the nearest point of the difference to the origin. In general GJK picks a direction towards the origin, adds the farthest point found there, and repeats with the triangle (in 3D, the tetrahedron) of points found so far, until a triangle encloses the origin (overlap) or no new point gets past the origin (apart); each step costs one farthest point per shape (dyn4j GJK). A bounding-volume hierarchy speeds up distance queries as it speeds up yes-or-no checks, as in the collision libraries PQP and FCL (Hauser ch.7). With distances in hand, the second question of the opening problem, whole segments, can be answered.
6. Checking a path segment


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A segment cannot be checked point by point, so we check points at most a step apart: too large a step misses thin collisions, and checking in halving order (ends, middle, quarter points, …) finds a collision sooner. With clearances, a piece of segment is free once the free circles at its two ends meet.


6.1 A segment holds infinitely many configurations
The second question of the opening problem: is the straight segment from a = (2, 2) to b = (4, 3.6) free? Both ends are free and so is its middle, (3, 2.8). A planner cannot test every point, because a segment holds infinitely many configurations (LaValle §5.3.4), so it tests some points and hopes the rest are free. Checking a segment by testing points along it is edge resolution (G-2679)Edge resolution (segment checking): Checking a straight path segment in C-space for collisions by testing points along it, spaced at most a chosen step apart; too long a step can miss a thin collision, too short a step wastes time. Explained in §6.1 A segment holds infinitely many configurations., also called dynamic collision checking (Hauser ch.10).
The segment is 2.561 m long. The notebook finds its colliding stretch: from 0.620 to 0.777 of the way along, 0.403 m round the table’s corner, (3.5, 3.2) among it.
6.2 Step size and order
Step size. Split the segment into k equal steps no longer than a chosen step \varepsilon (Hauser ch.10, “Dynamic collision checking”):

d(a, b) is the segment’s length, 2.561 m;
\varepsilon is the longest step allowed, in m;
\lceil \cdot \rceil rounds up to a whole number;
k is the number of steps; the checks are its k + 1 end points.

k = \left\lceil \frac{d(a, b)}{\varepsilon} \right\rceil
With \varepsilon = 0.6 m:
k = \lceil 2.561 / 0.6 \rceil = \lceil 4.27 \rceil = 5
\text{step} = 2.561 / 5 = 0.512 \text{ m}
The checks sit at 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1 of the way. The colliding stretch runs from 0.620 to 0.777, between the checks at 0.6 and 0.8, so all six checks are free and the segment wrongly passes. A step shorter than the thinnest obstacle a collision can hide in is needed; too short a step wastes time (Hauser ch.10; LaValle §5.3.4). With \varepsilon = 0.1 m we halve the segment until each piece is shorter than 0.1 m, so that the halving order below can use the same points:
2.561 \to 1.281 \to 0.640 \to 0.320
\to 0.160 \to 0.080 \text{ m}
Five halvings give 32 steps of 0.080 m, so 33 points.
Order. Checking those 33 points from a towards b, the first collision is check 21, at 0.625 of the way. Checking them in halving order instead (both ends, then the middle point, then the two quarter points, then the eighths, and so on), the fifth check, three quarters of the way, is the point (3.5, 3.2), and it hits (LaValle §5.3.4). When both ends are free, the point most likely to be in collision is the one farthest from both, the middle (Hauser ch.10); the halving order keeps checking the points farthest from those already checked, so its early checks spread over the whole segment and a collision anywhere is found soon (LaValle §5.3.4). If the segment is free, every point must be checked in either order, so the order costs nothing then (LaValle §5.3.4).
Figure 6 runs the three checks. Watch the stage “5 even steps: every check is free, yet the segment is not”, then the long row of checks from a until the hit, then “the same 33 points in halving order”, which hits at the fifth check.

6.3 Checking with clearance
A step of 0.1 m is a guess: a thinner obstacle could still hide between two checks. Clearances remove the guess (Hauser ch.10). Around a configuration with clearance c, the robot can move up to c in any direction without touching anything, so the circle of radius c round it is free. If the free circles at the two ends of a piece of segment reach each other, the piece is covered and free. With:

a and b the two ends of a piece of segment;
d(a, b) its length, in m;
c(a) and c(b) the clearances at its ends, in m.

d(a, b) \le c(a) + c(b)
If the length passes this test, the piece is free. Otherwise, check its middle and repeat on both halves (Hauser ch.10, “Visible-Exact1”; KAIST proximity slides). so the middle is checked, and so on. Figure 7 draws each check with its free circle. Watch the circles shrink as the checks approach the table’s corner and grow again towards the door. The check nearest the corner, at (3.2, 3.25), has a clearance of 0.141 m; the drive’s closest point to the grown table, 0.132 m, lies between two checks. A distance query costs more than a yes-or-no check, which is why planners mostly use the step method (Hauser ch.10; LaValle §5.3.4). Both answer the first two questions; the third needs a distance between configurations, not between bodies.
7. Distances in C-space


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A metric (G-2681)Metric (distance function): A distance between points that is never negative, is 0 only between equal points, is the same both ways and obeys the triangle inequality; search trees rely on these rules to skip far regions safely. 7.1 The rules a distance must follow
The third question of the opening problem: which stored configuration is nearest? “Nearest” needs a distance between two configurations. The Euclidean distance (G-715)Euclidean distance: The straight-line distance between two points. Explained in: Handling Missing Data: KNN Imputer, §4.1 The Euclidean distance, the straight-line distance, is one, and the nearest neighbours (G-1306)Nearest neighbours (neighbours): The observations at the smallest distance from a given point; in KNN, the k training points closest to the query point, whose values or labels decide the prediction. Explained in: Handling Missing Data: KNN Imputer, §3.2 The k nearest neighbours of a point are the stored points at the smallest distance from it. For any distance function a planner relies on, four rules must hold (LaValle §5.1.1; KAIST C-space slides). With:

d(p, q) the distance from p to q.

The rules, each followed by its formula:

d(p, q) \le d(p, r) + d(r, q)
A function that obeys all four is a metric (G-2681)Metric (distance function): A distance between points that is never negative, is 0 only between equal points, is the same both ways and obeys the triangle inequality; search trees rely on these rules to skip far regions safely. Explained in §7.1 The rules a distance must follow. (LaValle §5.1.1). The Euclidean distance is a metric, and so is the Manhattan distance, the sum of the absolute differences; both belong to the Minkowski distance (G-1227)Minkowski distance: A family of distances between two points, \left(\sum_i \lvert x_i - y_i \rvert^p\right)^{1/p}, set by the number p: p = 2 gives the Euclidean distance and p = 1 the Manhattan distance; KNN uses it to find the nearest neighbours. Explained in: K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN), §2.1 The steps family (KAIST C-space slides). Why the rules matter: the k-d tree search of Section 8 skips a whole box when the box is farther than the best point found so far, which is only safe if no detour is shorter than the straight distance (Hauser ch.10, “k-d trees”; Wikipedia, “Metric tree”).
7.2 The distance between two headings
Headings break the plain distance. The query at 350° and the stored 15° of Figure 1:
|350 - 15| = 335^\circ
but turning the other way, across 0°, is 25°. Worse, 0° and 360° are the same heading, yet:
|0 - 360| = 360^\circ
so plain subtraction breaks rule 2: two equal headings at a distance of 360°. Angle wrapping (G-2404)Angle wrapping: Adding or subtracting full turns until an angle or angle difference lies between −180° and 180°, so that 175° and −178° count as 7° apart, not 353°; needed whenever bearings or headings are compared. Explained in: Landmark Measurement Model, §3.3 Why angle differences must be wrapped fixes it: add or subtract full turns until the difference lies between −180° and 180°. Its size is the angular distance (G-2684)Angular distance: The distance between two headings measured the short way round the circle, the smaller of \lvert \theta_1 - \theta_2 \rvert and 360° minus it, so 350° and 15° are 25° apart, not 335°. Explained in §7.2 The distance between two headings., the length of the short way round the circle (LaValle §5.1.2, eq. 5.7; Hauser ch.4, “Geodesic distance and interpolation”). With headings \theta_1 and \theta_2 in degrees:
d = \min(|\theta_1 - \theta_2|,\ 360 - |\theta_1 - \theta_2|)
For 350° and 15°:
d = \min(335,\ 360 - 335) = 25^\circ
Figure 8 (left) shows the two ways round. The angular distance obeys the four rules (LaValle §5.1.2): on the right of Figure 8, A at 350°, B at 0° and C at 15°, and the detour through B is no shorter:
d(A, C) = 25
d(A, B) + d(B, C) = 10 + 15 = 25
