7.3 Metres and radians in one distance
A configuration of the floor robot has a position in metres and a heading in radians, and a distance must combine them. One radian of turn moves the rim of the 0.25 m footprint 0.25 m (the arc rule of radians (G-2285))Radian: The unit of angle at which the arc of a circle is as long as its radius; a full turn is 2\pi rad, and with radians an arc is simply radius times angle. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.3 Why angles are measured in radians, so we count 0.25 m for each radian of angular distance (LaValle §5.3.4, eq. 5.30; KAIST C-space slides). A longer robot, such as one carrying a 1.4 m board, would need a larger weight: a small turn moves its far end a lot (LaValle §5.3.4). With:

q_1 = (x_1, y_1, \theta_1) and q_2 = (x_2, y_2, \theta_2) two configurations;
\Delta\theta the angular distance between \theta_1 and \theta_2, in rad;
w the weight, 0.25 m per rad;
d(q_1, q_2) their distance, in m.

d(q_1, q_2) = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2 + (w\thinspace\Delta\theta)^2}
where \Delta x and \Delta y are the differences in x and y (KAIST C-space slides). The weighted distance is a metric: it is the Euclidean distance on positions and on scaled headings measured the short way (LaValle §5.1.1, “Cartesian products of metric spaces”). For the query at x = 3.55 m, 350°, and the stored configuration E at x = 3.60 m, 15° (y equal), the heading part is 25°, which is 0.436 rad:
0.25 \times 0.436 = 0.109 \text{ m}
d = \sqrt{0.05^2 + 0.109^2} = 0.120 \text{ m}
With plain subtraction, 335° would make the heading part 1.462 m and E look far. A distance that wraps is half of the answer; the search must wrap too.
8. Nearest neighbours when headings wrap


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A k-d tree search skips a cell when the cell is farther than the best point found so far. If headings are treated as numbers from 0 to 360, a cell just across 0° looks a long way off and is skipped; measuring the cell’s distance the short way round fixes the search.


The opening problem’s third trap, in a search tree. A k-d tree stores points in cells split one coordinate at a time, so a nearest-neighbour search can skip every cell that lies farther away than the best point found so far (Hauser ch.10, “k-d trees”; LaValle §5.5.2). Figure 9 stores 8 configurations in one, with two coordinates so that it fits a page, x and heading; y would work like x. The tree splits on x, then heading, then x. The query is at x = 3.55 m, heading 350°. Distances use the weight of Section 7.3, 0.25 m per radian, and the heading axis is drawn in those metres, so a circle of equal distance is round.
Plain search. The search goes first into the cell that holds the query (Hauser ch.10). The search finds C and then D, at 0.371 m, and then reaches the cell of headings 0° to 175° beside it. Measured as plain numbers, that cell is 175° below the query:
350 - 175 = 175^\circ = 3.054 \text{ rad}
0.25 \times 3.054 = 0.764 \text{ m}
The gap of 0.764 m is more than the best so far, 0.371 m, so the cell is skipped, and with it E. The search ends at H (3.40 m, 320°), 0.199 m away. Wrong: E is nearer, at 0.120 m (Section 7.3).
Search with wrap-around. The heading 0° is the same as 360°, so the cell of headings 0° to 175° starts 10° above the query, across the top edge:
360 - 350 = 10^\circ = 0.175 \text{ rad}
0.25 \times 0.175 = 0.044 \text{ m}
Less than 0.371 m, so the cell is visited, and E, at 0.120 m, becomes the best. Measuring a cell’s distance the short way round the circle, and its points’ distances with the angular distance, is all that changes; we call this a nearest-neighbour search with wrap-around (G-2685)Nearest-neighbour search with wrap-around: A k-d tree search that measures a cell’s distance from the query the short way round the circle of headings, so a cell just across 0° is not skipped and the true nearest configuration is found. Explained in §8. Nearest neighbours when headings wrap.. LaValle §5.5.2 warns that the tree search must respect the places where the space wraps round, and Hauser ch.10 notes that headings need their own point-to-cell distance.
Figure 9 runs both searches. Watch the stage “plain search, step 3”, where the cell holding E is pruned as 0.764 m away, then “with wrap-around search, step 3”, where the same cell is 0.044 m away and E is found. The circle of the best distance so far wraps from the top edge to the bottom.

Figure 9: Animation: nearest-neighbour search in a k-d tree over 8 stored configurations A to H (x in m across, heading up, the heading axis drawn at 0.25 m per radian so circles are round), for the query at x = 3.55 m, 350 degrees (red star). Visited cells turn green, pruned cells red; the dotted orange circle is the best distance so far. Plain search visits C, then D (0.371 m), prunes the cell of headings 0 to 175 degrees as 0.764 m away (350 − 175 = 175 degrees), and returns H at 0.199 m. Search with wrap-around measures that cell the short way, 360 − 350 = 10 degrees, 0.044 m, visits it and returns E at 0.120 m; its circle wraps from the top edge to the bottom
A planner that grows a tree of configurations asks this question at every step (Hauser ch.10, “Nearest-neighbor queries”), so the wrap-around must be right every time. The configurations it adds come from random sampling, which has a trap of its own: random orientations that favour some directions.
9. Uniform random rotations and directions


                  
                  Key point 
                  
                

A random heading must favour no direction: drawn evenly from 0° to 360°, every arc of 30° gets the same share, 1/12, wherever it lies. Directions and rotations in 3D need care: a uniform latitude angle crowds the poles, a point in a cube favours the corners; a normal sample scaled to length 1, the bread-slicer recipe and Shoemake’s recipe for 3D rotations are uniform.


9.1 What uniform means for headings
Sampling planners draw random configurations, so the random headings must not favour any direction. For the floor robot this is easy. Draw the heading from the continuous uniform distribution (G-467)Continuous uniform distribution U(a, b): A continuous variable spread evenly between a and b, with density 1/(b - a). Explained in: Uniform and Log-normal Distributions, §2. The uniform distribution from 0° to 360°, every value equally likely. Then any arc of 30° gets the same share of the draws, wherever on the circle it lies (notebook, 100,000 draws: 8.4 percent for 10° to 40°, 8.3 percent for 200° to 230°):
30 / 360 = 0.083
Equal shares for equal arcs, wherever they lie, is what uniform means for rotations. A uniform random rotation (G-2686)Uniform random rotation: A random rotation drawn so that every orientation is equally likely: turning the whole set of samples by any fixed rotation does not make some orientations more common; for headings, a draw evenly from 0° to 360°. Explained in §9.1 What uniform means for headings. makes every orientation equally likely: turning the whole set of samples by any fixed rotation must not make some orientations more common (LaValle §5.1.4, §5.2.2). The circle of headings has no favoured place, so the plain uniform draw is right. Directions and rotations in 3D, as for a drone or the gripper of an arm, are where the traps are.
9.2 Random directions
A uniform random direction (G-2689)Uniform random direction: A random unit vector drawn so that every direction is equally likely; a normal sample scaled to length 1 gives one, while a point in a square or cube scaled to length 1 favours the diagonals. Explained in §9.2 Random directions. is a unit vector (a vector of length 1) drawn so that every direction is equally likely: every patch of the circle, or of the sphere, of the same size gets the same share (LaValle §5.2.2).
Two traps and two fixes, with the shares from the notebook (Figure 10):

A point in a square, scaled to length 1. Draw x and y evenly from −1 to 1 and divide by the length. The square reaches 1.41 times as far along a diagonal as along an axis, so a thin wedge along a diagonal holds about twice the area, and diagonal directions come up more often: within 5° of a diagonal 16.2 percent of the time, within 5° of an axis 8.6 percent, against a fair share of 11.1 percent (LaValle §5.2.2 warns of this bias towards a cube’s corners).
A normal sample, scaled to length 1. Draw each coordinate from a normal distribution with the same spread. Its density depends only on the distance from the centre, so every direction is equally likely: 11.1 percent near the diagonals and 11.1 percent near the axes (LaValle §5.2.2).
On the sphere, a uniform latitude angle. Drawing the latitude evenly from −90° to 90° packs as many points into the short circles near the poles as into the long equator. The two caps above height 0.9 and below −0.9 hold 10 percent of the sphere’s surface but get 28.7 percent of the points.
On the sphere, a uniform height: the bread slicer. Drawing the height evenly from −1 to 1 and the longitude evenly from 0° to 360° is uniform, because slices of a sphere of equal thickness have equal crust area, like a loaf through a bread slicer (LaValle §5.2.2). The caps get 10.1 percent.

The caps by the two recipes, the height 0.9 being at latitude 64.2°:
\arcsin 0.9 = 64.2^\circ
\text{latitude: } 2 \times (90 - 64.2) / 180 = 0.287
\text{height: } 2 \times (1 - 0.9) / 2 = 0.1
The latitude recipe gives each degree of latitude the same share; the height recipe gives each slice of height the same share, which is right because equal slices have equal area.

9.3 Random rotations in 3D
A rotation in 3D, such as the orientation of a gripper, can be stored as four numbers h = (h_1, h_2, h_3, h_4) whose squares add up to 1, so h is a point on a sphere in four dimensions (LaValle §5.2.2):
h_1^2 + h_2^2 + h_3^2 + h_4^2 = 1
Uniform rotations are uniform points on that sphere, and the bread-slicer idea carries over one dimension up. Shoemake’s recipe (LaValle §5.2.2, eq. 5.15), with:

u_1, u_2, u_3 three numbers drawn evenly from 0 to 1;
h the four random numbers that describe the rotation.

h = (\sqrt{1 - u_1}\sin 2\pi u_2,
\sqrt{1 - u_1}\cos 2\pi u_2,
\sqrt{u_1}\sin 2\pi u_3,
\sqrt{u_1}\cos 2\pi u_3)
Check that the squares add up to 1. For u_1 = 0.3, u_2 = 0.6 and u_3 = 0.9 the recipe gives (−0.492, −0.677, −0.322, 0.443) (notebook). The squares of the first two entries, then of the last two:
0.242 + 0.458 = 0.700 = 1 - 0.3
0.104 + 0.196 = 0.300 = 0.3
0.700 + 0.300 = 1
The same steps in symbols, with s = 2\pi u_2, the first two entries squared:
(1 - u_1)\sin^2 s + (1 - u_1)\cos^2 s
= (1 - u_1)(\sin^2 s + \cos^2 s)
= 1 - u_1
The last two give u_1 the same way, and together:
(1 - u_1) + u_1 = 1
Check that it is uniform. Turn the arrow pointing straight up by 20,000 of these rotations. If every rotation is equally likely, the arrow’s tip lands evenly on the sphere, so the caps above height 0.9 should get 10 percent. The caps get 10.0 percent (notebook; Figure 10, bottom right). Drawing three angles evenly (turns about z, y and x, each from 0° to 360°) and turning the arrow puts 6.5 percent there, not 10: three uniform angles do not make a uniform rotation (notebook), as LaValle §5.2.2 warns.

The robot’s planner can now test configurations and segments quickly, measure how far configurations are from each other, find the nearest stored one and draw random configurations evenly. Still missing: a planner that puts these together, drawing random configurations, joining each to its nearest neighbours with checked segments, and growing a route to the door: the sampling-based planners of a later chapter.

12. Key terms
Terms taught in this Note come first; linked terms are recaps, taught in the Note the link opens.





















































































































TermMeaningCollision detection (G-2665)Collision detection: Deciding, yes or no, whether two bodies overlap, such as the robot’s disk and the table; planners call it thousands of times instead of building the obstacle region. Explained in §2.1 The yes-or-no question and what it costs.Deciding, yes or no, whether two bodies overlap, such as the robot’s disk and the table; planners call it thousands of times instead of building the obstacle region.Broad phase (G-2666)Broad phase: The first, cheap step of collision detection: wrap each body in a simple shape such as a box and keep only the pairs whose shapes overlap, so the costly exact test runs on few pairs. Explained in §2.2 Broad phase and narrow phase.The first, cheap step of collision detection: wrap each body in a simple shape such as a box and keep only the pairs whose shapes overlap, so the costly exact test runs on few pairs.Narrow phase (G-2667)Narrow phase: The second step of collision detection: the exact overlap test on the pairs the broad phase kept, such as the distance from the robot’s centre to the table compared with its 0.25 m radius. Explained in §2.2 Broad phase and narrow phase.The second step of collision detection: the exact overlap test on the pairs the broad phase kept, such as the distance from the robot’s centre to the table compared with its 0.25 m radius.Bounding volume (G-2668)Bounding volume: A simple shape that encloses a body, such as a sphere or a box; if two bounding volumes do not overlap, neither do the bodies, so it gives a quick test before an exact one. Explained in §2.2 Broad phase and narrow phase.A simple shape that encloses a body, such as a sphere or a box; if two bounding volumes do not overlap, neither do the bodies, so it gives a quick test before an exact one.Sweep and prune (G-2670)Sweep and prune: A broad phase that sorts the boxes by their left edge and sweeps along x, comparing each box only with the boxes it overlaps along x; it cuts the pairs tested, though long boxes that span the axis defeat it. Explained in §2.3 Sweep and prune.A broad phase that sorts the boxes by their left edge and sweeps along x, comparing each box only with the boxes it overlaps along x; it cuts the pairs tested, though long boxes that span the axis defeat it.Bounding-volume hierarchy (BVH) (G-2671)Bounding-volume hierarchy (BVH): A tree of nested bounding volumes, each holding its two children’s down to one per body; a query skips every body inside a box that misses, so it needs about \log_2 n box tests for n bodies (9 among the room’s 25). Explained in §3.1 Why a tree of boxes.A tree of nested bounding volumes, each holding its two children’s down to one per body; a query skips every body inside a box that misses, so it needs about \log_2 n box tests for n bodies (9 among the room’s 25).Self-collision (G-2672)Self-collision: Two links of the same robot overlapping, such as an arm’s third link folding back across its first; a configuration with a self-collision is not free, so planners test the robot’s own link pairs too. Explained in §4. Self-collision.Two links of the same robot overlapping, such as an arm’s third link folding back across its first; a configuration with a self-collision is not free, so planners test the robot’s own link pairs too.Distance query (G-2674)Distance query: A geometric query that returns the shortest distance between two bodies, 0 if they overlap; it tells a planner how much room the robot has, not only whether it is free. Explained in §5.1 How far, not only whether.A geometric query that returns the shortest distance between two bodies, 0 if they overlap; it tells a planner how much room the robot has, not only whether it is free.GJK algorithm (G-2678)GJK algorithm: The Gilbert-Johnson-Keerthi algorithm: it decides whether two convex shapes overlap, or how far apart they are, by searching their Minkowski difference for the origin using each shape’s farthest point in chosen directions, without building the difference. Explained in §5.2 The Minkowski difference and GJK.The Gilbert-Johnson-Keerthi algorithm: it decides whether two convex shapes overlap, or how far apart they are, by searching their Minkowski difference for the origin using each shape’s farthest point in chosen directions, without building the difference.Edge resolution (segment checking) (G-2679)Edge resolution (segment checking): Checking a straight path segment in C-space for collisions by testing points along it, spaced at most a chosen step apart; too long a step can miss a thin collision, too short a step wastes time. Explained in §6.1 A segment holds infinitely many configurations.Checking a straight path segment in C-space for collisions by testing points along it, spaced at most a chosen step apart; too long a step can miss a thin collision, too short a step wastes time.Metric (distance function) (G-2681)Metric (distance function): A distance between points that is never negative, is 0 only between equal points, is the same both ways and obeys the triangle inequality; search trees rely on these rules to skip far regions safely. Explained in §7.1 The rules a distance must follow.A distance between points that is never negative, is 0 only between equal points, is the same both ways and obeys the triangle inequality; search trees rely on these rules to skip far regions safely.Triangle inequality (G-2683)Triangle inequality: The rule that a detour through a third point is never shorter than going straight, d(p, q) \le d(p, r) + d(r, q); it is what lets a nearest-neighbour search skip a region farther than its best point. Explained in §7.1 The rules a distance must follow.The rule that a detour through a third point is never shorter than going straight, d(p, q) \le d(p, r) + d(r, q); it is what lets a nearest-neighbour search skip a region farther than its best point.Angular distance (G-2684)Angular distance: The distance between two headings measured the short way round the circle, the smaller of \lvert \theta_1 - \theta_2 \rvert and 360° minus it, so 350° and 15° are 25° apart, not 335°. Explained in §7.2 The distance between two headings.The distance between two headings measured the short way round the circle, the smaller of \lvert \theta_1 - \theta_2 \rvert and 360° minus it, so 350° and 15° are 25° apart, not 335°.Nearest-neighbour search with wrap-around (G-2685)Nearest-neighbour search with wrap-around: A k-d tree search that measures a cell’s distance from the query the short way round the circle of headings, so a cell just across 0° is not skipped and the true nearest configuration is found. Explained in §8. Nearest neighbours when headings wrap.A k-d tree search that measures a cell’s distance from the query the short way round the circle of headings, so a cell just across 0° is not skipped and the true nearest configuration is found.Uniform random rotation (G-2686)Uniform random rotation: A random rotation drawn so that every orientation is equally likely: turning the whole set of samples by any fixed rotation does not make some orientations more common; for headings, a draw evenly from 0° to 360°. Explained in §9.1 What uniform means for headings.A random rotation drawn so that every orientation is equally likely: turning the whole set of samples by any fixed rotation does not make some orientations more common; for headings, a draw evenly from 0° to 360°.Uniform random direction (G-2689)Uniform random direction: A random unit vector drawn so that every direction is equally likely; a normal sample scaled to length 1 gives one, while a point in a square or cube scaled to length 1 favours the diagonals. Explained in §9.2 Random directions.A random unit vector drawn so that every direction is equally likely; a normal sample scaled to length 1 gives one, while a point in a square or cube scaled to length 1 favours the diagonals.Obstacle region (C-obstacle) (G-2650)Obstacle region (C-obstacle): The set of all configurations at which the robot’s body touches or overlaps an obstacle, C_{\text{obs}}; drawing it in C-space lets a planner test a placement as one point, such as the disk robot’s centre (3.5, 3.2), which lies in it 0.2 m from the table. Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §2.2 The obstacle region: every placement that touches an obstacleThe set of all configurations at which the robot’s body touches or overlaps an obstacle, C_{\text{obs}}; drawing it in C-space lets a planner test a placement as one point, such as the disk robot’s centre (3.5, 3.2), which lies in it 0.2 m from the table.Triangle mesh (G-2338)Triangle mesh: A set of triangles, each given by three corner points in space, that together cover an object’s surface (a table as 12 triangles on 8 corners); fast to draw in 3D, but it does not say what is inside. Explained in: Maps and Landmarks, §5.1 Triangle meshesA set of triangles, each given by three corner points in space, that together cover an object’s surface (a table as 12 triangles on 8 corners); fast to draw in 3D, but it does not say what is inside.Grown obstacle (inflated obstacle) (G-2652)Grown obstacle (inflated obstacle): An obstacle with every point within the robot’s radius added, its edges pushed out and its corners rounded; for a disk robot it is exactly the obstacle region, so the robot can be treated as a point (the table, 3.625 m², grows to 5.747 m² for a 0.25 m radius). Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §2.3 Growing the obstacles by the robot’s radiusAn obstacle with every point within the robot’s radius added, its edges pushed out and its corners rounded; for a disk robot it is exactly the obstacle region, so the robot can be treated as a point (the table, 3.625 m², grows to 5.747 m² for a 0.25 m radius).Minkowski difference (G-2654)Minkowski difference: The set of all differences of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \ominus B, which equals A \oplus (-B); obstacle minus robot gives the obstacle region, and two convex bodies overlap exactly when their difference contains the origin. Explained in: Obstacles in C-space, §3.2 Minkowski sum and differenceThe set of all differences of a point of one shape and a point of the other, A \ominus B, which equals A \oplus (-B); obstacle minus robot gives the obstacle region, and two convex bodies overlap exactly when their difference contains the origin.Dot product (G-634)Dot product: Multiplying two vectors entry by entry and adding the products, u^{\mathsf T}x, which gives one number. It is large when the vectors point the same way, so it measures similarity and gives projections. Explained in: Dot Product and Cosine Similarity, §3. Computing the dot productMultiplying two vectors entry by entry and adding the products, u^{\mathsf T}x, which gives one number. It is large when the vectors point the same way, so it measures similarity and gives projections.Euclidean distance (G-715)Euclidean distance: The straight-line distance between two points. Explained in: Handling Missing Data: KNN Imputer, §4.1 The Euclidean distanceThe straight-line distance between two points.Nearest neighbours (neighbours) (G-1306)Nearest neighbours (neighbours): The observations at the smallest distance from a given point; in KNN, the k training points closest to the query point, whose values or labels decide the prediction. Explained in: Handling Missing Data: KNN Imputer, §3.2 The k nearest neighboursThe observations at the smallest distance from a given point; in KNN, the k training points closest to the query point, whose values or labels decide the prediction.Minkowski distance (G-1227)Minkowski distance: A family of distances between two points, \left(\sum_i \lvert x_i - y_i \rvert^p\right)^{1/p}, set by the number p: p = 2 gives the Euclidean distance and p = 1 the Manhattan distance; KNN uses it to find the nearest neighbours. Explained in: K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN), §2.1 The stepsA family of distances between two points, \left(\sum_i \lvert x_i - y_i \rvert^p\right)^{1/p}, set by the number p: p = 2 gives the Euclidean distance and p = 1 the Manhattan distance; KNN uses it to find the nearest neighbours.Angle wrapping (G-2404)Angle wrapping: Adding or subtracting full turns until an angle or angle difference lies between −180° and 180°, so that 175° and −178° count as 7° apart, not 353°; needed whenever bearings or headings are compared. Explained in: Landmark Measurement Model, §3.3 Why angle differences must be wrappedAdding or subtracting full turns until an angle or angle difference lies between −180° and 180°, so that 175° and −178° count as 7° apart, not 353°; needed whenever bearings or headings are compared.Radian (G-2285)Radian: The unit of angle at which the arc of a circle is as long as its radius; a full turn is 2\pi rad, and with radians an arc is simply radius times angle. Explained in: Pose and the Differential Drive, §2.3 Why angles are measured in radiansThe unit of angle at which the arc of a circle is as long as its radius; a full turn is 2\pi rad, and with radians an arc is simply radius times angle.Continuous uniform distribution U(a, b) (G-467)Continuous uniform distribution U(a, b): A continuous variable spread evenly between a and b, with density 1/(b - a). Explained in: Uniform and Log-normal Distributions, §2. The uniform distributionA continuous variable spread evenly between a and b, with density 1/(b - a).

IDTermMeaningHomeConceptG-11/(1-\beta)Roughly how many recent values a running average that favours new values (the EWMA) covers: about 10 for \beta = 0.9.Note DL-033Exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA)G-25444-connected gridA grid made into a graph by joining each cell to the up to four cells that share a side with it (left, down, up, right); the simplest graph of a grid map, with every move the same length.Note RO-032Graphs and state spacesG-25648-connected gridA grid made into a graph by joining each cell to all 8 cells around it: 4 straight moves of one cell side and 4 diagonal moves of 1.414 cell sides (0.707 m for 0.5 m cells), usually without cutting the corner of a blocked cell; it gives shorter, less jagged routes than a 4-connected grid.Note RO-033Dijkstra’s algorithmG-2577A* searchDijkstra’s algorithm with the open list sorted by f = g + h, the cost so far plus a heuristic guess of the cost left; with a consistent heuristic it returns the shortest route while expanding far fewer states (9 cells against 54 on the room grid).Note RO-034A* searchG-2465Adaptive (dynamic) decompositionCutting the state space into cells that change with the belief: small cells where the belief is high, large cells where it is near zero, as in a quadtree; it gives fine detail with far fewer cells.Note RO-015Histogram filterG-3\alphaThe share of confidence intervals that miss the true value they are meant to catch (the parameter). projects/grid-pathfinding.title: Path-finding on a grid
projects/grid-pathfinding.content:
Twelve search algorithms find a route across a warehouse floor drawn as a grid, all with the same start and goal, so we can watch how each one explores, cell by cell.
The maps

Figure 1: The warehouse floor: shelves and walls dark, floor white, start S, goal G, three blue charging pads

The floor: 40 × 25 cells, each 1 m × 1 m. Dark cells are shelves and walls (blocked); white cells are floor (free).
Moves: the robot moves to any of the 8 cells around it. A straight move costs 1 m, a diagonal move 1.41 m. A diagonal move must not cut the corner of a shelf.
The graph: every free cell is a node (623 of them); every move between two free cells is an edge.
The trip: from S (green, the loading dock, bottom left) to G (red, in the corridor behind the shelves at the top). The shelf rows are closed at the top, so the corridor can be entered only at its two ends.
Blue cells: three charging pads, the goals of the multi-goal search.

The map is a picture, maps/warehouse.png, one pixel per cell. A second map, a maze, runs with the same code:

Figure 2: The maze: 31 × 21 cells of 1 m, start top left, goal bottom right
Reading the animations: pale green cells are the frontier (reached, waiting to be expanded); pale blue cells are visited (taken off the frontier and expanded). The yellow line is the route. The counts are above the map.
Breadth-first search
Breadth-first search (BFS) takes cells from a first-in, first-out queue, so the blue area grows in rings: every cell 1 move away, then 2 moves, and so on. It counts moves and ignores that a diagonal move is longer, so its route has the fewest moves (41), not necessarily the fewest metres. On this floor the fewest-move route is also a shortest one.

Figure 3: Breadth-first search on the warehouse floor

Visited: 597 cells · Route: 44.7 m · 100 % of Dijkstra’s

Taught in: breadth-first search
Depth-first search
Depth-first search (DFS) takes the newest cell from a stack, so it runs one way until it is stuck, then backs up. The orange line is the branch it is on. It reaches the goal after fewer visits than BFS, but along a 308 m zigzag, 6.9 times the shortest route.

Figure 4: Depth-first search on the warehouse floor

Visited: 299 cells · Route: 307.9 m · 688 % of Dijkstra’s

Taught in: depth-first search
Dijkstra
Dijkstra always expands the frontier cell with the smallest distance from the start, g. The blue area grows in bands of equal metres, the same way in every direction, also away from the goal. It stops when the goal is expanded; by then it has visited 596 of the 623 floor cells.

Figure 5: Dijkstra on the warehouse floor

Visited: 596 cells · Route: 44.7 m (the shortest) · 100 %

Taught in: Dijkstra’s algorithm
A*
A* expands the cell with the smallest f = g + h, where h is the straight-line distance to the goal. A cell that leads away from the goal has a large h and waits. A* visits 376 cells instead of Dijkstra’s 596, and its route is still the shortest, because the straight line is never longer than a real route.

Figure 6: A* on the warehouse floor

Visited: 376 cells · Route: 44.7 m · 100 % of Dijkstra’s

Taught in: A* search
Choosing the heuristic
The guess h decides how much A* explores. Four guesses race side by side; each tick, every search expands one cell.

h = 0: no guess, so A* is Dijkstra: 596 cells.
Straight line: never too big: 376 cells.
Octile: the length of the best 8-way route if no shelf were in the way. Never too big, and closer to the truth: 350 cells.
Manhattan: metres east-west plus metres north-south. It counts a diagonal move as 2 m where it costs 1.41 m, so it can overestimate: at the start it guesses 50.0 m, but the shortest route is 44.7 m. It visits only 42 cells. Here its route is still the shortest, but once h can overestimate, A* no longer promises that.


Figure 7: A* with four heuristics: h = 0, Manhattan, straight line, octile

h = 0: 596 cells · Straight line: 376 · Octile: 350 · Manhattan: 42; all four routes 44.7 m

Taught in: heuristics
Greedy best-first search
Greedy best-first search expands the cell with the smallest h only, and ignores the metres already driven. It heads for the goal, runs up the shelf rows that are closed at the top, one after another, and finally goes round the right end. It visits few cells, but its route is a quarter longer than the shortest.

Figure 8: Greedy best-first search on the warehouse floor

Visited: 134 cells · Route: 56.1 m · 126 % of Dijkstra’s

Taught in: best-first search
Iterative deepening A* (IDA*)
IDA* is depth-first search with a bound on f = g + h: a branch is cut as soon as its f goes over the bound. If the goal is not reached, the bound rises to the smallest f that went over it, and the search starts again. It stores only the branch it is on (orange), but it visits the same cells again in every round.
On the whole trip, IDA* had not finished after 1,000,000 visits (193 rounds), and not on the trip to a point halfway along the route either. So the animation shows a nearer goal, 14.3 m from the start.

Figure 9: IDA* on the warehouse floor, to a goal 14.3 m away

Visits: 1,560 in 31 rounds (A* to the same goal: 29) · Route: 14.3 m, the shortest to that goal

Taught in: iterative deepening
Bidirectional search
Two Dijkstra searches run at once, one from the start (blue) and one from the goal (purple); each step expands whichever side’s next cell is nearer its own end. The route is complete where they meet. Together they visit 354 cells, against 596 for one Dijkstra.

Figure 10: Bidirectional search on the warehouse floor

Visited: 354 cells · Route: 44.7 m · 100 % of Dijkstra’s

Taught in: bidirectional search
Weighted A*
Weighted A* uses f = g + ε h with ε = 2: it trusts the guess twice as much. It visits 206 cells, about half of A*‘s, and its route is 56.1 m. The promise is a route at most ε times the shortest (89.5 m).

Figure 11: Weighted A* with ε = 2 on the warehouse floor

Visited: 206 cells · Route: 56.1 m · 126 % of Dijkstra’s

Taught in: weighted A*
Anytime A*
Weighted A* runs three times, with ε = 2.5, then 1.5, then 1. Each round starts afresh and gives a better route; the dotted lines are the earlier routes. The first route arrives after 169 visits; the shortest after 948 visits in all.

Figure 12: Anytime A* on the warehouse floor

Rounds: ε = 2.5: 56.1 m after 169 visits · ε = 1.5: 46.5 m after 403 · ε = 1: 44.7 m after 376
Route: 44.7 m · 100 % of Dijkstra’s

Taught in: anytime A*
Theta*
Theta* is A* whose route may run at any angle. When it reaches a cell, it checks whether the cell can be seen in a straight line from the parent of the cell it came from; if so, it links to that parent and cuts the corner. The route is 4 straight pieces, shorter than the 8-way route, which can only run along the 8 grid directions.

Figure 13: Theta* on the warehouse floor

Visited: 381 cells · Route: 43.6 m · 98 % of Dijkstra’s (Dijkstra may only make 8-way moves)

Taught in: any-angle search (Theta*)
Multi-goal A*
Which of the three charging pads (blue) is nearest by route? One A* run answers it: we add a virtual goal joined to each pad by a 0 m move, and h is the straight line to the nearest pad. It reaches the pad in the middle aisle, not the one nearest in a straight line (in the office, behind a wall with one door).

Figure 14: Multi-goal A* to the nearest of three charging pads

Visited: 148 cells · Route: 24.3 m to the pad in the middle aisle

Taught in: multi-goal A*
Jump point search
Jump point search (JPS) is A* that skips cells. From a cell it scans straight or diagonally across open floor (pale yellow) and stops only at the goal or beside a shelf corner, where a shortest route might turn. Only these jump points go on the frontier. It visits 67 cells against A*‘s 376, with the same route; its scans step over cells 1,696 times.

Figure 15: Jump point search on the warehouse floor

Visited: 67 jump points · Route: 44.7 m · 100 % of Dijkstra’s

Taught in: jump point search
The race
Six searches on one clock: each tick, every search expands one cell. Each map shows its cells visited and, once done, its route length.

Figure 16: Race on the warehouse floor: BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, greedy, A*, bidirectional
The same race on the maze, run by changing one argument (--map maze):

Figure 17: Race on the maze
The same functions also run on the streets of Chicago: Path-finding on real streets.
Run it yourself
In the campusx environment, from projects/grid-pathfinding/:
python check_algorithms.py                  # every search against networkx, on every map in maps/
python run.py                               # the warehouse: numbers, preview, all animations
python run.py --map maze                    # another map in maps/
python run.py --map path/to/my_floor.png    # a map you drew
python run.py --only a_star race            # only some animations
jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute grid-pathfinding.ipynb
A new map is a PNG drawn in any paint program with these colours:

black: blocked (shelf, wall);
white: free floor;
pure green (0, 255, 0): the start, one pixel;
pure red (255, 0, 0): the goal, one pixel;
pure blue (0, 0, 255), optional: goals for the multi-goal search.

One pixel is one cell. A JSON file with the same name gives the cell size: {"label": "My floor", "cell_m": 1.0, "pixels_per_cell": 1} (set pixels_per_cell if each cell is drawn as a block of pixels).
Files: algorithms.py (every search), map_interface.py (what a map gives the searches), grid.py (PNG maps), render.py (the drawings), run.py, check_algorithms.py, gifkit.py (frames to GIF).
Sources
Built from:

The video A* (A-Star) Pathfinding Algorithm Visualization on a Real Map by ones and zeros, as the inspiration.
S. M. LaValle, Planning Algorithms, Cambridge University Press, 2006, chapter 2 (BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, A*, best-first, iterative deepening, bidirectional search).
R. E. Korf, “Depth-first iterative-deepening: an optimal admissible tree search”, Artificial Intelligence 27, 1985 (IDA*).
I. Pohl, “Heuristic search viewed as path finding in a graph”, Artificial Intelligence 1, 1970 (weighted A*); M. Likhachev, G. Gordon, S. Thrun, “ARA*: Anytime A* with provable bounds on sub-optimality”, NIPS 2003 (anytime A*).
D. Harabor, A. Grastien, “Online graph pruning for pathfinding on grid maps”, AAAI 2011 (jump point search); the no-corner-cutting jump rules follow PathFinding.js by Xueqiao Xu, whose look the animations borrow.
A. Nash, K. Daniel, S. Koenig, A. Felner, “Theta*: any-angle path planning on grids”, AAAI 2007.

projects/real-map-pathfinding.title: Path-finding on real streets
projects/real-map-pathfinding.content:
The searches of Path-finding on a grid, unchanged, run on the streets of central Chicago and are drawn in the look of the video that inspired this project.
The map

Figure 1: Central Chicago: 1,670 intersections and 2,694 streets; start cyan, goal red, seven train stations blue

The streets: OpenStreetMap’s streets for cars in a 5 km × 5 km square around the Loop, downloaded once with OSMnx.
The graph: a node is an intersection (1,670); an edge is a street between two intersections (2,694). The cost of an edge is the street’s length in metres. We treat every street as two-way.
The trip: from the start (cyan) on the Near West Side, in the south-west corner, to the goal (red) in Streeterville, by Navy Pier. They are 4,894 m apart in a straight line; the shortest drive is 6,426 m.
Blue: the seven train stations of the map, the goals of the multi-goal search.

Reading the animations: a street glows orange when the search looks along it from an intersection it expands; the newest streets glow brightest. At the end the glow fades and the route glows yellow. “Explored” counts the different streets looked at.
Breadth-first search
BFS counts streets, not metres. Its route uses 34 streets where the shortest uses 40, and it is 921 m longer. It explores almost every street of the map before it reaches the goal.

Figure 2: Breadth-first search on the streets of Chicago

Explored: 2,597 streets · Route: 7,347 m · 114 % of Dijkstra’s

Taught in: breadth-first search
Depth-first search
DFS follows one street after another as far as it can, then backs up. It reaches the goal, but its route winds through most of the map: 665 streets and 88.8 km, 14 times the shortest.

Figure 3: Depth-first search on the streets of Chicago

Explored: 2,505 streets · Route: 88,841 m · 1,383 % of Dijkstra’s

Taught in: depth-first search
Dijkstra
Dijkstra expands intersections in order of their distance from the start, so the glow spreads evenly in every direction. The goal is one of the farthest intersections, so Dijkstra explores 2,682 of the 2,694 streets before it stops.

Figure 4: Dijkstra on the streets of Chicago

Explored: 2,682 streets · Route: 6,426 m (the shortest) · 100 %

Taught in: Dijkstra’s algorithm
A*
A* adds the straight-line distance to the goal, so streets that lead away from the goal wait. The streets run north-south and east-west while the goal lies diagonally, so the straight line (4,894 m) is well below the real distance (6,426 m), and A* still explores 64 % of the streets Dijkstra explores. The route is the same shortest one.

Figure 5: A* on the streets of Chicago

Explored: 1,709 streets · Route: 6,426 m · 100 % of Dijkstra’s

Taught in: A* search
Greedy best-first search
Greedy best-first search follows only the straight-line distance, so it runs almost directly at the goal. It explores 154 streets, and its route is 412 m longer than the shortest.

Figure 6: Greedy best-first search on the streets of Chicago

Explored: 154 streets · Route: 6,838 m · 106 % of Dijkstra’s

Taught in: best-first search
Iterative deepening A* (IDA*)
IDA* searches depth-first under a bound on f = g + h and raises the bound each round. On the whole trip it had not finished after 1,000,000 visits and 1,415 rounds: street lengths are all different, so each round raises the bound by a few metres only. The animation shows the trip to the point halfway along the shortest route.

Figure 7: IDA* on the streets of Chicago, to the halfway point

Visits: 652 in 36 rounds (A* to the same point: 36) · Explored: 82 streets · Route: 2,600 m, the shortest to that point

On the small map below, IDA* finishes the whole trip.
Taught in: iterative deepening
Bidirectional search
One Dijkstra grows from the start and one from the goal; the route is complete where they meet. Together they explore 2,295 streets, 86 % of one Dijkstra’s.

Figure 8: Bidirectional search on the streets of Chicago

Explored: 2,295 streets · Route: 6,426 m · 100 % of Dijkstra’s

Taught in: bidirectional search
Weighted A*
With f = g + 2h the straight line counts twice, and the search runs almost straight at the goal, like greedy search. It explores 155 streets, 9 % of A*‘s, for a route 6 % longer.

Figure 9: Weighted A* with ε = 2 on the streets of Chicago

Explored: 155 streets · Route: 6,809 m · 106 % of Dijkstra’s

Taught in: weighted A*
Anytime A*
Weighted A* with ε = 2.5, then 1.5, then 1. The first route comes almost at once; each round improves it, and the last one is the shortest. The earlier routes stay dim yellow.

Figure 10: Anytime A* on the streets of Chicago

Rounds: ε = 2.5: 6,860 m after 59 visits · ε = 1.5: 6,790 m after 80 · ε = 1: 6,426 m after 1,009
Route: 6,426 m · 100 % of Dijkstra’s

Taught in: anytime A*
Multi-goal A*
Which of the seven train stations is nearest by road? One A* run to a virtual goal joined to every station by a 0 m street, with h the straight line to the nearest station. It is Halsted Street station, 1.3 km south-east of the start.

Figure 11: Multi-goal A* to the nearest of seven train stations

Explored: 49 streets · Route: 1,279 m to Halsted Street station

Taught in: multi-goal A*
On a grid made from the map
Jump point search and Theta* need a grid. We cover the map with cells of 15 m and call a cell free if its centre is within 11 m of a street: 328 × 331 cells, 24,906 of them free. Every street becomes a band of free cells; blocks, the river and the lake are blocked. The glow shows the moves that reached a cell.
Grid A*
The same A* function, now on the grid. A grid route may cut corners inside the band of free cells, so its length differs a little from the street graph’s.

Figure 12: Grid A* on the grid made from the streets

Visited: 15,090 cells · Route: 6,373 m

Taught in: A* search
Theta*
Theta* lets the route run straight from a cell to any cell it can see, so it cuts the corners where the route turns from one street into the next. It is 3 % shorter than grid A*‘s.

Figure 13: Theta* on the grid made from the streets

Visited: 13,870 cells · Route: 6,172 m · 97 % of grid A*‘s

Taught in: any-angle search (Theta*)
Jump point search
JPS scans along the street bands and puts only the cells where a route might turn on the frontier: 3,179 instead of 15,090. The route is the same as grid A*‘s. Its scans step over cells 75,951 times, more than the 36,641 moves grid A* looks at: the saving is in the frontier, not in the cells looked at.

Figure 14: Jump point search on the grid made from the streets

Visited: 3,179 jump points · Route: 6,373 m · 100 % of grid A*‘s

Taught in: jump point search
Travel time instead of distance
A driver wants the quickest route, not the shortest. The cost of a street is now the seconds it takes: OSMnx’s add_edge_speeds takes each street’s speed limit from its OpenStreetMap maxspeed tag and gives a street without one the average speed of streets of the same road type; add_edge_travel_times divides the length by the speed. Speeds on this map run from 24 to 89 km/h. The quickest route takes 478 s (8.0 min) and is 6,486 m long, 60 m longer than the shortest.
A* now needs a guess of the seconds still to go that is never too big. The better the guess, the fewer streets A* explores:

h = 0: no guess; A* is Dijkstra.
Straight line ÷ top speed: the straight line driven at the map’s top speed (88.5 km/h). No street is faster, so it is never too big, but most streets allow 32–44 km/h, so it is far too small.
Landmarks (ALT): we pick 8 landmarks spread over the map (each the farthest, by time, from those already chosen) and work out the time from each landmark to every intersection once. For an intersection n, the goal t and a landmark L, the triangle inequality gives time(n → t) ≥ |time(L → t) − time(L → n)|; h is the largest of these over the landmarks.
Exact: one Dijkstra backwards from the goal gives the true time still to go from every intersection. A* then explores little more than the route itself. No guess can do better, but it costs a full Dijkstra first, and only for this goal.


Figure 15: h = 0 (Dijkstra) on travel time

Figure 16: Straight line ÷ top speed on travel time

Figure 17: Landmarks (ALT) on travel time

Figure 18: Exact time to go on travel time

Figure 19: The four heuristics side by side on travel time

h = 0: 2,662 streets explored · straight line ÷ top speed: 2,251 · landmarks: 360 · exact: 107; every route 478 s (8.0 min)

CH-Potentials (Strasser and Zeitz, 2021) is the research answer for continent-sized road maps: a guess close to the exact one (4), ready quickly for any goal. Live traffic would change the costs as it changes; we have no traffic data, so we do not simulate it.
Taught in: heuristics
The race
Six searches on one clock: each tick, every search explores one more street. Each map shows its explored count and, once done, its route.

Figure 20: Race on the streets of Chicago: BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, greedy, A*, bidirectional
Explore it yourself: the interactive map below shows one search at a time (pick it from the menu), with its explored streets coloured by the order it reached them: dark red first, pale yellow last.
Open interactive playground
Interactive playground: tap Open, then move the controls.
Another map
The same code on a small part of Chicago, the West Loop: 140 intersections and 216 streets, cut from the Chicago file and saved under another name, with Union Station and Ogilvie as its two stations. Only the map argument changes: python run.py --map chicago-west-loop.

Figure 21: The West Loop map
On this small map IDA* finishes the whole trip, but it needs 87,822 visits in 419 rounds where A* needs 56.

Figure 22: IDA* on the West Loop map

Visits: 87,822 in 419 rounds · Route: 1,723 m, the shortest

Run it yourself
In the campusx environment, from projects/real-map-pathfinding/:
python check_algorithms.py                      # every search against networkx, on every map in data/
python run.py                                   # Chicago: numbers, preview and all animations
python run.py --map chicago-west-loop           # another map in data/
python run.py --only a_star race                # only some animations
jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute real-map-pathfinding.ipynb
The West Loop map was cut from the Chicago file, with no download:
python get_map.py --cut-from chicago --point 41.8820 -87.6395 --dist 550 --name chicago-west-loop --label "Chicago, West Loop"
A new city needs the internet once. For example, Rome:
python get_map.py --place "Rome, Italy" --name rome --label Rome --dist 2500
python run.py --map rome
get_map.py saves data/rome.graphml.gz (the streets), data/rome.json (label, start, goal and multi-goal goals) and the preview data/rome.png. Without --start and --goal it picks the intersections nearest two opposite corners; --goals-tag picks the multi-goal goals from OpenStreetMap tags (hospitals by default). The Chicago map was made with python get_map.py and no arguments, which runs the command written at the top of get_map.py.
Files: get_map.py (download), streets.py (the street map behind the map interface, the grid made from it, and FreeSpace, the streets as free space for sampling planners such as RRT and PRM), render.py (the drawings), run.py, check_algorithms.py. The searches are imported from ../grid-pathfinding/algorithms.py.
Sources
Built from:

The video A* (A-Star) Pathfinding Algorithm Visualization on a Real Map by ones and zeros, as the inspiration for the look.
Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors, available under the Open Database License (ODbL).
G. Boeing, OSMnx: “Modeling and analyzing urban networks and amenities with OSMnx”, Geographical Analysis, 2025 (download, speeds and travel times).
S. M. LaValle, Planning Algorithms, Cambridge University Press, 2006, chapter 2.
A. V. Goldberg, C. Harrelson, “Computing the shortest path: A* search meets graph theory”, SODA 2005 (landmarks, ALT).
B. Strasser, T. Zeitz, “A fast and tight heuristic for A* in road networks”, SEA 2021 (CH-Potentials).
The searches and their sources: Path-finding on a grid.

projects/sampling-planning.title: Sampling-based planning
projects/sampling-planning.content:
Four planners (RRT, RRT*, RRT-Connect and PRM) find a path for a round robot across a floor plan by trying random points, and every step they take is drawn.
The worlds
A world is a floor plan in metres: outer walls, blocked areas (shelves, walls, desks), a start, a goal and the robot’s size. Each world is one file in worlds/, and its picture is drawn beside it.

Figure 1: Small warehouse: 20 m by 12.5 m, six shelves, a 0.8 m gap in the middle one

Small warehouse, 20 m × 12.5 m, six shelves. The long middle shelf has one 0.8 m gap.
The robot is a disk of radius 0.25 m, so in the gap it has 0.15 m to spare on each side.
Start (2, 1.5), goal (2, 11): 9.5 m apart in a straight line.
Shortest path: 12.8 m, through the gap. With the gap closed it would be 34.2 m, round the right end of the shelf.
All the animations below run in this world.


Figure 2: Warehouse floor: 40 m by 25 m, from the grid project’s map

Warehouse floor, 40 m × 25 m: the grid project’s warehouse, read from its map picture (one pixel per 1 m cell).
The goal sits in a 1 m wide aisle along the top wall. Shortest path: 43.0 m.


Figure 3: Office: 12 m by 8 m, six rooms off a corridor

Office, 12 m × 8 m: three rooms below a corridor and three above, with 1.0 m doors. Shortest path: 12.9 m.

How a planner asks “is this free?”:

A point. The robot fits at a point when its disk, centred there, touches nothing. Shrinking the free floor by the robot’s radius turns this into one question: is the centre inside the shrunk floor?
A straight step. The step is tested at points 5 cm apart (the edge resolution): both ends first, then the middle, then the two quarter points, and so on. In the RRT run below, the 169 blocked steps took 1.1 tests each on average; testing point by point from the near end would have taken 8.0.
Corners. Two free test points 5 cm apart can still let the step clip a corner between them, by up to 1.25 mm. So every point is tested with the robot 2.5 mm larger. Without this, one RRT-Connect step in the office (seed 2) passes 0.2 mm too close to a wall corner, and the re-check with points 1 mm apart in check_planners.py catches it.
Each point test is one collision check. The check counts below are these tests.

Taught in: checking a path segment
RRT
What to watch:

In the first frames: a random point (black ×), the tree node nearest to it (orange ring), and one 1 m step from that node toward the point (orange). A step that would hit a shelf is dropped (red).
On average one sample in 20 is the goal itself (goal bias; 16 of the 331 here). Once a new node is within 1 m of the goal with a free line to it, the goal joins the tree and RRT stops.
RRT keeps the first path it finds. Here the tree found the gap, but its path zig-zags.


Figure 4: RRT growing in the small warehouse
Seed 2: 331 samples, 164 nodes in the tree, 169 steps blocked, 2,828 collision checks, path 24.5 m (shortest possible 12.8 m).
Taught in: RO-051 (being written)
RRT*
What to watch:

RRT* draws the same random points as RRT (same seed), so it grows the same nodes and reaches the goal at the same sample, 331. Its first path is shorter, 22.5 m against 24.5 m: each new node joins through the neighbour that gives it the shortest way back to the start, not just the nearest node.
Then rewiring: neighbours within 1 m that are reached more cheaply through the new node switch to it. The close-up shows sample 630, where one new node re-routes 3 neighbours and the path drops from 22.1 m to 14.5 m.
It keeps sampling after the first path. The lower panel shows the path length never rising.


Figure 5: RRT* rewiring in the small warehouse, with its path length falling
Seed 2: 1,500 samples, 895 nodes, 819 rewires, 31,625 collision checks (11 times RRT’s), path 13.8 m, 1.0 m above the shortest possible. Karaman and Frazzoli (2011) prove that RRT*‘s path tends to the shortest as the samples grow, and that RRT’s does not.
Taught in: RO-051 (being written)
RRT-Connect
What to watch:

Two trees: blue from the start, purple from the goal. Each round one tree takes a step toward a random point; the other then steps straight at that new node, again and again, until it gets there or hits a shelf. Then they swap roles.
The long orange lines are those straight runs. Kuffner and LaValle (2000) add this greedy step so the two trees meet quickly: here after 210 samples, against RRT’s 331.


Figure 6: RRT-Connect: two trees reaching for each other
Seed 2: the trees met after 210 samples (44 nodes from the start, 51 from the goal), 1,950 collision checks, the fewest of the four. The path goes round the right end: 44.2 m, the longest of the four.
Taught in: RO-051 (being written)
PRM
What to watch:

Step 1: points are scattered over the floor. Points that land on a shelf are thrown away.
Step 2: each point is joined to its 10 nearest points wherever the straight line between them is free. This network of free lines is the roadmap; it serves any start and goal in the same world.
Step 3: the start and the goal are joined to the roadmap the same way, and A* (the grid project’s own) finds the shortest route in it.


Figure 7: PRM: samples, roadmap, then the route
Seed 2: 772 points drawn, 500 kept, 272 thrown away; 2,881 roadmap edges; 53,744 collision checks; route 37.2 m, round the right end.
The gap is a narrow passage: few random points land in it or line up with it. Here one point landed in the gap, but no roadmap edge passes through it. More points fix this. Over seeds 1 to 10:



































pointsthrough the gapmedian routemedian checks2504 of 1036.5 m38,1395004 of 1036.8 m53,6081,00010 of 1013.9 m77,3182,0009 of 1013.5 m113,010
A route under 25.6 m (twice the shortest) must use the gap, since the way round is at least 34.2 m.
Taught in: RO-052 (being written)
The race
All four planners side by side. The shared clock is the number of collision checks: each panel shows what that planner had built after that many checks.

Figure 8: The race: four planners on one clock
Seed 2:








































plannersamplescheckspathtimeRRT3312,82824.5 m0.026 sRRT*1,50031,62513.8 m0.584 sRRT-Connect2101,95044.2 m0.018 sPRM77253,74437.2 m0.335 s
One seed can be lucky. Medians over seeds 1 to 10:








































plannersamplescheckspaththrough the gapRRT4783,59142.2 m3 of 10RRT*1,50030,56336.7 m3 of 10RRT-Connect1721,69242.5 m4 of 10PRM78053,60836.8 m4 of 10

RRT-Connect uses the fewest samples and checks.
RRT* and PRM pay the most checks. RRT* spends them on shorter paths; PRM spends them on a roadmap that serves every later query.
Most runs of every planner go round the right end: the 0.8 m gap is hard to find by chance.

The same code on other worlds
Nothing in the planners or the drawing code changes; only the world file does.

Figure 9: The race on the office floor
Office, seed 2:








































plannersamplescheckspathtimeRRT17592116.3 m0.005 sRRT*1,50017,09313.5 m0.271 sRRT-Connect1,0812,13717.0 m0.019 sPRM82535,05513.8 m0.180 s

Figure 10: The race on the grid project’s warehouse
Warehouse floor, seed 2:








































plannersamplescheckspathtimeRRT6,01826,92764.3 m1.398 sRRT*12,036232,38252.6 m11.041 sRRT-Connect5504,16846.7 m0.030 sPRM3,013165,32444.9 m1.128 s
The goal’s 1 m aisle is a narrow passage for a tree grown from the start: RRT needed 6,018 samples. RRT-Connect also grows a tree from the goal, which starts inside the aisle, and needed 550.
Run it yourself
From this folder, with the campusx environment:
python run.py --world small-warehouse        # numbers, checks, animations into images/small-warehouse/
python run.py --world office --no-gifs       # another world, numbers and checks only
python run.py --world ../grid-pathfinding/maps/warehouse.png   # any grid map from the grid project
python run.py --world worlds/my_world.json   # your own world
python run.py --sweep                        # add the 10-seed tables
python check_planners.py                     # every check, on every world in worlds/

Swap the world. Copy worlds/office.json, change its bounds, obstacles (rectangles [x0, y0, x1, y1] or polygons [[x, y], ...]), start, goal and robot_radius, and pass it with --world. Its picture is drawn on the first run.
Grid maps. A PNG from ../grid-pathfinding/maps/ is read with the grid project’s own loader (black blocked, white free, green start, red goal, cell size from the JSON beside it) and saved as a world file.
Street maps. street_world in world.py is the place for a road network: the free floor is the roads widened to their width.
Files. world.py loads worlds, collision.py answers “is this free?”, planners.py holds the four planners, render.py draws, run.py runs and prints, check_planners.py checks.
The notebook sampling-planning.ipynb runs everything on this page. The numbers above come from its last run (times vary from run to run):

PYTHONNOUSERSITE=1 /home/anshu/miniforge3/envs/campusx/bin/python -m nbconvert --to notebook --execute sampling-planning.ipynb --output-dir /home/anshu/campusx/.logs
Sources
Built from:

S. M. LaValle, Planning Algorithms, Cambridge University Press, 2006, chapter 5, “Sampling-Based Motion Planning” (collision checking of segments in section 5.3.4). Free online: lavalle.pl/planning/
S. M. LaValle, “Rapidly-exploring random trees: a new tool for path planning”, TR 98-11, Iowa State University, 1998 (RRT).
S. Karaman and E. Frazzoli, “Sampling-based algorithms for optimal motion planning”, International Journal of Robotics Research 30(7), 846–894, 2011 (RRT*).
J. J. Kuffner and S. M. LaValle, “RRT-Connect: an efficient approach to single-query path planning”, IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation, 2000 (RRT-Connect).
L. E. Kavraki, P. Švestka, J.-C. Latombe and M. H. Overmars, “Probabilistic roadmaps for path planning in high-dimensional configuration spaces”, IEEE Transactions on Robotics and Automation 12(4), 566–580, 1996 (PRM).
